6.1.4 Power Management
1051 Power Management is considered to be system implementation specific, and as a result this Specification
1052 cannot provide a comprehensive statement on the Host Controller’s support for Power Management, for
1053 every system or platform implementation. In particular the System Bus, OS, and platform-specific
1054 implementations may drive different needs, or pose different limitations, for Host Controller power
1055 management flows. For flexibility and effectiveness, Power Management support at the HCI level should
1056 be designed to avoid limiting the Host Controller functionality during normal operation.
1057 For most system implementations, a Host Controller must still be responsive to the system’s power
1058 management approach, especially if the system uses a power management schema that attempts to
1059 minimize power consumption upon detection of idleness for attached Devices (including the Host
1060 Controller). A lack of activity on the interface that connects the Host Controller to the system (i.e., PCI*,
1061 USB) may not be a reliable indicator that the Host Controller can safely reduce its power allocation without
1062 impact to its functionality. For example, the Host Controller may require specific minimal power state to
1063 continue processing queued command transactions, or in order to process In-Band Interrupts from Target
1064 Devices. As such, the Host Controller may need to carefully manage its link state, using an interface-
1065 specific method, or send a remote-wakeup signal to the system during situations when it knows it has
1066 received an unexpected Bus event (i.e., an Interrupt from a Target), in order to ensure required power state.
1067 As link states and power states are typically closely associated, the Host Controller’s interface logic needs
1068 to be aware of the current state of any queued command transactions, as well as the arrival of unexpected
1069 Bus events, and drive changes appropriately.
1070 In some cases, the Host Controller may be forced into a lower-power state by the system, from which it
1071 cannot reliably pull itself back into a higher-power state in order to remain responsive to Bus events. In
1072 these cases, the Host Controller shall automatically NACK any Hot-Join Requests, In-Band Interrupt
1073 Requests, or Controller Role Requests from any other Devices, even if they would otherwise be permitted
1074 and acknowledged.
1075 The Driver expectation is that any Host Controller initiated power management capability is autonomous
1076 (i.e., doesn’t need Driver intervention). The Driver may choose to manually manage power by disabling /
1077 resetting the Controller, in which case Host Controller re-initialization would be taken care of by the
1078 Driver. The Driver shall also work within the OS power management framework to keep the Host
1079 Controller sufficiently powered when possible, so that it can continue processing queued command
1080 transactions, or respond to unexpected Bus events appropriately.

6.1.4.1 Power Management in Standby Controller Mode
1081 A Host Controller that supports Secondary Controller functionality (see Section 6.17) requires additional
1082 support for power management, in order to remain responsive to I3C Bus activity that might signal a
1083 potential transfer of the Controller Role. The process for passing the Controller Role, with steps necessary
1084 to fully prepare for Controller Role Handoff, is defined in the I3C Specification [MIPI02] at
1085 Section 5.1.7.1. A successful Controller Role Handoff would require the Secondary Controller Logic to
1086 remain active and respond to CCCs sent by the Active Controller, so that the Active Controller can
1087 determine whether the Secondary Controller Logic needs to be re-synchronized (i.e., after returning from a
1088 Deep Sleep state).
1089 A Host Controller that supports Standby Controller mode shall attempt to monitor the Bus for events that
1090 might indicate that the Active Controller is trying to pass the Controller Role to it. If field
1091 AC_FSM_OP_SELECT in register STBY_CR_CONTROL is set, or if the Host Controller has sent a Controller
1092 Role Request, then the Secondary Controller Logic shall remain active and shall respond to CCCs sent by
1093 the Active Controller, which may indicate that the Active Controller has started the steps to prepare for
1094 handoff. The Secondary Controller Logic shall also monitor the Bus for any Broadcast DEFTGTS or
1095 DEFGRPA CCCs that the Active Controller might send; if these are received, then they would be captured
1096 and stored in the IBI Data Queue (for PIO Mode) or an IBI Ring Pair (for DMA Mode) per
1097 Section 6.17.3.2.
1098 If field AC_FSM_OP_SELECT in register STBY_CR_CONTROL is not set, then the Secondary Controller Logic
1099 shall respond to the GETSTATUS Format 1 CCC (i.e., no Defining Byte) with Bits[7:6] set to 2'b11 to
1100 indicate that the Host Controller and its Secondary Controller Logic may not participate in the steps to
1101 prepare for handoff, and will not accept the Controller Role at this time since it has not been allowed to do
1102 so by its connected Host (see the I3C Specification [MIPI02] at Section 5.1.9.3.15).
1103 If such a Host Controller supports Power Management capabilities, then it shall also support the
1104 GETSTATUS Format 2 CCC with the PRECR Defining Byte (see the I3C Specification [MIPI02] at Section
1105 5.1.7.3) which serves as the definitive indicator that the Active Controller is reading its status, to determine
1106 whether it has returned from a Deep Sleep state and needs to be re-synchronized. From the time the
1107 Secondary Controller Logic receives and ACKs this CCC, it should remain active and responsive, and not
1108 re-enter a Deep Sleep state that would interrupt the re-synchronization and successful preparation for
1109 handoff. To prevent any interruption of the re-synchronization, the Host Controller shall decline any
1110 attempts by the system to put it into a lower-power state based on assumption of inactivity, when possible.
1111 The Driver must also work within the OS power management framework to keep the system sufficiently
1112 awake and powered, and avoid going into a sleep state if possible, since the Driver is also a key actor in the
1113 process of re-synchronization (as shown by Figure 33).
1114 The transition to Active Controller mode can be interrupted if the system sends a power management event
1115 or link state transition that cannot be declined and that would put the Host Controller or its connected Host
1116 into a lower-power state from which it would be unable to complete re-synchronization or commit to
1117 actively managing the I3C Bus as the Active Controller. In such cases, any pre-Handoff re-synchronization
1118 flows would be interrupted, and the Secondary Controller Logic: shall decline the GETACCCR CCC from
1119 the Active Controller; shall NACK any subsequent CCCs relating to Handoff preparation; and shall make
1120 itself unavailable to receive the Controller Role while in this lower-power state. The Secondary Controller
1121 Logic shall also respond to the GETSTATUS Format 1 CCC (i.e., no Defining Byte) with Bits[7:6] set to
1122 2'b11 (see the I3C Specification [MIPI02] at Section 5.1.9.3.15) to indicate that the Host Controller and its
1123 Secondary Controller Logic may not participate in the steps to prepare for handoff, and will not accept the
1124 Controller Role at this time due to its lower-power state as well as the power state of its connected system.

6.2 Host System Memory Access
1125 If the Host Controller implements support for DMA to access the Host’s system memory, then it shall
1126 expose pairs of 32-bit registers for the Driver to provide the base address to regions of Driver-allocated
1127 memory for specific purposes, and the Host Controller’s Memory Access Engine (i.e., DMA engine) shall
1128 use these registers to access the regions of memory. Such registers are arranged into LO / HI pairs, and each
1129 register pair shall be concatenated to hold a full 64-bit address pointer for the Host system. The Host
1130 Controller shall support up to 64-bit addressing for the Host system’s memory address space.
1131 • Register pair DEV_CTX_BASE_LO / DEV_CTX_BASE_HI (see Section 7.4.19 and Section 7.4.20) together
1132 hold the base address pointer for the Device Context, which are used for the DAT and/or the DCT.
1133 • If DMA Mode is supported, then each Ring Header provides four register pairs for the Rings within the
1134 associated Ring Bundle:
1135 • Register pair RH_CMD_RING_BASE_LO / RH_CMD_RING_BASE_HI (see Section 7.6.10.12 /
1136 Section 7.6.10.13) together hold the base address pointer for the Command Ring.
1137 • Register pair RH_RESP_RING_BASE_LO / RH_RESP_RING_BASE_HI (see Section 7.6.10.14 /
1138 Section 7.6.10.15) together hold the base address pointer for the Response Ring.
1139 • Register pair RH_IBI_STATUS_RING_BASE_LO / RH_IBI_STATUS_RING_BASE_HI (see Section 7.6.10.16
1140 / Section 7.6.10.17) together hold the base address pointer for the IBI Status Ring.
1141 • Register pair RH_IBI_DATA_RING_BASE_LO / RH_IBI_DATA_RING_BASE_HI (see Section 7.6.10.18 /
1142 Section 7.6.10.19) together hold the base address pointer for the IBI Data Ring.
1143 • If Scheduled Commands with Handler Type 3 is supported (per Section 6.16.4), then each such instance
1144 of the Scheduled Commands logic provides one register pair for the Schedule Buffer:
1145 • Register pair SCHEDULE_BUF_BASE_LO / SCHEDULE_BUF_BASE_HI (Section 7.7.10.7 /
1146 Section 7.7.10.8) together hold the base address pointer for the Schedule Buffer.

6.2.1 Scatter-Gather for Host System Memory
1147 Note:
1148 This section applies only for Host Controller implementations that support access to the Host’s
1149 system memory via DMA, and also support additional Scatter-Gather capabilities, for specific
1150 regions of allocated memory. Note that some of these Scatter-Gather capabilities are specific to
1151 DMA Mode.
1152 In order to support systems with fragmented physical memory, the Host Controller may support additional
1153 Scatter-Gather capabilities. The Host Controller shall expose the level of support for Scatter-Gather when
1154 accessing Host system memory for specific purposes, including Rings (for DMA Mode) and Device
1155 Context. The Host Controller advertises its capabilities with three capability fields in register
1156 HC_CAPABILITIES (see Section 7.4.4):
1157 • Field SG_CAPABILITY_DC_EN: Allows Device Context memory to be physically fragmented
1158 • If DMA Mode is supported, then each Ring Header may optionally provide up to four registers for the
1159 Rings within the associated Ring Bundle:
1160 • Field SG_CAPABILITY_IBI_EN: Allows memory for IBI Status and IBI Data Rings to be physically
1161 fragmented
1162 • Field SG_CAPABILITY_CR_EN: Allows memory for Command and Response Rings to be physically
1163 fragmented
1164 Note:
1165 The Scatter-Gather capability fields for Rings apply to all Ring Bundles in the Host Controller.
1166 As such, the Scatter-Gather registers for Ring Headers shall either be supported for all Ring
1167 Headers, or not supported for any Ring Headers. However, each Scatter-Gather register may
1168 be configured individually for the Ring in conjunction with its LO / HI register pair for such a
1169 Ring’s memory region (per Table 3), if a Ring Header provides the Scatter-Gather register
1170 and if its Ring Bundle supports the Scatter-Gather capability.
1171 Upon enabling Scatter-Gather for any Ring (or any other context) that supports it, the pointer to physical
1172 memory shall point to a physically contiguous list of Memory Descriptor structures, with each entry
1173 describing one chunk of physically contiguous memory. The use of a Scatter-Gather List is indicated in the
1174 related setup register, in the BLP bit. The length of the table, in entries, is provided in the LIST_SIZE field.

Note:
1181  Scatter-Gather  for  the  Command/Response  Rings  and  IBI  Status/Data  Rings  are  optional
1182  capabilities. If a Host Controller supports DMA Mode, then it implicitly supports standard Scatter-
1183  Gather capabilities for typical Transfer Commands, as indicated by fields in the Data Buffer
1184  Descriptor (see Section 8.3.1) that allow it to indicate a Buffer List Pointer with non-contiguous
1185  memory. These standard Scatter-Gather capabilities were previously defined in earlier versions of
1186  this I3C HCI Specification, as a required capability of DMA Mode. The additional capability fields in
1187  register HC_CAPABILITIES offer additional Scatter/Gather capabilities that go beyond the standard
1188  capabilities.
1189  Similarly, if a Host Controller supports one or more instances of Scheduled Commands logic with
1190  Handler Type 3, then it implicitly supports standard Scatter-Gather capabilities for each Schedule
1191  Buffer that is used to hold Transfer Commands for this purpose.
1192  For both cases listed above, implementers should ensure that the Memory Access Engine (i.e.,
1193  DMA engine) can support Scatter-Gather for additional memory regions (such as Device Context,
1194  Scheduled Commands, or Rings) when considering whether to also support the optional Scatter-
1195  Gather capabilities.

6.3 Device Management
1196 The Host Controller provides capabilities for managing the I3C and I2C Devices on the I3C Bus, as well as
1197 configuring automatic response to various Bus conditions such as Interrupt Requests.
1198 Note:
1199 For additional context, refer to the I3C TCRI Specification at Section 6.1 [MIPI06].
6.3.1 Device Attach, Enumeration, and Initialization
1200 After the Host Controller is initialized, the initial I3C Bus enumeration should be performed. The Host
1201 Controller shall support the Dynamic Address Assignment process, during which the Host Controller
1202 assigns Addresses to multiple Devices on the Bus, based on an ENTDAA command issued by the Driver
1203 through a Command Descriptor structure. For every Device on the Bus that participates in Dynamic
1204 Address Assignment, a single DAT entry must be assigned. Within each DAT entry, field STATIC_ADDRESS
1205 is programmed by the Driver, based on a priori knowledge of the connected Devices on the Bus (i.e., only
1206 those that have an assigned Static Address). Additionally, for every Dynamic Addressing capable Device,
1207 field DYNAMIC_ADDRESS shall be set for each valid DAT entry, as part of the Dynamic Address Assignment
1208 process.
1209 Once the DAT table is set up, the software may choose to assign the Address using either the SETDASA
1210 CCC (Direct), the SETAASA CCC (Broadcast), and/or the ENTDAA procedure.
1211 • SETDASA and SETAASA: These CCCs rely on prior knowledge of Devices that have Static Addresses
1212 assigned.
1213 • ENTDAA: When the Host Controller executes the ENTDAA command, the first Device that wins
1214 Arbitration is assigned the Dynamic Address contained in the first index, as indicated in the Address
1215 Assignment Command (field DEV_INDEX). The order of Address assignment is determined by the
1216 contents of the DAT table, the provided index in the Address Assignment Command, and Arbitration
1217 priority on the Bus. Note that the Driver may choose to address just a subset of the Devices present on
1218 the Bus.
1219 The DCT table is updated by Host Controller only when the ENTDAA CCC method is used. For the
1220 SETDASA and SETAASA method, the software may read the BCR, the DCR, and the PID with separate
1221 transfers to the Device.

Figure 7 Example Flow for Initial Bus Enumeration
1224 For the initial Bus enumeration, the Driver shall perform the following steps:
1225 1. Check the Device Address Table (DAT) and Device Context Table (DCT) sizes.
1226 A. Check the size of the DAT table, by reading the TABLE_SIZE and ENTRY_SIZE fields of register
1227 DAT_SECTION_OFFSET (Section 7.4.11). The TABLE_SIZE field value bounds the overall number
1228 of addressable Devices.
1229 B. Check the size of the DCT table, by reading the TABLE_SIZE and ENTRY_SIZE fields of register
1230 DCT_SECTION_OFFSET (Section 7.4.12). The TABLE_SIZE field value bounds the number of entries
1231 addressable with a single DAA command (see I3C’s ENTDAA CCC).
1232 2. Set up the Device Address Table (DAT) entries (see Section 8.1) with the preferred Dynamic Addresses
1233 (for I3C Devices having Static Address), and enqueue appropriate Command Descriptors to assign
1234 Dynamic Addresses based on Static Addresses (see Section 6.4.2).
1235 3. Set up the Device Address Table (DAT) entries (see Section 8.1) with the preferred Dynamic Addresses
1236 (for I3C Devices not having Static Address), and enqueue appropriate Command Descriptors to assign
1237 Dynamic Addresses using the ENTDAA procedure (see Section 6.4.1).
1238 4. If any I3C Devices need to change any assigned Dynamic Addresses:
1239 A. Enqueue one or more Command Descriptors of Immediate Data Transfer Command type for the
1240 SETNEWDA Direct CCC, as a standard CCC (i.e., not an Address Assignment Command).
1241 B. Wait for a response, using polling or interrupts (as appropriate for the operating mode). Ensure
1242 that field ERR_STATUS of the Response Descriptor indicates a successful result.

1243  After the Dynamic Addressing procedure completes, it’s possible that some dedicated Devices might not
1244  have been assigned the intended Dynamic Addresses (i.e., the Dynamic Address intended for a Device with
1245  a specific PID was instead assigned to another Device). For example, this can occur when some Devices
1246  are either missing on the Bus, or else not yet ready to be addressed. In some cases, the software may change
1247  the  Dynamic Address  for  another  Device  that  was  assigned  successfully,  by  enqueueing  a  Transfer
1248  Command with the SETNEWDA CCC. In other cases the software must either reset all Dynamic Addresses
1249  using the RSTDAA Broadcast CCC; repeat the Dynamic Addressing procedure by enqueueing new Address
1250  Assignment Commands; or else use the Target Reset Pattern to reset some or all I3C Target Devices on the
1251  I3C Bus.

1258 The Host Controller shall receive and handle Hot-Join Requests from I3C Target Devices. Hot-Join
1259 Requests shall be automatically handled (i.e., either ACKed or NACKed) according to the current value of
1260 field HOT_JOIN_CTRL in register HC_CONTROL (see Section 7.4.2). Upon receiving a Hot-Join Request
1261 from an I3C Target, the Host Controller shall conditionally notify the Host, by generating an IBI Status
1262 Descriptor (see Section 8.6). Such an IBI Status Descriptor shall indicate the Hot-Join ID in field IBI_ID,
1263 with a value of 7'h02 (i.e., the reserved Hot-Join Address) in Bits[15:9], and 1'b0 (i.e., RnW = 0) in Bit[8].
1264 If the Hot-Join Request was rejected (i.e., NACKed), then the Host Controller shall conditionally notify the
1265 Host, according to the current value of field NOTIFY_HJ_REJECTED in register IBI_NOTIFY_CTRL (see
1266 Section 7.4.17).
1267 Note:
1268 The I3C Bus Controller Logic does not distinguish whether an I3C Target might have used either
1269 the standard method or a passive method to send a Hot-Join Request (see version 1.1.1+ of the
1270 I3C Specification [MIPI05], Section 5.1.5). In effect, any valid IBI from the reserved Hot-Join
1271 Address of 7'h02 / W shall be handled as a Hot-Join Request, regardless of the method that the
1272 I3C Target might use.
1273 In response to an incoming Hot-Join IBI, the software shall populate a single new entry in the DAT table,
1274 and shall issue an Address Assignment Command pointing to this entry in the DAT table, using fields
1275 DEV_COUNT and DEV_INDEX. Since Hot-Join requires Dynamic Address Assignment with the ENTDAA
1276 procedure, software shall assign an initial Dynamic Address in field DYNAMIC_ADDRESS.
1277 To schedule the transfer, the software indicates the target Device Address by using its index in the DAT
1278 table. The Host Controller shall use the appropriate Address from the DAT table for the Bus transaction,
1279 depending upon the Device type:
1280 • For Transactions to I3C Devices: The Dynamic Address shall be used, if defined.
1281 Exceptions:
1282 • Address Assignment Command with SETDASA CCC: This is always sent to the Static Address.
1283 • Address Assignment Command with ENTDAA CCC: The ENTDAA procedure is used, and the initial
1284 Dynamic Address (i.e., in field DYNAMIC_ADDRESS) is assigned to the Device during this procedure.
1285 • Transfer Commands that are Broadcast CCCs: No DAT entry is used, per Section 6.7. This includes
1286 the SETAASA CCC.
1287 • For Transactions to I2C Devices: The Static Address shall always be used.
1288 The Driver shall not change the DAT table entry’s Dynamic Address while the Device is in the Addressed
1289 state, with exception of a successful completion of an Address change request (i.e., using the SETNEWDA
1290 CCC).
1291 As field MODE is not present for the Address Assignment command, the HCI controller shall automatically
1292 select the appropriate transmission rate, based on the CCC provided:
1293 • For the SETDASA or SETAASA CCC: Push-Pull Mode
1294 • For the ENTDAA CCC: Open-Drain Mode
1295 Any I2C Devices that might be present on the Bus do not take part in dynamic enumeration. To set up a
1296 DAT entry for I2C Devices:
1297 • Set the DEVICE field to indicate the Device’s type (i.e., I2C).
1298 • Set the STATIC_ADDRESS field to indicate the Static Address, which is configured by the Bus designer.

6.3.2 Device Detach, Reset, and Power Management
1299 Per the I3C Specification [MIPI02], the Controller-capable Device is not aware of a Device detaching from
1300 the Bus (including powering down the Device).
1301 Upon a Device detach event (i.e., an unexpected removal of a Device from the Bus) the DAT shall not be
1302 altered. The assigned Address is reserved (see the I3C Specification at Section 5.1.4). The Driver can re-use
1303 the specific entry (e.g. if it needs to recycle it) by executing an Address Assignment command using the
1304 specific index of the DAT table. In this operation, Device discovery (re-enumeration) may be required. If
1305 the Device is gracefully removed, then the software shall clear the DAT table entry.
1306 Once an I3C Device joins the Bus or exits from reset, it shall wait for Dynamic Address assignment. The
1307 Driver shall assign a Dynamic Address to the Device, and once a Dynamic Address has been assigned to it,
1308 the Device shall respond to all transfers addressed to it. The Device may be driven to a power-gated state,
1309 or it may enter a detached state. If the Device retains its Address while in the detached state (as in an
1310 Offline Capable Device), then it can re-attach using its existing Address. Optionally, if the Device loses its
1311 Address then it can go through the regular enumeration flow.

1313 Because Offline Capable Devices might not instantly respond to directed commands, it is essential for the
1314 software to allow Devices to take time to respond, with retries and/or longer timeout. Functionally, from the
1315 HCI perspective, such Devices are in the Addressed state.

6.3.3 Device Context
1316 The context for Devices present on the Bus is realized through the standard Device Context tables,
1317 including the DAT (see Section 8.1) and the DCT (see Section 8.2).
1318 The standard DAT contains information on Devices on the Bus that could be the target of a command or
1319 transfer. Due to the nature of the I3C Bus, specific Devices may be described in dedicated DAT entries,
1320 even though they might currently be either detached from the Bus, or not responding according to the I3C
1321 protocol. DAT entries also contain fields that control the Host Controller’s automatic response to certain
1322 types of Interrupt Requests.
1323 The DCT is a transient table of entries, having fields intended to be populated by the Host Controller during
1324 the Dynamic Address Assignment procedure with the ENTDAA CCC. Note that the DCT size could be
1325 significantly smaller than the DAT size. Since DCT entries can be reused for new Devices that would need
1326 to have a Dynamic Address assigned, the Driver shall copy the contents of a DCT entry to the internal
1327 Driver context, on a per-Device basis.
1328 A DAT table entry is associated with a given DCT table entry if the DAT entry’s DYNAMIC_ADDRESS field
1329 has the same value as the DCT entry’s DYNAMIC_ADDRESS field.
1330 The Host Controller supports automatic disabling of Controller Role Request (CRR) or In-Band Interrupt
1331 (IBI) from specific Devices, using the CRR_REJECT or IBI_REJECT fields of the DAT table, and also using
1332 the Target’s credit counter (i.e., if the Target IBI credit counting mechanism is supported and enabled, per
1333 Section 6.9.5).
1334 • If CRRs are disabled using the CRR_REJECT field of the DAT table, then the software is responsible for
1335 re-enabling CRRs using the ENEC CCC.
1336 • If IBIs are disabled using the IBI_REJECT field of the DAT table, then the software is responsible for re-
1337 enabling IBIs using the ENEC CCC.
1338 • If IBIs are disabled using the Target IBI credit counting mechanism (i.e., if supported and enabled) in
1339 response to a NACKed IBI Request when the Target’s credit counter is zero, then the Host Controller
1340 shall automatically re-enable IBIs for that Target using the ENEC CCC, once the Host Controller
1341 increments the Target’s credit counter, i.e., after the Driver writes to that Target’s register
1342 TARGET_CREDIT_N (see Section 7.7.5.3).
1343 Figure 10 shows the flow for the Host Controller automatically disabling Controller Role Requests and In-
1344 Band Interrupts based on DAT entries.
1345 Optionally, the software may configure an interrupt source for getting information on whether Controller
1346 Role Requests and/or In-Band Interrupts might have been disabled (i.e., fields NOTIFY_CRR_REJECTED and
1347 NOTIFY_IBI_REJECTED in register IBI_NOTIFY_CTRL, see Section 7.4.17). In this case, the IBI Status
1348 Queue/Ring shall be populated with notifications of NACKed CRRs and/or IBIs.

6.4 Device Addressing
1350 The Host Controller supports the I3C-defined methods of assigning a Dynamic Address to I3C Target
1351 Devices:
1352 • The Address Assignment Command type of the Command Descriptor (see Section 8.4.1) shall be used to
1353 perform Dynamic Address Assignment using either the ENTDAA CCC or the SETDASA CCC.
1354 • The Immediate Data Transfer Command (see the I3C TCRI Specification [MIPI06] at Section 7.1.2.1)
1355 shall be used to perform Dynamic Address Assignment using the SETAASA CCC, which is a Broadcast
1356 CCC that applies to all such Target Devices on the Bus.
1357 The Host shall initiate and direct the steps for Dynamic Address Assignment, using software to enqueue the
1358 appropriate Command Descriptors. Once an I3C Target Device has been assigned a Dynamic Address,
1359 software may also use the SETNEWDA CCC to change the assigned Dynamic Address, by enqueuing an
1360 Immediate Data Transfer Command type of the Command Descriptor.
1361 Note:
1362 If the Transfer Command that sends the SETNEWDA CCC is successful, then software must then
1363 update the appropriate DAT entry for that I3C Target Device to use the new Dynamic Address,
1364 before enqueueing any new Transfer Commands intended for that I3C Target Device.
1365 In DMA Mode, if the DAT entry has not yet been updated, and if the Host Controller receives any
1366 incoming IBIs from such an I3C Target Device that has recently changed its Dynamic Address, then
1367 such IBI Requests would be sent to Ring Bundle 0 (per Section 6.6.1 and Section 6.9.2), as there
1368 would not yet be any dedicated DAT entry with the new Dynamic Address.
1369 The Host Controller may also use the RSTDAA CCC to reset the Dynamic Address of all I3C Target
1370 Devices. After using this Broadcast CCC, all assigned Dynamic Addresses would be reset, and any DAT
1371 entries for such I3C Target Devices should be reused or updated, as they are likely to become invalid.
1372 The Host Controller also supports I2C Target Devices, which have Static Addresses that are assigned by the
1373 Bus Designer (i.e., with a priori knowledge) and which cannot be changed with I3C standard CCCs. If such
1374 I2C Target Devices are known to be on the I3C Bus, then the Host:
1375 • Shall not attempt to use any of the I3C standard CCCs for Dynamic Address Assignment to assign these
1376 same Static Addresses to any I3C Target Devices, and
1377 • Shall not attempt to use the SETNEWDA CCC to change the assigned Dynamic Address of any I3C
1378 Target Device to conflict with any of these same Static Addresses.

6.4.1 Dynamic Address Assignment with ENTDAA
1379 For I3C Target Devices that support the ENTDAA procedure and that have not been assigned Static
1380 Addresses by the Bus Designer, software shall issue Command Descriptors to assign Dynamic Addresses,
1381 according to the defined Bus Initialization Sequence with Dynamic Address Assignment (see
1382 Section 5.1.4.2 of the I3C Specification [MIPI02]).
1383 Each I3C Target Device that will be used with the ENTDAA Procedure shall have its own DAT entry,
1384 populated by software.
1385 For each such DAT entry, software shall:
1386 • Set the DEVICE field to indicate the Device’s type (i.e., I3C).
1387 • For DMA Mode: Set the RING_ID field to indicate which Ring Bundle (in DMA Mode only) will be used
1388 to receive IBIs from this Device.
1389 • Set the DYNAMIC_ADDRESS field to indicate the Device’s preferred Dynamic Address.
1390 1. Enqueue one or more Command Descriptors of Address Assignment Command type for the ENTDAA
1391 CCC, using the steps listed in Section 8.4.1.1.
1392 2. Wait for a response, using polling or interrupts (as appropriate for the operating mode). Ensure that the
1393 Response Descriptor indicates a successful result (i.e., field ERR_STATUS).
1394 3. For each successful response: read the PID, BCR and DCR values from the appropriate fields of the
1395 indicated entries in the DCT (see Section 8.2) for the assigned Dynamic Address(es) as part of the
1396 ENTDAA process.
1397 A. Note that these values are transient, so software must read them and save them internally before
1398 performing subsequent Address Assignment commands with the ENTDAA CCC.
1399 B. Each DCT entry for a successful assignment with the ENTDAA modal flow shall have the same
1400 value in field DYNAMIC_ADDRESS as the corresponding DAT entry that was used for the I3C
1401 Device to which this Dynamic Address was assigned.
1402 If the Address Assignment command is successful, then the Host Controller shall generate a Response
1403 Descriptor with a SUCCESS response in the Response Descriptor’s ERR_STATUS field (see Section 8.4.1.1
1404 and Section 8.5).
1405 In specific cases, the Address Assignment Command might complete with a NACK response in field
1406 ERR_STATUS of the Response Descriptor, for these reasons:
1407 • A NACK on the I3C Broadcast Address (7'h7E) with Read during the ENTDAA modal flow indicates that
1408 no I3C Devices are available for participation in the DAA (ENTDAA) procedure.
1409 • If the ENTDAA procedure did assign some Dynamic Addresses, this will be indicated in the Response
1410 Descriptor, with field DATA_LENGTH having a value greater than zero (i.e., the number of remaining
1411 entries before the NACK) but less than field DEV_COUNT of the Address Assignment Command.
1412 • If the ENTDAA procedure did not assign any Dynamic Addresses, this will be indicated in the
1413 Response Descriptor, with field DATA_LENGTH equal to field DEV_COUNT of the Address Assignment
1414 Command (i.e., no I3C Devices responded).
1415 Note:
1416 If the I3C Bus Controller Logic sees a NACK on the I3C Broadcast Address (7'h7E) before the
1417 ENTDAA Broadcast CCC (which usually indicates an Address Header error due to no I3C Devices
1418 responding to CCC framing in SDR Mode), then it shall indicate this status by setting field
1419 ERR_STATUS to the value 0x4 (i.e., ADDR_HEADER, see Section 6.13.1.1).
1420 After assignment, software may use the SETNEWDA CCC with an Immediate Data Transfer Command to
1421 change the assigned Dynamic Address for any I3C Target Device, per Section 6.3.1.

6.4.2 Using Static Addresses
1422 For I3C Target Devices that have been assigned Static Addresses by the Bus Designer, software shall issue
1423 Command Descriptors to assign Dynamic Addresses according to the defined Bus Initialization Sequence
1424 with Dynamic Address Assignment (see Section 5.1.4.2 of the I3C Specification [MIPI02]).
1425 Each I3C Target Device that has an assigned Static Address shall have its own DAT entry. I3C Target
1426 Devices that are assigned with the Address Assignment Command for SETDASA must be populated in
1427 advance with the known Static Address.
1428 For each such DAT entry, software shall:
1429 • Set the DEVICE field to indicate the Device’s type (i.e., I3C).
1430 • For DMA Mode: Set the RING_ID field to indicate which Ring Bundle (in DMA Mode only) will be used
1431 to receive IBIs from this Device.
1432 • Set the DYNAMIC_ADDRESS field to indicate the Device’s preferred Dynamic Address.
1433 1. For those I3C Devices which will be configured with the SETDASA CCC:
1434 A. Use prior configuration from the Host to set up one DAT entry for each known I3C Target Device
1435 that will be configured with the SETDASA CCC. Each DAT entry shall include the assigned Static
1436 Address in field STATIC_ADDRESS.
1437 B. Enqueue one or more Command Descriptors of Address Assignment Command type for the
1438 SETDASA CCC, using the steps listed in Section 8.4.1.2.
1439 C. Wait for a response, using polling or interrupts (as appropriate for the operating mode). Ensure
1440 that the Response Descriptor indicates a successful result (i.e., field ERR_STATUS).
1441 2. For those I3C Devices which will be configured with the SETAASA CCC:
1442 A. Use prior configuration from the Host to set up one DAT entry for each known I3C Target Device
1443 that will be configured with the SETAASA CCC.
1444 B. Enqueue one Command Descriptor of Immediate Data Transfer Command type for the SETAASA
1445 Broadcast CCC, as a standard CCC (i.e., not an Address Assignment Command).
1446 C. Wait for a response, using polling or interrupts (as appropriate for the operating mode). Ensure
1447 that the Response Descriptor indicates a successful result (i.e., field ERR_STATUS).
1448 If the Address Assignment command for SETDASA is successful, then the Host Controller shall generate a
1449 Response Descriptor with a SUCCESS response in field ERR_STATUS (see Section 8.4.1.2 and Section 8.5).
1450 In specific cases, the Address Assignment Command for SETDASA might complete with a NACK response
1451 in the Response Descriptor’s ERR_STATUS field. An explicit NACK on the SETDASA Direct CCC might
1452 indicate that the I3C Device with the indicated Static Address is not present, or was not ready, or did not
1453 detect the SETDASA CCC on the I3C Bus.
1454 Note:
1455 If the I3C Bus Controller Logic sees a NACK on the I3C Broadcast Address (7'h7E) before the
1456 SETAASA Broadcast CCC or the SETDASA Direct CCC (which usually indicates an Address
1457 Header error due to no I3C Devices responding to CCC framing in SDR Mode), then it shall
1458 indicate this status by setting field ERR_STATUS to the value 0x4 (ADDR_HEADER, see
1459 Section 6.13.1.1).
1460 If the Immediate Data Transfer Command for the SETAASA CCC is successful, then the Host Controller
1461 shall conditionally generate a Response Descriptor with a SUCCESS response in field ERR_STATUS, just as
1462 it would for any other Broadcast CCC that would be sent via a Transfer Command. Note that the SETAASA
1463 CCC has no method for determining the status of any individual I3C Target Device that is asked to assign
1464 its own Static Address as a Dynamic Address.
1465 After assignment, software may choose to use the SETNEWDA CCC with an Immediate Data Transfer
1466 Command to change the assigned Dynamic Address for any I3C Target Device, per Section 6.3.1.

6.4.3 Grouped Addressing
1467 In Active Controller mode, software may issue Command Descriptors that are Transfer Commands (see
1468 Section 6.7) to manage the assignment of I3C Devices to any Group Addresses. Software shall track the
1469 Group Addresses and maintain the assignments in memory. I3C Group Addresses share the same address
1470 space as valid I3C Dynamic Addresses, so software must avoid assigning conflicting addresses (i.e., a
1471 Dynamic Address and a Group Address having the same value).
1472 The following CCCs may be used:
1473 • To assign an I3C Device to a Group Address, software may issue a Direct SETGRPA CCC addressed to a
1474 Dynamic Address (see the I3C Specification [MIPI02] at Section 5.1.9.3.27).
1475 • To remove I3C Devices from a Group Address, software may issue a Direct RSTGRPA CCC addressed
1476 to either a Dynamic Address or the Group Address (see the I3C Specification [MIPI02] at
1477 Section 5.1.9.3.28).
1478 • To disband all Groups, software may issue a Broadcast CCC for the RSTGRPA CCC (see the I3C
1479 Specification [MIPI02] at Section 5.1.9.3.28).
1480 Write-Type Transfers: A Group Address may be used in the same manner as any Target’s Dynamic Address
1481 for a Write-Type Transfer Command. Each Group Address must have a dedicated DAT entry in order to be
1482 used for Transfer Commands. Software shall only enqueue any Write-Type Transfer Commands directed to
1483 that Group Address if a dedicated DAT entry already exists for that Group Address.
1484 Read-Type Transfers: Software shall not enqueue a Command Descriptor that would attempt to perform a
1485 Read-Type transfer directed to a Group Address, because the I3C Specification specifies that Group
1486 Addresses shall only be used for Write-Type transfers (see the I3C Specification [MIPI02] at
1487 Section 5.1.4.4).

6.5 PIO Queue Management
1488 Note:
1489 This section applies only for Host Controller implementations that implement PIO Mode, and thus
1490 accept all Transfer Commands and associated data via register reads and writes. PIO Mode does
1491 not require connection to a System Bus that supports DMA.
1492 In the I3C HCI Register Map, the PIO Section Offset (see Section 7.4.14) register provides the starting
1493 location of the PIO Register Section. The PIO Register section is the structure of registers that allows for
1494 scheduling transfers and reception of IBI without need of memory access.
1495 The PIO Register section includes four mailbox registers that are used to accept all Transfer Commands
1496 and associated data:
1497 • A write-only register as the Command Queue Port (i.e., register COMMAND_QUEUE_PORT,
1498 Section 7.5.1) that accepts Command Descriptor structures (Section 8.4).
1499 • A read-only register as the Response Queue Port (i.e., register RESPONSE_QUEUE_PORT,
1500 Section 7.5.2) that provides Response Descriptor structures (Section 8.5).
1501 • A bi-directional port register as the Transfer Data Port (i.e., register XFER_DATA_PORT, Section 7.5.3)
1502 that accepts write (Tx) data or provides read (Rx) data. The data queues accessed with this Port are called
1503 the Tx Data Queue and Rx Data Queue.
1504 • A read-only register as the IBI Port (i.e., register IBI_PORT, Section 7.5.4) that provides IBI Status
1505 Descriptor (Section 8.6) and IBI payload data.
1506 In addition to these PIO port registers, the PIO Register section contains one or more read-only registers
1507 that provide information on sizes of the PIO queues, i.e., register QUEUE_SIZE (Section 7.5.7) and register
1508 ALT_QUEUE_SIZE (Section 7.5.8), and a set of registers that allow for programming thresholds for efficient
1509 batch-based operation. The PIO thresholds are described in Section 6.5.5.
1510 Note:
1511 In version 1.1 of this I3C HCI Specification, the Command Queue and Response Queue were
1512 required to have the same size. In this version of the I3C HCI Specification, these sizes may be
1513 defined independently; if so, then register ALT_QUEUE_SIZE shall report the size of the Response
1514 Queue, if it is different from the size of the Command Queue. Implementers may choose whether to
1515 define these sizes independently, or whether to keep them linked together (i.e., in the same manner
1516 as version 1.1 of this I3C HCI Specification).
1517 However, in all other aspects, Command Queue and Response Queue operations in PIO Mode are
1518 the same as in previous versions of this I3C HCI Specification.
1519 The Command Queue and Response Queue may support up to 255 Commands and Responses,
1520 respectively. The maximum size of the Transfer Data Queue is 256 DWORDs in each direction.
1521 The set of PIO-specific interrupt registers shall be used for enabling and reporting interrupts. The interrupts
1522 are related to threshold conditions, as well as indications of possible transfer errors. On detecting any
1523 transfer error, the Host Controller transitions to Suspended state (i.e., field RESUME in register
1524 HC_CONTROL has a read value of 1'b1; see Section 7.4.2). The operation of the PIO Queues can be aborted
1525 by software as needed, by writing a value of 1'b1 to the ABORT field in register PIO_CONTROL. The
1526 operation of the PIO Queues can also be paused or disabled by software, by writing to fields RS and/or
1527 ENABLE in register PIO_CONTROL (see Section 7.5.13).
1528 There is only one instance of a PIO Register section (i.e., a single set of PIO queues) per Bus Controller
1529 instance. Registers HC_CONTROL and PIO_CONTROL shall determine the operating status of the PIO queues.
1530 The PIO queues are running if the following conditions are true:
1531 • If both PIO Mode and DMA Mode are supported: Field MODE_SELECTOR in register HC_CONTROL is
1532 set to PIO (see Section 5.3 for details)
1533 • Field BUS_ENABLE in register HC_CONTROL is set to ENABLED (not DISABLED).
1534 This enables all operation involving the I3C Bus Controller Logic.

1535 • Field RESUME in register HC_CONTROL is set to RUNNING (not SUSPENDED).
1536 • If the Host Controller was in the Halt state due to an error, then writing a value of 1'b1 shall resume
1537 operations from the Halt state.
1538 • Field ENABLE in register PIO_CONTROL is set to ENABLED (not SUSPENDED).
1539 This enables access to the PIO Queues via the registers in the PIO Register section. Once
1540 enabled, if the I3C Bus Controller receives In-Band Interrupt Requests from any I3C
1541 Targets, then these will be populated into the IBI Queue (per Section 6.5.4).
1542 • Field RS in register PIO_CONTROL is set to 1ꞌb1 (i.e., running)
1543 If set to run, this enables processing of any Command Descriptors that are enqueued into
1544 the Command Queue, and allows the Host Controller to populate Response Descriptors
1545 into the Response Queue (per Section 6.5.2 and Section 6.5.3).
1546 Note:
1547 In version 1.1 of this I3C HCI Specification, the operation of PIO Queues was always implicitly
1548 enabled if the Host Controller was enabled (i.e., via register HC_CONTROL) and PIO Mode (not
1549 DMA Mode) was selected. This version of the HCI Specification provides more finely-grained
1550 control over PIO Queue operation and Command Descriptor processing, using register
1551 PIO_CONTROL. The structure of register PIO_CONTROL is similar to the equivalent register
1552 RH_CONTROL for a Ring Bundle.
1553 For reference, in version 1.0 of this I3C HCI Specification, the operating mode for a Host Controller
1554 that supported both PIO Mode and DMA Mode was determined by the number of enabled Ring
1555 Headers, such that PIO Mode was only enabled if no Ring Headers were enabled. This version of
1556 the HCI Specification defines a field in register HC_CONTROL to explicitly set the operating mode.
1557 See Section 5.3 for more details.

1564 The Debug Specific (ID = 0x0C) Extended Capability (if implemented) might provide additional

1570 In PIO Mode, the IBI data payload is described with DATA_LENGTH of the IBI Status Descriptor structure

1579 • The Response Descriptor is optional, and shall only be generated when a Transfer Command generates

1581 • For Read-Type transfers (i.e., when field RnW in the Command Descriptor structure has a value of
1582 1'b1):
1583 • The Response Descriptor is required, and shall always be generated.
1584 Software may individually reset specific PIO Queues, using fields in register RESET_CONTROL (see
1585 Section 7.4.5).

6.5.1 PIO Section Initialization
1586 Before software may use the PIO Queues to enqueue Transfer Commands, software needs to know the size
1587 of each queue, and optionally set batch thresholds for optimal performance.
1588 To initialize a PIO Mode, the Driver shall:
1589 1. Get the sizes of the Command FIFO, Response FIFO, and related Data FIFOs from registers
1590 QUEUE_SIZE (Section 7.5.7) and (if present:) ALT_QUEUE_SIZE (Section 7.5.8):
1591 A. Read QUEUE_SIZE register, evaluate CR_QUEUE_SIZE.
1592 B. Read QUEUE_SIZE register, evaluate RX_DATA_BUFFER_SIZE.
1593 C. Read QUEUE_SIZE register, evaluate TX_DATA_BUFFER_SIZE.
1594 D. If register ALT_QUEUE_SIZE is present, read it and evaluate field ALT_RESP_QUEUE_SIZE (i.e., if
1595 field ALT_RESP_QUEUE_EN is 1'b1).
1596 E.
1597 2. If any IBI is enabled, then get the size of IBI FIFO from register QUEUE_SIZE (see Section 7.5.7) and
1598 (if present:) register ALT_QUEUE_SIZE (Section 7.5.8):
1599 A. Read QUEUE_SIZE register, evaluate IBI_ STATUS_SIZE.
1600 B. If register ALT_QUEUE_SIZE is present, then read it and evaluate field EXT_IBI_QUEUE_EN (i.e., if
1601 field EXT_IBI_QUEUE_EN is 1'b1).
1602 3. Optionally, set the thresholds of the Command Queue, Response Queue and related Transfer Data
1603 FIFOs:
1604 A. Write QUEUE_THLD_CTRL register, set CMD_EMPTY_BUF_THLD field.
1605 B. Write QUEUE_THLD_CTRL register, set RESP_BUF_THLD field.
1606 C. Write DATA_BUFFER_THLD_CTRL register, set TX_BUF_THLD field.
1607 D. Write DATA_BUFFER_THLD_CTRL register, set RX_BUF_THLD field.
1608 4. Optionally, set the starting thresholds of the Data FIFOs:
1609 A. Write DATA_BUFFER_THLD_CTRL register, set TX_START_THLD field.
1610 B. Write DATA_BUFFER_THLD_CTRL register, set RX_START_THLD field.
1611 5. If any IBI is enabled: optionally, set the thresholds of the IBI Queue:
1612 A. Write QUEUE_THLD_CTRL register, set IBI_STATUS_THLD field.
1613 B. Write QUEUE_THLD_CTRL register, set IBI_DATA_THLD field.
1614 6. If both PIO Mode and DMA Mode are supported, ensure that the Host Controller is configured to
1615 operate in PIO Mode (see Section 5.3):
1616 A. Write HC_CONTROL register, set MODE_SELECTOR to 1'b1 (PIO) (see Section 7.4.2).
1617 7. Ensure Host Controller is in running state:
1618 A. Read HC_CONTROL register, check if BUS_ENABLE is set to 1'b1 (ENABLED).
1619 B. Read HC_CONTROL register, check if RESUME is set to 1'b0 (RUNNING).
1620 C. Read HC_CONTROL register, check if ABORT is set to 1'b0 (RUNNING).
1621 8. Ensure that the PIO Queues are enabled and running:
1622 A. Read register PIO_CONTROL, check whether field ENABLE is set to 1'b1 (ENABLED).
1623 B. To start the PIO Queues, set bit field RS in register PIO_CONTROL.

6.5.2 Command Queue Operation
1624 While the PIO Queues are enabled and running, the Host Controller Driver shall check for available entries
1625 on the Command Queue and, for a write transfer, available space on Tx Data Queue. The Tx Data Queue
1626 might not be able to fit an entire transfer. The Driver shall populate the Tx Data Queue with data until the
1627 Tx Data Buffer threshold condition is not met (i.e., fewer entries than the threshold), preferably in
1628 threshold-size batches. Once the Tx Queue is populated (or once all data is posted to the Tx Data Queue),
1629 the Driver shall populate the Command Queue with a Command Descriptor. If not all Tx Data for the
1630 transfer was posted to the Tx Data Queue, then the interrupt shall indicate to software to load the next batch
1631 of data (or threshold batch size). On completion of the transfer, the Response Queue shall be populated with
1632 a Response Descriptor per Section 6.5. The interrupt indicating successful transfer, and/or transfer errors,
1633 shall be flagged in the PIO Interrupt Status register. The software shall read the Response Queue and clear
1634 the interrupt.
1635 For read requests, the data may flow before the Response Queue is populated with the Response Status, as
1636 it is populated after the Rx Data. If insufficient space is available on the Rx Data Queue, then the Driver
1637 shall service the interrupt by reading a threshold-size batch of data from the Rx Data Buffer and clearing
1638 the interrupt.
1639 There shall be a 1:1 mapping between the Command Queue’s Command Descriptor structures and the
1640 Response Queue’s Response Descriptor structures, unless the Command Descriptor’s WROC field indicates
1641 that the Host Controller should not generate (i.e., should not provide) a Response Descriptor for successful
1642 Write-type transfers.

6.5.3 Response Queue Operation
1645 While the PIO Queues are enabled and running, upon completion of a Bus transaction and availability of its
1646 response status, the Host Controller shall appropriately populate a Response Descriptor structure on the
1647 Response Queue as required:
1648 • For successful transfers, this shall be determined by field WROC in the corresponding Command
1649 Descriptor as well as the transfer type (i.e., Write-type vs. Read-type) (see Section 6.5).
1650 • For transfers that generate an error, the Host Controller shall always populate a Response Descriptor.
1651 The Host Controller shall conditionally flag an interrupt to the Driver, depending on the interrupt threshold
1652 for the Response Queue (i.e., the value of field RESP_BUF_THLD in register QUEUE_THLD_CTRL). Note that
1653 the interrupt is subject to both masking and signal enabling, per Section 6.14.
1654 Upon processing Response Descriptor entries in the Response Queue, the Driver should observe the change
1655 to Response Ready Status (i.e., the de-assertion of interrupt RESP_READY_STAT in register
1656 PIO_INTR_STATUS) to allow for the Host Controller to flag another interrupt when new Response
1657 Descriptors become available, subject to the threshold configuration. This allows for the Driver to process
1658 more than a batch of Response Descriptors, based on the threshold configuration; in this manner, the Driver
1659 may optionally process a batch in one run, but may choose not to drain the Response Queue fully for
1660 certain use cases.
1661 Any read from Response Queue shall evict (i.e., shall dequeue) the Response Descriptor from Response
1662 Queue. If the Driver attempts to read from an empty Response Queue, this yields undefined behavior.

6.5.4 IBI Queue Operation
1666 For PIO Mode, IBI handling is performed with a single IBI Queue. This IBI Queue is active when the PIO
1667 Queues are enabled (i.e., when field ENABLE in register PIO_CONTROL is set to 1'b1), meaning that the Bus
1668 Controller Logic will accept (i.e., will ACK) incoming IBIs unless the IBI Queue becomes full.
1669 Note:
1670 If the PIO Queues are not enabled (i.e., if field ENABLE in register PIO_CONTROL is set to 1'b0),
1671 then the Bus Controller Logic will not accept (i.e., will NACK) any incoming IBIs.
1672 The IBI Queue supports either up to 255 DWORDs of data, or (if extended IBI Queue sizes are supported,
1673 per register ALT_QUEUE_SIZE; see Section 7.5.8) up to 2040 DWORDs of data. The IBI Queue stores IBI
1674 Status Descriptor structures (see Section 8.6), each of which describes how much IBI Payload data follows
1675 it. The payload data is padded with ‘0’s to fill the DWORD entries as appropriate.
1676 A single IBI event can use multiple IBI Status Descriptor structures, depending on the amount of memory
1677 needed to store the data associated with the IBI event. There may be up to 255 Bytes associated with each
1678 IBI Status Descriptor. An IBI with less than 256 Bytes of data will require one IBI Status Descriptor
1679 structure; an IBI event with 256 Bytes of data will require at least two IBI Status Descriptor structures; and
1680 so on. The IBI Status Descriptor structure includes a LAST_STATUS bit, which must be set to 1'b1 for the
1681 last IBI Status Descriptor for a given IBI event. To continue an IBI event into an additional IBI Status
1682 Descriptor (i.e., for additional storage), set bit field LAST_STATUS to 1'b0.
1683 Note:
1684 Per Section 6.9.4, the Driver may also abort an IBI data payload, if the Host Controller supports
1685 this capability.
1686 The IBI Queue has the capability to issue an interrupt when a specific threshold of data or IBI Statuses are
1687 reached.
1688 Example: Figure 14 shows an IBI payload that exceeds 255 Bytes, so a second IBI Status Descriptor is
1689 used to store the additional received IBI packet data. IBI #1 (blue) contains 257 data Bytes and therefore
1690 requires two IBI Status Descriptor entries, whereas IBI #2 (yellow) only needs one IBI Status Descriptor as
1691 it only contains three data bytes.

6.5.5 PIO Thresholds
1695 PIO Mode includes configurable PIO thresholds, which allows the Host Controller and controlling software
1696 to use the PIO Queue registers to process Transfer Commands either one at a time, or in batches. The
1697 Queue Threshold Control register (i.e., register QUEUE_THLD_CTRL, see Section 7.5.5) and the Transfer
1698 Data Buffer Threshold Control register (i.e., register DATA_BUFFER_THLD_CTRL, see Section 7.5.6) provide
1699 configurable threshold settings, to allow software to set interrupt triggers for the following events and
1700 conditions:
1701 • A batch of new Commands may be written to the Command Queue
1702 • A batch of Responses is pending processing in the Response Queue
1703 • A batch of IBIs and any related payload data are pending in the IBI Queue
1704 • A batch of Read transfer related data is pending processing in the Rx Data Queue
1705 • A batch of Write transfer related may be written to the Tx Data Queue
1706 The definition allows for setting the size of any batch, to balance latency and performance. For some use
1707 cases, the batch size might be decreased with lower threshold values in order to reduce latency for time-
1708 critical applications, where controlling delay of processing is required. For other use cases, the batch size
1709 might be increased with higher threshold values, which allows for Host system configurations where higher
1710 latency might be tolerated.
1711 The Transfer Data Buffer Threshold Control register (i.e., register DATA_BUFFER_THLD_CTRL, see
1712 Section 7.5.6) allows software to configure the appropriate balance of latency and performance for
1713 outgoing Write-Type transfers using the Tx Data Queue, as well as incoming Read-Type transfers using the
1714 Rx Data Queue.
1715 • The Transmit Buffer Threshold (i.e., field TX_BUF_THLD) is set by software. The Host Controller shall
1716 send an interrupt of type TX_THLD_STAT when the number of available entries (i.e., DWORDs) in the Tx
1717 Data Queue reaches or exceeds the configured threshold level.
1718 • This interrupt is useful during Write-Type transfers, when not all data DWORDs might initially be
1719 enqueued into the Tx Data Queue at the start of the transfer. In such cases, software may need to be
1720 notified at the appropriate time to write additional data DWORDs, in order to prevent an underflow
1721 condition, which would cause early transaction termination (see Section 6.8.1).
1722 • Upon sending this interrupt, the Host Controller asserts that software may write the indicated number
1723 of data DWORDs into the Tx Data Queue (i.e., based on the configured threshold level, per
1724 Section 7.5.9). As software writes data DWORDs into the Tx Data Queue, this interrupt shall be
1725 automatically de-asserted once the Tx Data Queue is filled (i.e., once the number of available entries
1726 becomes less than the configured threshold level).
1727 • The Receive Buffer Threshold (i.e., field RX_BUF_THLD) is set by software. The Host Controller shall
1728 send an interrupt of type RX_THLD_STAT when the number of entries (i.e., DWORDs) in the Rx Data
1729 Queue reaches or exceeds the configured threshold level.
1730 • This interrupt is useful during Read-Type transfers, when data DWORDs are written into the Rx Data
1731 Queue during the transfer. In such cases, software may need to be notified at the appropriate time to
1732 read (i.e., to consume) the data DWORDs, in order to prevent an overflow condition, which would
1733 cause early transaction termination (see Section 6.8.1).
1734 • Upon sending this interrupt, the Host Controller asserts that software may read the indicated number of
1735 data DWORDs from the Rx Data Queue (i.e., based on the configured threshold level, per
1736 Section 7.5.9). As software reads data DWORDs from the Rx Data Queue, this interrupt shall be
1737 automatically de-asserted once the Rx Data Queue is drained (i.e., once the number of populated
1738 entries becomes less than the configured threshold level).
Copyright © 2018–2023 MIPI Alliance, Inc. 63
Public Release Edition

Specification for I3C HCI Version 1.2
15-Feb-2023
1739 In addition to the thresholds listed above, it is possible to set the Transfer Start thresholds, in the Transfer
1740 Data Buffer Threshold Control register (i.e., register DATA_BUFFER_THLD_CTRL, see Section 7.5.6). Using
1741 this register, software may set these thresholds to configure a minimum number of bytes that must be
1742 present in the Tx Data Queue to initiate the next enqueued Write-Type transfer; and a minimum number of
1743 free entries that must be available in the Rx Data Queue to initiate the next enqueued Read-Type transfer.
1744 This method allows for postponing the next enqueued Transfer Command until the indicated Data Queue
1745 has reached an appropriate level (i.e., a margin of safety), in order to avoid PIO Queue overrun/underrun
1746 conditions that would otherwise cause a stall or timeout. These starting thresholds can be changed by
1747 software as needed, depending on the current Data Queue levels, changing system latency, and the size of
1748 enqueued Transfer Commands.
1749 • The Transmit Start Threshold (i.e., field TX_START_THLD) is set by software. It applies when not all data
1750 DWORDs have been enqueued into the Tx Data Queue to initiate a Write-Type transfer, when the Host
1751 Controller begins processing this transfer as next enqueued Command Descriptor (i.e., the head of the
1752 Command Queue).
1753 • If the next enqueued Command Descriptor is an Immediate Data Transfer Command, or a Regular
1754 Data Transfer Command that has a zero-byte payload (i.e., does not rely on the Tx Data Queue), then
1755 the Transmit Start Threshold is not considered and the Transfer Command is always allowed to
1756 proceed.
1757 • If the number of data DWORDs that have been written into the Tx Data Queue is sufficient to satisfy
1758 the number of bytes indicated by the next enqueued Command Descriptor, then the Transmit Start
1759 Threshold is met, so the Transfer Command shall be allowed to proceed.
1760 • If the number of data DWORDs that have been written into the Tx Data Queue is not sufficient to
1761 satisfy the number of bytes indicated by the next enqueued Command Descriptor, then the Transmit
1762 Start Threshold is not met, so the Transfer Command shall be postponed until software writes more
1763 data DWORDs into the Tx Data Queue.
1764 • If software subsequently writes additional data DWORDs to meet this threshold condition, then the
1765 Transfer Command shall be allowed to proceed.
1766 • Alternately, if software changes the Transfer Start Threshold to a lower value that causes the
1767 threshold condition to be met earlier, then the Transfer Command shall be allowed to proceed.
1768 • The Receive Start Threshold (i.e., field RX_START_THLD) is set by software. It applies when there are not
1769 enough available DWORD entries in the Rx Data Queue to hold data that would be received after
1770 initiating a Read-Type transfer, when the Host Controller begins processing this transfer as the next
1771 enqueued Command Descriptor (i.e., the head of the Command Queue).
1772 • If the number of available DWORD entries in the Rx Data Queue is sufficient to satisfy the number of
1773 bytes indicated by the next enqueued Command Descriptor, then the Receive Start Threshold shall be
1774 met, so the Transfer Command shall be allowed to proceed.
1775 • If the number of available DWORD entries in the Rx Data Queue is not sufficient to satisfy the number
1776 of bytes indicated by the next enqueued Command Descriptor, then the Receive Start Threshold is not
1777 met, so the Transfer Command shall be postponed until software reads data DWORDs from the Rx
1778 Data Queue.
1779 • If software subsequently reads these data DWORDs (i.e., from prior Read-Type transfers) from the
1780 Rx Data Queue and causes it to drain, then the threshold condition would eventually be met, and the
1781 Transfer Command shall be allowed to proceed at that time.
1782 • Alternately, if software changes the Receive Start Threshold to a lower value that causes the
1783 threshold condition to be met earlier, then the Transfer Command shall be allowed to proceed.
1784 • The Host Controller’s ability to notify software of data DWORDs in the Rx Data Queue from prior
1785 Read-Type transfers shall depend on the current value of the Receive Buffer Threshold (i.e., field
1786 RX_BUF_THLD), so software must provide values for both Receive thresholds that appropriately
1787 balance performance and latency of the system. Software must manage frequent Read-Type transfers
1788 properly, and prevent stall conditions that turn into aborted transactions, if the Rx Data Queue
1789 becomes full during a transfer and is not drained in a timely manner.

1790 Note:
1791 In PIO Mode, if the Host Controller must postpone a Transfer Command due to either of the starting
1792 thresholds not being met, then all enqueued Transfer Commands are blocked from processing until
1793 the threshold condition is met, or until software reduces the starting threshold (if possible).
1794 The Transmit Start Threshold may be set to a minimum value of 2 DWORDs, whereas the smallest
1795 possible Write-Type transfer that relies on the Tx Data Queue might only use 1 DWORD entry (i.e.,
1796 between 1 and 4 data bytes). For such small Write-Type transfers, the threshold would always be
1797 met regardless of the value written to field TX_START_THLD, since the single data DWORD written
1798 into the Tx Data Queue would always satisfy the starting condition. The Host Controller shall
1799 compare the length of the transfer in the Command Descriptor (i.e., field DATA_LENGTH in bytes)
1800 with the number of DWORD entries currently written, and handle such short Write-Type transfers by
1801 allowing them to proceed if the Tx Data Queue contains enough DWORD entries based on the
1802 length of the transfer.

6.5.6 PIO Abort Operation
1803 The Driver may trigger the PIO Abort operation for the PIO Queues by setting the ABORT bit in register
1804 PIO_CONTROL (Section 7.5.12) to 1'b1.
1805 If the PIO Queues are enabled and running, then:
1806 • The Host Controller shall at the earliest opportunity abort (i.e., terminate) any in-progress transfers for
1807 the PIO Queues that the I3C Bus Controller Logic is currently driving.
1808 In terminating transfers, the I3C Bus Controller Logic shall observe all requirements of the I3C
1809 Specification [MIPI02] for the current I3C Mode (i.e., shall not cause any I3C Bus errors).
1810 The transactions that were aborted shall be indicated accordingly in the corresponding Response
1811 Descriptors; field ERR_STATUS shall contain 0x8 (HC_ABORTED). The Host Controller shall also
1812 trigger the TRANSFER_ABORT_STAT interrupt (if enabled for notification) via register
1813 PIO_INTR_STATUS (see Section 7.5.9).
1814 Note:
1815 If the Host Controller is instructed to cancel a transaction sequence (i.e., Command Descriptor with
1816 field TOC=0) in order to process the PIO Abort operation, then it shall also trigger an interrupt via
1817 field HC_SEQ_CANCEL_STAT in register INTR_STATUS (Section 7.4.7) to inform the Host that the
1818 sequence was terminated before processing a Command Descriptor with field TOC=1 (see
1819 Section 6.12).
1820 If the PIO Queues are enabled and running but not currently active for processing, or if the PIO Queues
1821 were enabled but not currently running, then no transactions shall be aborted (because the I3C Bus
1822 Controller Logic was not actively processing any Command Descriptors).
1823 Note:
1824 Any subsequent Command Descriptors that might have been enqueued after any aborted transfers
1825 shall remain unprocessed in the Command Queue once the PIO Queues enter the ABORTED state.
1826 The Driver should determine whether such Command Descriptors should remain enqueued for
1827 future processing, or whether the Command Queue should be flushed (i.e., via register
1828 RESET_CONTROL) before the Driver enqueues new Command Descriptors.
1829 To resume operation for the PIO Queues, the Driver shall perform the following steps:
1830 1. If any transfers were aborted (as specified above), then clear the Transfer Abort Status interrupt
1831 notification for the PIO Queues by writing 1'b1 to field TRANSFER_ABORT_STAT in register
1832 PIO_INTR_STATUS (Section 7.5.9).
1833 2. Clear the PIO Abort Request state by writing 1'b0 to field ABORT in register PIO_CONTROL
1834 (Section 7.5.13).
1835 3. Re-enable processing of PIO Queues by writing 1'b1 to field RS in register PIO_CONTROL. Per
1836 Section 6.8.1, this resumes PIO Queue operation for Command Descriptors and Response Descriptors,
1837 unless the PIO Queues entered the ABORTED state via the Host Controller Abort operation (see
1838 Section 6.8.4) or unless the Host Controller remains in ABORTED state.
1839 Note:
1840 A PIO Abort can also be triggered by a global Host Controller Abort operation (see Section 6.8.4).
1841 If this occurs, then both register HC_CONTROL (i.e., at the global level) and register PIO_CONTROL
1842 shall report the ABORTED state. However, if only a PIO Abort was triggered on its own (i.e., via
1843 register PIO_CONTROL), then this does not necessarily cause, and does not necessarily imply, a
1844 global Host Controller Abort operation.

6.6 Ring Management
1845 Note:
1846 This section applies only for Host Controller implementations that implement DMA Mode, and thus
1847 connect to a System Bus that supports memory-mapped IO and DMA.
1848 In the I3C HCI Register Map, at the Section Offset for Ring Headers Descriptor (see Section 7.4.13), a
1849 metadata area appears containing information on the number of Ring Headers that the Host Controller
1850 supports, and the Header structure size (see Section 7.6.1). Every Header describes a single Ring Bundle,
1851 which includes:
1852 • One Command/Response Ring Pair (i.e., a Command Ring and a Response Ring) that provide a
1853 Command/Response interface to software; and
1854 • One IBI Ring Pair (i.e., an IBI Status Ring and an IBI Data Ring) that provide IBI notification status and
1855 data.
1856 A Host Controller may support up to 8 Ring Bundles. Each Ring Bundle is described by its own Ring
1857 Header (see Section 7.6.10). Each Ring Header supports up to 255 (a static number) valid Ring entries for
1858 Command, Response, and IBI Status Rings.
1859 Every Ring Header includes:
1860 • A Run/Stop bit, which stops processing on all Rings described by that Ring Header (see Section 7.6.10.8
1861 and Section 7.6.10.9).
1862 • An Enable/Disable bit, which enables or disables all Rings described by specific Ring Header. A
1863 Disable/Enable sequence is used to reset a given Ring Header (see Section 7.6.10.8 and
1864 Section 7.6.10.9).
1865 Note:
1866 Support for multiple Rings allows the software to direct separate pipes to different Device groups,
1867 which may be useful for some Device classes. For example, each individual pipe may feature
1868 different behavior in terms of processing latency.
6.6.1 Ring Bundle Initialization
1869 Before a Ring Bundle can be used, the software needs to know how many Ring Headers the specific Host
1870 Controller implementation supports, and to provide allocated memory for all Rings that it wishes to use.
1871 • The minimum memory required for the Command Ring and Response Ring shall be derived from the
1872 number of entries multiplied by the minimum size of the data structure used for each Ring.
1873 For the Command Ring, the Host Controller may use additional DWORDs for storing context, at the
1874 discretion of the implementer.
1875 • The minimum memory required for the IBI Status Ring and IBI Data Ring is arbitrary, and is not related
1876 to the Command Ring or Response Ring. This shall be derived from the size of the IBI Status Descriptor
1877 structure (see Section 8.6) and the desired size of the IBI Data Ring.
1878 To initialize a specific Ring Bundle, the Driver shall:
1879 1. Set the sizes of the Command and Response Rings, and set up the IBI Status and IBI Data Ring
1880 (optional; see note below).
1881 A. In register CR_SETUP, evaluate the sizes of the Transfer Descriptor (XFER_STRUCT_SIZE) and
1882 Response Descriptor (RESP_STRUCT_SIZE) structures (Section 7.6.10.1).
1883 B. In register IBI_SETUP, evaluate the size of the IBI Status Descriptor structure
1884 (IBI_STATUS_STRUCT_SIZE, see Section 7.6.10.2).
1885 C. In register CR_SETUP, set the RING_SIZE field (Section 7.6.10.1).
1886 D. In register IBI_SETUP, set fields IBI_STATUS_RING_SIZE, CHUNK_SIZE, and CHUNK_COUNT
1887 (Section 7.6.10.2) (optional; see note below).
Copyright © 2018–2023 MIPI Alliance, Inc. 67
Public Release Edition

Specification for I3C HCI Version 1.2
15-Feb-2023
1888 2. Allocate memory for the Rings:
1889 A. The Command Ring size is XFER_STRUCT_SIZE * RING_SIZE
1890 B. The Response Ring size is RESP_STRUCT_SIZE * RING_SIZE
1891 C. The IBI Status Ring size is IBI_STATUS_STRUCT_SIZE * IBI_STATUS_RING_SIZE
1892 D. The IBI Data Ring size is (2CHUNK_SIZE+2 * CHUNK_COUNT)
1893 3. Enable the Ring Header:
1894 A. To enable the Ring Header, set the ENABLE bit in register RH_CONTROL (Section 7.6.10.9).
1895 4. Upon Ring Header being enabled, the Host Controller shall zero the Host-Controller-managed fields in
1896 the following registers:
1897 • RH_OPERATION1 (Section 7.6.10.10)
1898 • RH_OPERATION2 (Section 7.6.10.11)
1899 • CHUNK_CONTROL (Section 7.6.10.3)
1900 5. Set up the memory pointer registers for each Ring:
1901 Note:
1902 The memory allocated for each Ring must be physically contiguous, unless Scatter-Gather is
1903 supported and enabled for each Ring Pair (see Section 6.2.1).
1904 A. For the Command Ring, set registers RH_CMD_RING_BASE_LO and RH_CMD_RING_BASE_HI
1905 (Section 7.6.10.12 and Section 7.6.10.13).
1906 B. If field SG_CAPABILITY_CR_EN in register HC_CAPABILITIES is 1'b1 (ENABLED per Section 7.4.4):
1907 Optionally configure the Command Ring for Scatter-Gather:
1908 Set register RH_CMD_RING_SG (Section 7.6.10.20) to accept a non-contiguous
1909 memory allocation (i.e., an array of Memory Descriptors per Section 8.7).
1910 C. For the Response Ring, set registers RH_RESP_RING_BASE_LO and RH_RESP_RING_BASE_HI
1911 (Section 7.6.10.14 and Section 7.6.10.15).
1912 D. If field SG_CAPABILITY_CR_EN in register HC_CAPABILITIES is 1'b1 (ENABLED per Section 7.4.4):
1913 Optionally configure the Response Ring for Scatter-Gather:
1914 Set register RH_RESP_RING_SG (Section 7.6.10.21) to accept a non-contiguous
1915 memory allocation (i.e., an array of Memory Descriptors per Section 8.7).
1916 E. For the IBI Status Ring, set registers RH_IBI_STATUS_RING_BASE_LO and
1917 RH_IBI_STATUS_RING_BASE_HI (Section 7.6.10.16 and Section 7.6.10.17).
1918 F. If field SG_CAPABILITY_IBI_EN in register HC_CAPABILITIES is 1'b1 (ENABLED per Section 7.4.4):
1919 Optionally configure the IBI Status Ring for Scatter-Gather:
1920 Set register RH_IBI_STATUS_RING_SG (Section 7.6.10.22) to accept a
1921 non-contiguous memory allocation (i.e., an array of Memory Descriptors per
1922 Section 8.7).
1923 G. For the IBI Data Ring set registers RH_IBI_DATA_RING_BASE_LO and RH_IBI_DATA_RING_BASE_HI
1924 (Section 7.6.10.18 and Section 7.6.10.19).
1925 H. If field SG_CAPABILITY_IBI_EN in register HC_CAPABILITIES is 1'b1 (ENABLED per Section 7.4.4):
1926 Optionally configure the IBI Data Ring for Scatter-Gather:
1927 Set register RH_IBI_DATA_RING_SG (Section 7.6.10.23) to accept a
1928 non-contiguous memory allocation (i.e., an array of Memory Descriptors per
1929 Section 8.7).
1930 6. Zero the Host Controller Driver-managed fields (R/W) in the following registers:
1931 • RH_OPERATION1 (Section 7.6.10.10)
1932 • RH_OPERATION2 (Section 7.6.10.11)
1933 • CHUNK_CONTROL (Section 7.6.10.3)

1935 A. To enable interrupts, set registers RH_INTR_STATUS_ENABLE and RH_INTR_SIGNAL_ENABLE

1937 B. To start the Ring Header, set the RS bit in register RH_CONTROL (Section 7.6.10.9).

1952 Note:
1953 The Dequeue Pointer serves two purposes, since the Host Controller must simultaneously process
1954 any enqueued Transfer Descriptors (from the Command Ring) and populate Response Descriptors
1955 (into the Response Ring) for each such Transfer Descriptor, while the Ring Bundle is enabled and
1956 running. See Section 6.6.2.1 and Section 6.6.2.2.
1957 Within a Command/Response Ring Pair, the Command and Response Rings always have the same length
1958 (number of structures). The Command Ring contains Transfer Descriptor structures (see Section 8.3), and
1959 the Response Ring contains Response Descriptor structures (see Section 8.5).
1960 Each Command/Response Ring Pair serves as an independent interface to software. If the Ring Bundle is
1961 enabled, then Transfer Commands (i.e., Command Descriptors contained within Transfer Descriptors) that
1962 are enqueued by software into the Command Ring would be processed by the Host Controller, and the
1963 corresponding results for each Transfer Command (i.e., Response Descriptors) would be written into the
1964 Response Ring contained in the same Ring Bundle.
1965 In addition to the ability to gracefully stop execution by software request, transfers enqueued in a
1966 Command Ring Pair may also be aborted upon detection of any malfunction. In this case, any transfer
1967 currently executing on the Bus may be interrupted (i.e., may be completed with an error condition) and the
1968 Host Controller shall then stop the Command/Response Ring Pair, and wait for recovery by the software.
1969 • If the Host Controller detects a transfer error, then it shall stop processing and transition the Ring Bundle
1970 into Stopped status. The Host Controller shall also indicate that a transfer error has occurred, by asserting
1971 the TRANSFER_ERR_STAT interrupt (if enabled for notification) for the associated Ring Header (see
1972 Section 7.6.10.4).
1973 • If software changes the Ring Bundle into Running or Stopped status, then the Host Controller shall also
1974 indicate that the Ring Bundle’s state has changed by asserting the RING_OP_STAT interrupt (if enabled for
1975 notification) for the associated Ring Header (see Section 7.6.10.4).
1976 • Software may also initiate a Ring Abort operation per Section 6.6.6.

6.6.2.1 Command Ring Operation
1977 The Host Controller Driver shall check for available entries on the Command Ring for an already enabled
1978 and started Ring Bundle, and shall schedule transfer(s) by putting Transfer Descriptor(s) (see Section 8.3)
1979 onto the Command Ring, and then shall update the Enqueue Pointer (EnqPtr), which shall serve as a
1980 Doorbell to the Host Controller. Upon detecting a Doorbell ring, the Host Controller shall check the
1981 Enqueue Pointer and shall process Transfer Descriptors in the Command Ring, in order, until reaching the
1982 Enqueue Pointer (and no further) (see Section 7.6.10.10 and Section 7.6.10.11). For each processed
1983 Transfer Descriptor, upon completion of the corresponding transaction on the Bus, the Host Controller shall
1984 populate a Response Descriptor (see Section 8.5) structure in the Response Ring.
1985 There shall be a 1:1 mapping between the Command Ring’s Transfer Descriptor structures and the
1986 Response Ring’s Response Descriptor structures. As a result, the Ring management related registers for a
1987 given Ring Pair are shared between these two Rings.
1988 Transfers shall be split according to the width of the DATA_LENGTH field. E.g., for a 16-bit DATA_LENGTH
1989 field a single Transfer Descriptor can describe a transfer of up to 65535 Bytes (0xFFFFh). If the transfer is
1990 larger than that, then it should be split into multiple transfers, each with a maximum length of 65535 Bytes.

6.6.2.2 Response Ring Operation
1992 Upon completion of a Bus transaction and availability of its response status, the Host Controller shall
1993 populate a Response Descriptor structure (see Section 8.5) on the Response Ring, update Dequeue Pointer
1994 (DeqPtr), and optionally trigger a TRANSFER_COMPLETION_STAT interrupt to the Driver, depending on the
1995 value of the Transfer Descriptor’s IOC bit. Note that the interrupt is subject to both masking and signal
1996 enabling. If enabled, this interrupt shall appear in register RH_INTR_STATUS (see Section 7.6.10.4) in the
1997 Ring Header for the associated Ring Bundle. Upon successful completion of the transaction, the Host
1998 Controller shall populate the Response Descriptor’s ERR_STATUS field with the value 0x0.
1999 The list position of the newly populated Response Descriptor in the Response Ring shall be the same as the
2000 list position of the Transfer Descriptor that caused the transfer (or command) in the Command Ring.
2001 Example: If a Bus transfer is caused by the third Transfer Descriptor in the Command Ring, then the
2002 Response Descriptor that reports the response to that transfer shall appear in the third position in the
2003 Response Ring.
2004 Upon processing Response Descriptor entries in the Response Ring, the Driver shall indicate its current
2005 processing position in the Response Ring (i.e., shall indicate which Response Descriptor entries in the
2006 Response Ring are now available for the Host Controller to populate) by updating the Software Dequeue
2007 Pointer (SwDequeuePointer) (see Section 7.6.10.10 and Section 7.6.10.11). A write to SwDequeuePointer
2008 notifies the Host Controller that the software event handler has exited. If any Response Descriptors remain
2009 unprocessed (outstanding) at that time, then the Host Controller shall repeat the interrupt to the Driver so
2010 that processing of received Responses can continue to completion.

2012 For a given Ring Bundle, IBI handling is shared between the IBI Status Ring and the IBI Data Ring.
