2017 The IBI Status Ring supports up to 255 valid IBI Status Descriptor structures (see Section 8.6), each
2018 describing a number of chunks of memory on the IBI Data Ring in the same Ring Bundle.
2019 Each Data buffer consists of one or more equally-sized Data Chunks. This Data Chunk size is variable, and
2020 is determined by the Driver via field CHUNK_SIZE in register IBI_SETUP (see Section 7.6.10.2). For
2021 example, a 4kB total buffer block could be processed either as 1000 DWORD chunks, or as 500 QWORD
2022 chunks, etc.
6.6.3.1 IBI Status Ring Operation
2023 A single IBI event can use from one to 255 IBI Status Descriptor structures, depending on the amount of
2024 memory in the IBI Data Ring needed to store the IBI payload data associated with the IBI event. There may
2025 be up to 255 Data Chunks associated with each IBI Status Descriptor (see Section 6.6.3.2). Note that all
2026 Data Chunks for an IBI Status Descriptor shall be “full” (i.e., fully populated with IBI payload data), except
2027 for the last Data Chunk: the Host Controller shall write incoming IBI payload data into all such Data
2028 Chunks for an IBI Status Descriptor, without gaps, until the end of the IBI payload.
2029 The Host Controller shall automatically create IBI Status Descriptor structures and enqueue them onto the
2030 IBI Status Ring, based on the overall length of the IBI data payload. An IBI needing one Data Chunk of
2031 storage (or less, for shorter payloads) will require one IBI Status Descriptor structure. However, an IBI
2032 event needing 256 Data Chunks of storage will require at least two consecutive IBI Status Descriptor
2033 structures; and so on. The IBI Status Descriptor structure includes a LAST_STATUS bit, which shall be set to
2034 1'b1 for the last IBI Status Descriptor for a given IBI event. To continue an IBI event into an additional IBI
2035 Status Descriptor (i.e., for additional storage), the Host Controller shall set field LAST_STATUS to 1'b0.
2036 Note:
2037 Considering the two paragraphs above: For an IBI event that has a longer data payload and
2038 requires two or more IBI Status Descriptors, the Host Controller should generally write incoming IBI
2039 payload data to completely fill all Data Chunks associated with the first IBI Status Descriptor.
2040 Additionally, all Data Chunks associated with each subsequent IBI Status Descriptor should be “full”
2041 Data Chunks, up until the last IBI Status Descriptor where field LAST_STATUS is set to 1'b1.
2042 The Driver may also abort an IBI data payload, if the Host Controller supports this capability (per
2043 Section 6.9.4).
2044 To enqueue one or more IBI Status Descriptor structures for an IBI event, the Host Controller shall
2045 populate these IBI Status Descriptor structures into the IBI Status Ring, update the Enqueue Pointer, and
2046 then optionally trigger the IBI_READY_STAT interrupt to the Driver. Note that this interrupt is subject to both
2047 masking and signal enabling. If enabled, this interrupt shall appear in register RH_INTR_STATUS (see

2050  Once the Driver receives this interrupt, it may write to the Dequeue Pointer, which notifies the Host

2053  The Host Controller shall ensure that it does not enqueue any new IBI Status Descriptor structures that

6.6.3.2 IBI Data Ring Operation
2077 A single IBI Status Descriptor may require up to 255 Data Chunks from the IBI Data Ring. Since the Host
2078 Controller does not always know the full (i.e., intended) length of the IBI payload when the I3C Bus
2079 Controller Logic receives and accepts the IBI, and since the memory regions for the IBI Status Ring and
2080 IBI Data Ring are allocated separately by the Driver, the Host Controller shall manage the IBI Ring Pair in
2081 an efficient manner, for IBI payloads of varying length.
2082 The Host Controller shall allocate (i.e., shall mark as used) up to 255 Data Chunks as needed for each IBI
2083 Status Descriptor, starting at the first free Data Chunk. An allocation of Data Chunks shall either be
2084 adjacent (i.e., allocated in a single region) within the IBI Data Ring, or, if the end of the IBI Data Ring is
2085 reached, an allocation shall “wrap” around the end of the IBI Data Ring and continue from the start of the
2086 IBI Data Ring (i.e., from position 0). The Host Controller may allow an allocation to grow until a
2087 maximum of 255 Data Chunks. At the end of an allocation, the Host Controller shall automatically attempt
2088 to create a new IBI Status Descriptor, per Section 6.6.3.1, if the IBI has not been terminated.
2089 If the IBI Data Ring becomes completely full during an IBI event, then the Host Controller shall trigger the
2090 IBI_RING_FULL_STAT interrupt, and shall either terminate reception of the IBI payload (i.e., only accept a
2091 partial entry for this IBI Status Descriptor and mark its field LAST_STATUS as 1'b1, per Section 6.6.3.1), or
2092 instruct the I3C Bus Controller Logic to stall the Bus (if possible) until the Driver can resolve the situation
2093 by freeing existing Data Chunks in the IBI Data Ring. If the Driver cannot resolve the situation in a timely
2094 manner, then the Host Controller shall terminate reception of the IBI payload. If a new IBI event occurs and
2095 the IBI Data Ring does not have any free Data Chunks, the Host Controller shall trigger the interrupt, and
2096 shall also NACK such an IBI event.
2097 Within each Data Chunk, the Host Controller shall write the IBI payload data according to the current byte
2098 ordering mode that was selected, when the IBI was received and processed by the Host Controller’s I3C
2099 Bus Controller Logic, per Section 6.8.3.
2100 Allocations in the IBI Data Ring are circular in nature, i.e., the oldest Data Chunk allocations are always
2101 freed first. The oldest allocation is associated with the oldest IBI Status Descriptor, at the position where
2102 the Dequeue Pointer for the IBI Status Ring is pointing. Field CHUNK_COUNTER in register
2103 CHUNK_CONTROL (see Section 7.6.10.3) shall provide the position for the first Data Chunk for this IBI
2104 Status Descriptor’s Data Chunk allocation. This register is read by the Driver, which shall allow the Host
2105 Controller to know when the Driver has started processing enqueued IBI Status Descriptor structures with
2106 Data Chunks (per Section 6.9.2).
2107 The Driver shall also write to this register to notify the Host Controller that the Driver has consumed the
2108 oldest Data Chunk allocation, and intends to free the allocation that is associated with the oldest IBI Status
2109 Descriptor structure. The Host Controller shall clear this field (i.e., reset to zero) when the Ring Bundle is
2110 transitioned to the Enabled state.
2111 Field CHUNK_COUNTER allows the Host Controller and the Driver to communicate updates on freed Data
2112 Chunks, assuming that the Driver has read from register CHUNK_CONTROL while the IBI Status Ring’s
2113 Dequeue Pointer was pointing to this IBI Status Descriptor structure (i.e., the structure that it intends to
2114 free), or some previous IBI Status Descriptor structure (per the conditions below for freeing adjacent IBI
2115 Status Descriptor structures):
2116 • The Driver shall subsequently advance the Dequeue pointer, and shall write the new value to field
2117 IBI_DEQ_PTR in register RH_OPERATION1 (see Section 7.6.10.10), indicating that the Driver has
2118 consumed the oldest IBI Status Descriptor structure from the IBI Status Ring (per Section 6.6.3.1).
2119 • The Driver shall then add the number of Data Chunks indicated by this IBI Status Descriptor (i.e., the
2120 value of field CHUNKS) to its cached value of register CHUNK_CONTROL, and shall write this value back
2121 to register CHUNK_CONTROL. This operation shall not use circular (i.e., “modulo”) arithmetic, as it would
2122 when advancing typical Ring pointers: the Driver simply needs to add the number of Data Chunks and
2123 write that new value back to the same register.
78 Copyright © 2018–2023 MIPI Alliance, Inc.
Public Release Edition

Version 1.2 Specification for I3C HCI
15-Feb-2023
2124 Note:
2125 The Driver may also free all Data Chunk allocations for several adjacent IBI Status Descriptor
2126 structures, starting with the oldest, by advancing the Dequeue pointer by two or more positions and
2127 writing the new value to field IBI_DEQ_PTR in register RH_OPERATION1, and then updating the
2128 Chunk Counter by adding a value equal to the total number of Data Chunks associated with all
2129 such IBI Status Descriptor structures. See Section 6.9.2.
2130 After writing to register CHUNK_CONTROL to free the Data Chunk allocations for one or more
2131 adjacent IBI Status Descriptor structures, the Driver shall read register CHUNK_CONTROL again
2132 before processing and freeing Data Chunks for the next IBI Status Descriptor structure, in order to
2133 capture the location of the first Data Chunk and inform the Host Controller of the state at the time of
2134 reading.
2135 Field CHUNK_COUNTER acts a monotonic counter. It may accept writes of values at least two times the
2136 largest possible configured value of CHUNK_COUNT in register IBI_SETUP (see Section 7.6.10.2), i.e., values
2137 larger than 2048. This ensures that the Driver can always perform the following operations:
2138 • Read the value of field CHUNK_COUNTER at its largest possible value (i.e., position 0x3FE in the IBI Data
2139 Ring).
2140 • Add the number of Data Chunks allocated for one or more IBI Status Descriptors, with each having up to
2141 the largest possible Data Chunk allocation size (i.e., 0xFF, as indicated by an IBI Status Descriptor), and
2142 adding up to the total number of Data Chunks in the IBI Data Ring, for a total of up to 0x3FE.
2143 • Write that new value (up to 0x7FC maximum) back to field CHUNK_COUNTER, to indicate that up to the
2144 maximum number of Data Chunks should be freed.
2145 A write to register CHUNK_CONTROL notifies the Host Controller that the Driver has consumed and
2146 subsequently freed one or more Data Chunk allocations for one or more IBI Status Descriptors, starting
2147 with the IBI Status Descriptor structure that was pointed to by the Dequeue Pointer when the Driver read
2148 register CHUNK_CONTROL. The Host Controller does not need to inspect the contents of each such IBI
2149 Status Descriptor structure (i.e., when the Driver advances the Dequeue Pointer) to determine how many
2150 Data Chunks were originally allocated. Instead, the Host Controller shall maintain an internal “Chunk
2151 Counter (HW)” pointer for the IBI Data Ring, and shall advance this pointer to free such Data Chunk
2152 allocations, as the Driver writes an updated value to register CHUNK_CONTROL.
2153 Note:
2154 Implementation details of the internal “Chunk Counter (HW)” pointer are vendor-specific, and are
2155 not covered by the scope of this I3C HCI Specification.
2156 Unlike the IBI Status Ring, the IBI Data Ring does not have an “enqueue” pointer that is visible to
2157 the Host (i.e., readable by the Driver). The Host Controller shall maintain its own internal pointer for
2158 the first available Data Chunk on the IBI Data Ring, and shall also ensure that this internal pointer
2159 never goes past the Chunk Counter (either its internal pointer, or the value that might be read from
2160 register CHUNK_CONTROL).

6.6.3.3 IBI Data Ring Configuration Changes
2161 If the Driver wishes to change the IBI Ring data buffer chunk size or data buffer area, then the Driver shall
2162 perform the following steps:
2163 1. Stop the Ring Bundle
2164 2. Store the current position (i.e., value) of the Enqueue Pointer in Old Enqueue Pointer
2165 3. Store the current data buffer chunk size in Old Data Chunk
2166 4. Disable the Ring Bundle
2167 5. Allocate the new data buffer, then update the Chunk Size and Data Head Pointer for the newly
2168 allocated buffer
2169 6. Start/run the IBI Ring
2170 7. Process the old IBI Ring until reaching Old Enqueue Pointer (still using Old Data Chunk for data
2171 chunk sizes)
2172 8. Switch to the new Data Head and new Chunk Size
2173 9. Enable the Ring Bundle
2174 10. Free memory for the old data buffer area
2175 11. Continue with the new buffer
2176 Making the Data Chunk size variable allows for optimal memory use (i.e., set Chunk Size to the typical IBI
2177 payload size), simpler data buffer management, and very large IBI payloads (i.e., with a very large Data
2178 Chunk size and using all 255 IBI Status Descriptor entries, the maximum data buffer size can be very large,
2179 i.e., up to 261,888 bytes, with 256 bytes per Data Chunk and 1023 maximum Data Chunks, per
2180 Section 7.6.10.2).
2181 The Data Chunk size can be regarded as a scaling factor: the same IBI Status Descriptor format can address
2182 either small or large data buffers. For smaller IBI payloads (which are generally expected), DWORD could
2183 be considered an optimal Data Chunk size.
2184 The Driver should only extend the IBI Data Ring or make similar changes to the configuration under
2185 special circumstances, namely: (a) upon receiving a Hot-Join event, and (b) in systems where memory use
2186 optimization is critical.

6.6.4 Ring Header Registers
2187 The Ring Headers section of the Host Controller memory map (at an offset defined in the Capabilities
2188 Registers section, see Section 7.4.13) begins with a Ring Headers Preamble register (RHS_CONTROL, see
2189 Section 7.6.1) which contains fields for the number of Ring Headers supported
2190 (MAX_HEADER_COUNT_CAPABILITY) and the Ring Header Structure Size (HEADER_SIZE). The Preamble
2191 register also contains control field MAX_HEADER_COUNT to enable or disable the supported Ring Headers
2192 for use by software.
2193 Following the Preamble register, the section contains offsets for up to eight Ring Headers in registers
2194 RH0_OFFSET through RH7_OFFSET (Section 7.6.2 through Section 7.6.9).
2195 Interrupt handling, memory pointers, pointer management, and Ring Bundle management registers are
2196 defined for each Ring Bundle in the Ring Header (see Section 7.6.10).
2197 Please refer to Section 7.6 for a detailed description of the Ring Headers Specific Registers.

6.6.5 Ring Bundle Servicing
2199 If the Host Controller supports multiple Ring Bundles that are exposed as separate instances of Ring
2200 Header register sections (see Section 6.6.4), then the Ring Controller shall use arbitration logic to
2201 automatically manage the servicing of all Ring Bundles that are enabled for software (via register
2202 RHS_CONTROL, see Section 7.6.1), configured for use with the Ring Header Base Address registers, and in
2203 an enabled and running state (via register RH_CONTROL, see Section 7.6.10.9). However, this arbitration
2204 logic shall never select any Ring Bundles that are in a DISABLED, STOPPED or ABORTED state.
2205 The Ring Controller’s arbitration logic shall attempt to fairly balance the servicing of such enabled and
2206 running Ring Bundles, to ensure that all enqueued Transfer Descriptors are processed without undue delay.
2207 Additionally, the arbitration logic should avoid breaking up any enqueued command sequences (as defined
2208 in Section 6.12) if the last Transfer Descriptor for such a command sequence (i.e., a Command Descriptor
2209 with TOC=1 that follows a Command Descriptor with TOC=0) was known to be enqueued by the arbitration
2210 logic.
2211 However, for specific use cases, an implementer may define other prioritization algorithms or balancing
2212 controls, with appropriate registers in an implementer-defined Extended Capability structure. In general,
2213 the arbitration logic should balance the priority of the enabled and running Ring Bundles, while also not
2214 interrupting any command sequences in progress, breaking the atomicity of any single sets of Transfer
2215 Descriptors enqueued with a single “doorbell” event (unless otherwise allowed with other directives) or
2216 causing any undue interruption for the various transfers that comprise an I3C content protocol.
6.6.5.1 Ring Bundle Switching
2217 Before switching from one valid (i.e., enabled and running) Ring Bundle to another valid Ring Bundle that
2218 has pending Transfer Descriptors yet to be processed, the Ring Controller’s arbitration logic shall test to see
2219 whether the previously processed Command Descriptor did not drive a STOP condition or the HDR Exit
2220 Pattern (i.e., when TOC=0) and the indicated I3C Mode (i.e., field MODE in the Command Descriptor) is the
2221 same as for the previously processed Command Descriptor. In such cases, where the framing for the
2222 previous I3C Mode has not been ended and the Speed and/or Mode changes on switching Ring Bundles,
2223 the rules in Section 6.2.5 of the I3C TCRI Specification [MIPI06] shall apply.
2224 For cases when a Speed and/or Mode change requires the Host Controller to insert either a STOP condition
2225 or the HDR Exit Pattern in order to process the first enqueued Transfer Descriptor in the new Ring Bundle
2226 (i.e., due to a different value of field MODE in the Command Descriptor), or when any interrupts must be
2227 reported due to any other unexpected conditions that would have been caused by switching to another valid
2228 Ring Bundle, the Host Controller shall report such interrupts via the Ring Interrupt Status register in the
2229 Ring Header for the new Ring Bundle that the Ring Controller’s arbitration logic had just switched to be
2230 processed.

6.6.5.2 Ring Bundle Locking
2231 Software may temporarily lock the Ring Controller to remain on a single valid (i.e., enabled and running)
2232 Ring Bundle using the Ring Bundle Lock sub-command, sent as an Internal Control Command (see
2233 Section 8.4.2.1 and Table 136) via the Command Ring of the Ring Bundle that will be locked.
2234 • If another Ring Bundle is currently locked, then the Ring Controller shall reject the Ring Bundle Lock -
2235 sub-command, and return a Response Descriptor with error code 0x5 (NACK) in field ERR_STATUS.
2236 • If no Ring Bundle is currently locked, then the Host Controller shall lock to the current Ring Bundle and
2237 shall not switch to other enabled and running Ring Bundles:
2238 • The Ring Bundle ID to be locked shall be implicit, based on the Command Ring to which the software
2239 enqueues the Transfer Descriptor containing such an Internal Control Command.
2240 • If the Ring Bundle is not the current Ring Bundle that is being processed when software enqueues the
2241 Transfer Descriptor containing the Internal Control Command, then the Ring Controller shall attempt
2242 to lock to that Ring Bundle once the Ring Controller’s arbitration logic switches to process it (per
2243 Section 6.6.5.1).
2244 • Once locked, the Ring Bundle shall remain locked until software enqueues a corresponding Ring
2245 Bundle Unlock sub-command, sent as an Internal Control Command via the same Command Ring of
2246 the currently locked Ring Bundle.
2247 • On receiving and successfully processing Ring Bundle Lock/Unlock sub-commands, the Ring
2248 Controller shall return a Response Descriptor with value 0x0 (SUCCESS) in field ERR_STATUS.
2249 Note:
2250 Once the Host Controller processes the Ring Bundle Lock sub-command (i.e., when that Command
2251 Ring is active and selected for processing by the Ring Controller’s arbitration logic), the Host
2252 Controller shall not reject the Ring Bundle Lock sub-command, unless there is an internal error or
2253 some other configuration issue that prevents a successful locked state. In the rare event that this
2254 occurs, the Host Controller shall reject the Ring Bundle Lock sub-command and return a Response
2255 Descriptor with error code 0x5 (NACK) in field ERR_STATUS.
2256 By definition, the Host Controller shall not process the Command Rings for any other valid Ring
2257 Bundles, so as a result there can be no contention for the locked state, and also no rejection of a
2258 Ring Bundle Lock sub-command due to another Ring Bundle currently being locked.
2259 While any Ring Bundle is operating in a locked state, if a Ring Bundle encounters an error and is halted,
2260 stopped or otherwise interrupted; or if the Ring operations are aborted by software (i.e., by writing to field
2261 ABORT in register RH_CONTROL, see Section 7.6.10.9), the Ring Controller’s arbitration logic shall not
2262 switch to any other Ring Bundles that might be enabled and in a running state and have pending Transfer
2263 Descriptors (i.e., those that might otherwise be available for Command/Response processing) until and
2264 unless the locked Ring Bundle is unlocked, or operation is resumed.
2265 Each Ring Header for a valid Ring Bundle shall indicate its current Lock/Unlock status in field LOCKED in
2266 register RH_STATUS (see Section 7.6.10.8).

6.6.6 Ring Abort Operation
2267 The Driver may trigger the Ring Abort operation for a Ring Bundle by setting the ABORT bit to 1'b1 in
2268 register RH_CONTROL (see Section 7.6.10.9) for the associated Ring Header.
2269 If the Ring Bundle is valid (i.e., enabled and running) and is currently the active Command/Response Ring
2270 for processing, then:
2271 • The Host Controller shall abort (i.e., shall terminate) any in-progress transfers for this Ring Bundle that
2272 the I3C Bus Controller Logic is currently driving, at the earliest opportunity.
2273 The I3C Bus Controller Logic shall terminate transfers according to the requirements of the I3C
2274 Specification for the current I3C Mode (i.e., without causing any I3C Bus errors).
2275 The transactions that were aborted shall be indicated accordingly in the corresponding Response
2276 Descriptors, with field ERR_STATUS having a value of 0x8 (HC_ABORTED). The Host Controller
2277 shall also trigger the TRANSFER_ABORT_STAT interrupt (if enabled for notification) for the
2278 associated Ring Header, via register RH_INTR_STATUS (see Section 7.6.10.4).
2279 • The Host Controller shall also indicate that the Ring Bundle’s state has changed to ABORTED, by
2280 asserting the RING_OP_STAT interrupt (if enabled for notification) for the associated Ring Header (see
2281 Section 7.6.10.4).
2282 Note:
2283 If the Host Controller is instructed to cancel a transaction sequence (i.e., Transfer Descriptor
2284 contains a Command Descriptor with field TOC=0) in order to process the Ring Abort operation,
2285 then it shall also trigger an interrupt via field HC_SEQ_CANCEL_STAT in register INTR_STATUS (see
2286 Section 7.4.7) to inform the Host that the sequence was terminated before processing a Transfer
2287 Descriptor containing a Command Descriptor having field TOC=1 (see Section 6.12).
2288 If the Ring Bundle is valid (i.e., is enabled and running) but is not currently active for processing; or if the
2289 Ring Bundle was enabled but not currently running, then:
2290 • No transactions shall be aborted, since no Transfer Descriptor was being actively processed by the I3C
2291 Bus Controller Logic.
2292 • The Host Controller shall indicate that the Ring Bundle’s state has changed to ABORTED, by asserting the
2293 RING_OP_STAT interrupt (if enabled for notification) for the associated Ring Header. The Ring Bundle
2294 shall immediately be removed from the list of valid Ring Bundles that may be selected by the Ring
2295 Controller’s arbitration logic for servicing (per Section 6.6.5).
2296 Once a Ring Bundle receives the Ring Abort request and stops processing Transfer Descriptors as a result
2297 (if it was active for processing), it shall trigger its RING_OP_STAT interrupt to indicate its ABORTED state, as
2298 indicated above. The Driver shall perform any needed Ring recovery steps upon receiving this notification.
2299 Note:
2300 Any subsequent Transfer Descriptors that might have been enqueued after any aborted transfers
2301 shall remain unprocessed in the Command Ring once the Ring Bundle enters the ABORTED state.
2302 The Driver should determine whether such Transfer Descriptors should remain enqueued for future
2303 processing, or replaced with other Transfer Descriptors (or, in some situations, replaced with
2304 “NoOp”-type Internal Control Commands; see Section 8.4.2).

2305 To resume operation for the Ring Bundle, the Driver shall perform the following steps:
2306 1. Clear the Ring Operation Status interrupt notification for the Ring Header, by writing 1'b1 to field
2307 RH_OP_STAT in register RH_INTR_STATUS (Section 7.6.10.4).
2308 2. Clear the Transfer Abort Status interrupt notification for the Ring Header, if any transfers were aborted
2309 (as specified above), by writing 1'b1 to field TRANSFER_ABORT_STAT in register RH_INTR_STATUS
2310 (Section 7.6.10.4).
2311 3. Clear the Ring Header’s Ring Abort Request state, by writing 1'b0 to field ABORT in register
2312 RH_CONTROL (Section 7.6.10.9).
2313 4. Write to the Ring Header’s Enqueue Pointer for the Command/Response Ring, i.e., field CR_ENQ_PTR
2314 in register RH_OPERATION1 (Section 7.6.10.10). This automatically resumes the Ring operation, and
2315 any remaining Transfer Descriptors that are enqueued will be processed, per Section 6.8.2., unless the
2316 Ring Bundle entered its ABORTED state via the Host Controller Abort operation (see Section 6.8.4) or
2317 the Host Controller remains in ABORTED state.
2318 Note:
2319 A Ring Abort can also be triggered by a global Host Controller Abort operation (see Section 6.8.4).
2320 If this occurs, then both register HC_CONTROL (at the global level) and register RH_CONTROL (for
2321 this Ring Bundle) shall report the ABORTED state. However, if only a Ring Abort was triggered on its
2322 own (i.e., via register RH_CONTROL) then this does not necessarily cause, nor necessarily imply, a
2323 global Host Controller Abort operation.

6.7 Transfer Command Handling
2324 A Host Controller includes I3C Bus Controller Logic and allows the Host to enqueue transfers via its
2325 Transfer Command/Response Interface (TCRI). While the Host Controller is the Active Controller of the
2326 I3C Bus, these transfers are driven to the I3C Bus by the Controller Logic, and the response status for each
2327 transfer can be read by the Host to determine whether the transfer succeeded or failed. This mode of
2328 operation is called Active Controller mode.
2329 For each enqueued transfer, the Controller Logic uses the transfer parameters that are encoded in the
2330 Command Descriptor structure. These parameters inform the Controller Logic which I3C/I2C Target Device
2331 is the recipient of the transfer, or (for Broadcast CCC commands) inform the Controller Logic that a
2332 transfer is directed to all I3C Target Devices on the I3C Bus.
2333 Note:
2334 Additional details on Transfer Command and Transfer Response handling are defined in
2335 Section 6.2 of the I3C TCRI Specification [MIPI06].
2336 In DMA Mode, since Command/Response Rings are bundled together into Ring Pairs, for every Command
2337 Descriptor structure populated on the Command Ring there shall be exactly one Response Descriptor
2338 structure populated on the corresponding Response Ring. The Driver provides the Transfer Descriptor in
2339 Driver-allocated memory. Refer to Section 6.6 for more details.
2340 In PIO Mode, the Command Descriptor structure is written to registers (the Command Queue Port), and
2341 related data is read from/written to the Transfer Data Port. Refer to Section 6.7 for more details.
2342 The size of the Command Descriptor is 2 DWORDs, and the size of the Response Descriptor is 1 DWORD.
2343 The format of the Command Descriptor is “Format 1: Legacy Format, Indexed” as defined in Section 7.1 of
2344 the I3C TCRI Specification [MIPI06].
2345 Note:
2346 It is possible that future versions of this I3C HCI Specification might use different formats and/or
2347 sizes for the Command Descriptor. In that event, the new format(s) and/or size(s) will be indicated
2348 by a different value in field CMD_SIZE.
2349 The Command Descriptor is defined in Section 8.4, and supports several types of Transfer Commands per
2350 Section 7.1.2 of the I3C TCRI Specification [MIPI06], in addition to the Internal Control type command,
2351 as indicated by field CMD_ATTR. Transfers are limited to 64 KB in size. For all Transfer Commands, the
2352 Command Descriptor includes a 5-bit DEV_INDEX field containing an index into the DAT table:
2353 • For private transfers and Direct CCCs: The Host Controller shall fetch the Dynamic Address from the
2354 DAT entry indicated by the DEV_INDEX field. Software shall provide a valid index to a DAT entry that has
2355 been populated with a valid Dynamic Address of a Device on the I3C Bus (or an assigned Group Address
2356 for Write-type transfers, if supported).
2357 • For Broadcast CCCs: The Host Controller shall not use the DEV_INDEX field. Software should set
2358 DEV_INDEX to 5'h00.
2359 Note:
2360 This version of the I3C HCI Specification does not support transfers using some of the new
2361 features enabled by version 1.1.1+ of the I3C Specification [MIPI05], such as HDR-BT (Bulk
2362 Transfer) Mode, Multi-Lane transfers in any supported I3C Modes, CCC flows in HDR Modes, or
2363 several types of Combo transfers that are necessary for specific use cases such as Device to
2364 Device Tunneling. Such transfer types or control capabilities may be added as extended
2365 capabilities, or could be supported in a future version of this I3C HCI Specification.

6.8 Transfers
6.8.1 Transfers in PIO Mode
2366 In PIO Mode, the Driver shall enqueue a Command Descriptor structure by writing it to the Command
2367 Queue Port (i.e., register COMMAND_QUEUE_PORT, see Section 7.5.1), starting with its least significant
2368 DWORD (since the Command Queue Port register is 32 bits wide). Before enqueueing the Command
2369 Descriptor structure, the Driver shall put the corresponding write data into the Tx Data Queue via the
2370 Transfer Data Port (i.e., register XFER_DATA_PORT, see Section 7.5.3), for Transfer Commands that are a
2371 Write-Type transfer request and also require the Tx Data Queue. After the transfer is completed, the Driver
2372 shall read its status from the Response Queue Port (i.e., register RESPONSE_QUEUE_PORT, see
2373 Section 7.5.2) as notified by a RESP_READY_STAT interrupt. Additionally, if the Transfer Command is a
2374 Read-Type transfer request, the Driver shall read any incoming data from the Rx Data Queue via the
2375 Transfer Data Port.
2376 The Tx Data Queue is drained by the Host Controller, whereas the Rx Data Queue is drained by Driver.
2377 Since the Tx/Rx Data Queues are finite in size, the Driver shall ensure that the I3C Bus Controller Logic
2378 does not encounter any situations where a transaction would be aborted due to Data Queue underflow (for
2379 Write-Type transfers) or overflow (for Read-Type transfers).
2380 Before initiating a Write-Type transfer, the Driver shall ensure that there is data in the Tx Data Queue for
2381 the hardware to read: either by limiting the request size and putting all data into the queue when possible,
2382 or else by initially loading the Tx Data Queue with partial data, and subsequently populating the Tx Data
2383 Queue with remaining data as the I3C Bus Controller Logic begins transferring the data on the I3C Bus, to
2384 avoid an underflow during the Write-Type transfer.
2385 For Write-Type transfers that are larger than the Tx Data Queue size, the Driver should set the Transmit
2386 Buffer threshold (i.e., field TX_BUF_THLD in register DATA_BUFFER_THLD_CTRL; see Section 7.5.6) in
2387 order to remain responsive and prevent underflow conditions. The Driver then populates the Tx Data Queue
2388 up to its full size (i.e., field TX_DATA_BUFFER_SIZE in register QUEUE_SIZE, see Section 7.5.7), enqueues
2389 the Command Descriptor, and then waits for the Tx FIFO to drain. When the Driver receives the
2390 TX_THLD_STAT interrupt, it knows that the Host Controller can accept additional data, so it writes more data
2391 into the TX Data Queue, up to the threshold value. In order to prevent an underflow condition and the
2392 resulting early transaction termination, for transactions larger than the size of the Tx Data Queue, the
2393 Driver shall ensure that the Tx Data Queue does not drain completely before it writes the last DWORD of
2394 data for the transfer.
2395 Note:
2396 Per Section 6.6.5, the Host Controller shall use the TX_THLD_STAT interrupt to indicate its
2397 readiness to accept additional data DWORDs in the Tx Data Queue, up to the threshold level
2398 provided in TX_BUF_THLD. When the Host receives this interrupt, it knows that it may write up to
2399 that number of DWORDs of data into the Tx Data Queue.
2400 Similarly, for Read-Type transfers, the Driver should set the Receive Buffer threshold (i.e., field
2401 RX_BUF_THLD in register DATA_BUFFER_THLD_CTRL, see Section 7.5.6) in order to remain responsive and
2402 prevent overflow conditions. The Driver then enqueues the Command Descriptor and waits for an interrupt
2403 notification that indicates that incoming data is ready to be read from the Rx Data Queue (i.e., field
2404 RX_THLD_STAT in register PIO_INTR_STATUS, see Section 7.5.9). The frequency of such interrupt
2405 notifications is determined by the value written into field RX_BUF_THLD (i.e., the Receive Buffer threshold).
2406 After receiving this interrupt notification, the Driver then reads the incoming data from the Rx Data Queue.
2407 In order to prevent an overflow condition and the resulting early transaction termination, the Driver shall
2408 ensure that incoming data is read from the Rx Data Queue before it becomes totally filled with data (i.e.,
2409 field RX_DATA_BUFFER_SIZE in register QUEUE_SIZE, see Section 7.5.7).

2410 Note:
2411 Per Section 6.6.5, the Host Controller shall use the RX_THLD_STAT interrupt to indicate that some
2412 data DWORDs (i.e., at least the number indicated in the threshold level provided in RX_BUF_THLD)
2413 are in the Rx Data Queue. When the Host receives this interrupt, it knows that it may read up to

2415 However, under certain circumstances, the last data DWORD for a particular Read-Type transfer
2416 might not trigger the RX_THLD_STAT interrupt, since the minimum threshold level that may be
2417 configured for RX_BUF_THLD for such interrupt notifications is 2 DWORD entries in the Rx Data
2418 Queue (see Section 7.5.6, Table 42). This is especially pertinent for very short Read transfers (i.e.,

2420 therefore not trigger the RX_THLD_STAT interrupt notification.
2421 The Driver shall inspect the Response Descriptor, check field DATA_LENGTH to determine the
2422 actual number of data bytes received, and consume an appropriate number of DWORDs from the
2423 Rx Data Queue for each Read-Type transfer that has completed, even if not all such DWORDs
2424 would have generated the RX_THLD_STAT interrupt. The Driver must also appropriately configure
2425 the Response Ready Buffer Threshold (i.e., field RESP_BUF_THLD in register QUEUE_THLD_CTRL,
2426 see Section 7.5.5, Table 45) to ensure that it receives RESP_READY_STAT interrupt notifications in
2427 a timely manner.
2428 Interrupts related to PIO Mode transfers are defined in the PIO Registers Section (see Section 7.5). Note
2429 that the PIO interrupt for Rx Data Buffer Threshold Status might be asserted before a Read-Type transfer is
2430 complete, for larger transfers, depending on the threshold settings in register QUEUE_THLD_CTRL (see
2431 Section 7.5.5). The Driver should be ready to read such incoming data in advance of receiving the
2432 Response Descriptor that describes this data, including its overall message length.
2433 Upon completion of the transfer, the Host Controller might indicate that a Response Descriptor is ready to
2434 be read, by setting field RESP_READY_STAT in register PIO_INTR_STATUS (see Section 7.5.9). This field
2435 might be automatically cleared upon the Driver reading out one or more Response Descriptors from the
2436 Response Queue (i.e., the readout operation might serve as an interrupt clear). Response Descriptor
2437 interrupts shall depend on the threshold setting for the Response Queue (i.e., field RESP_BUF_THLD in
2438 register QUEUE_THLD_CTRL).
2439 The Driver shall correlate the data DWORDs read from the Rx Data Queue to ensure that the data is
2440 correctly associated with the read transfer for the length indicated by the Response Descriptor. For I3C
2441 Read-type transfers, a successful Response Descriptor (i.e., field ERR_STATUS having a value of 0x0)
2442 might indicate a ‘short’ Read-Type transfer, per Section 6.2.7 of the I3C TCRI Specification [MIPI06]. In
2443 PIO Mode, the length of data received from the I3C Target Device would typically be fully understood in
2444 context only after most (or, in some cases, all) of the data DWORDs were been read from the Rx Data
2445 Queue and then compared with the Response Descriptor. Since the relevant PIO Queues are independently
2446 read for Read-Type transfers, but have an implied association of data that is available to be consumed, the
2447 Driver might not always read from the Rx Data Queue and the Response Queue in the same order, due to
2448 the threshold settings for such queues, as well as the presence of other enqueued Transfer Commands.
2449 However, the Driver must ensure that it correctly associates the received data DWORDs with the Response
2450 Descriptor for each Read-Type transfer, in order to determine whether it has received all the expected data
2451 DWORDs, or whether this is a ‘short’ Read-Type transfer.
2452 The Host Controller shall also generate interrupts for other Queue events, which shall be set and cleared

2455 interrupt events that must be explicitly cleared by the Driver:
2456 • Interrupt TRANSFER_ABORT_STAT: Transfer was aborted
2457 • Interrupt TRANSFER_ERR_STAT: Error

2458 For transfers that are aborted by the I3C Bus Controller Logic due to either an underflow condition in the
2459 Tx Data Queue, or an overflow condition in the Rx Data Queue (as described above), the Host Controller
2460 shall stop processing any subsequent Command Descriptors in the Command Queue after reporting this
2461 error. Additionally, if the aborted transfer was not the last transfer in a sequence (i.e., field TOC=0, as
2462 defined in Section 6.12) then the Host Controller shall also report this as a cancelled transaction sequence,

6.8.2 Transfers in DMA Mode
2464 Note:
2465 This section applies only for Host Controller implementations that implement DMA Mode, and thus
2466 connect to a System Bus that supports memory-mapped IO and DMA.
2467 In DMA Mode, the transfer to a Device is performed via Command and Response Rings, per Section 6.6.2.
2468 The Driver shall populate the Command Ring with Transfer Descriptor structures, and eventually update
2469 the Enqueue Pointer for the related Ring Bundle (see Table 4).
2470 The Transfer Descriptor supports either:
2471 • A Data Buffer Pointer to a single, physically contiguous memory block that data is fetched from and/or
2472 stored to, or
2473 • A pointer to a Driver-allocated table of Data Buffer Pointers containing the Addresses of multiple,
2474 potentially non-contiguous memory blocks (i.e., a Scatter-Gather List).
2475 • The Data Buffer Pointers shall take the form of an array of Memory Descriptor structures (see
2476 Section 8.7). This array shall be a single, physically contiguous allocation of memory.
2477 • Each Memory Descriptor shall contain an Address of a memory buffer, that the Driver shall allocate.
2478 Each memory buffer shall be DWORD-aligned.
2479 If a Transfer Descriptor uses a Scatter-Gather List, then there are two limitations on the sizes of the set of
2480 memory buffers that the Driver shall allocate for the Scatter-Gather structures:
2481 • The total size of the Data Buffer Pointers table shall be a multiple of the Memory Descriptor structure
2482 size; and
2483 • The sum of the memory buffer sizes in a Scatter-Gather List shall be ≤ the maximum transfer size.
2484 Additionally, each Data Buffer Pointers table should have a limited number of entries, i.e., to avoid
2485 memory fragmentation where possible. The Data Buffer Pointers table should be ≤ 0xFF entries, in order to
2486 limit the processing time for each Transfer Descriptor and reduce the number of memory read operations
2487 required to fetch all such Memory Descriptors. Although the maximum length is 0xFFFF (i.e., field
2488 BLOCK_SIZE in the Transfer Descriptor, when field BLP = 1'b1), the Driver should constrain this value to
2489 0xFF or lower (see Figure 49).
2490 An update of the Enqueue Pointer shall serve as a Doorbell for the Host Controller, which shall then
2491 evaluate the number of Transfer Descriptor entries to process. For each Transfer Descriptor that has been
2492 enqueued, the Host Controller shall perform the described transaction on the Bus. The order and sequence
2493 of such Transfer Descriptors shall be maintained per Section 6.12. For transactions with a data phase, the
2494 Host Controller shall move the data based on the Data Buffer (i.e., either as a single region, or Scatter-
2495 Gather, as indicated in the Transfer Descriptor). The Driver shall set field WROC in the Command
2496 Descriptor structure to 1'b1 for every command scheduled in the Command Ring.
2497 Example: Assume that the Command/Response Rings are initialized, with both the Enqueue Pointer
2498 and Dequeue Pointer having value 0. The Driver advances the Enqueue Pointer to value X, which
2499 triggers a Doorbell notification.
2500 • First the hardware processes all Transfer Descriptor entries, in order, from 0 through X-1 (i.e., X
2501 Transfer Descriptors are processed).
2502 • Next, the Driver advances the Enqueue Pointer by Y, to X+Y, to schedule Y additional commands.
2503 • After this write, the hardware processes Transfer Descriptor entries from X through X+Y-1 (i.e., Y
2504 additional Transfer Descriptors are processed).

2505 For every Transfer Descriptor on the Command Ring, the Host Controller shall populate one Response
2506 Descriptor on the Response Ring, indicating the status of the corresponding Bus transfer. When requested
2507 in the Transfer Descriptor (by setting the IOC bit to 1'b1), the Host Controller shall issue an interrupt to
2508 notify the Driver that outstanding Response Descriptors are available and should be processed. The Host
2509 Controller may process any number of outstanding Command Descriptor structures, in order, until reaching
2510 the Enqueue Pointer (and no further). The number of processed Command Descriptor structures is reflected
2511 in the Dequeue Pointer.
2512 The Driver shall notify the Host Controller of the number of Responses processed by advancing the
2513 Software Dequeue Pointer. The Driver may process an arbitrary number of Responses, in order, until
2514 reaching the Dequeue Pointer (and no further). This approach allows the Host Controller to re-generate the
2515 interrupt when necessary.
2516 Example: Assume that the hardware has produced N Response Descriptors, and that the software
2517 then receives the interrupt to process them, but for some reason the Driver is only able to process M
2518 of the Response Descriptors (where M < N). When the Host Controller detects that the Driver has
2519 advanced the Software Dequeue Pointer, it will know that N − M additional Responses are still
2520 pending for processing in Response Ring, and as a result the Host Controller may generate a new
2521 interrupt to remind the Driver to continue processing the remaining N − M Response Descriptors.
2522 When the Driver transitions a Ring Header to the Enabled state, the Host Controller shall set its own
2523 Dequeue Pointer to 0 and then wait for a write to the Enqueue Pointer. Upon transition to the Enabled state,
2524 the Host Controller shall re-read the Base Pointers for all Rings in that Ring Bundle.
2525 A Command/Response Ring Pair is considered idle when the Enqueue Pointer, Dequeue Pointer, and
2526 Software Dequeue Pointer are all equal to one another.
2527 To prevent Commands on the Ring from ever overflowing when advancing the Enqueue Pointer, the Host
2528 Controller Driver shall never permit the Enqueue Pointer to reach the value of the Software Dequeue
2529 Pointer. However, advancing the Software Dequeue Pointer may result in the Software Dequeue Pointer
2530 having the same value as the Enqueue Pointer.
2531 The Host Controller processes Ring Bundles individually:
2532 • The number of enabled Ring Bundles is set in the Ring Headers Preamble registers (Section 7.6.1). E.g.,
2533 the Driver shall configure the Host Controller to only look at enabled Ring Bundles: for example, 0, 1, 2,
2534 and 3.
2535 • The order in which the Host Controller starts to process Ring Bundles, and the order in which the Host
2536 Controller processes subsequent Ring Bundles, shall be hardware-implementation specific.
2537 • The Host Controller shall use its Ring Controller arbitration logic to switch processing to the next Ring
2538 Bundle that is valid (i.e., enabled and running) and has pending Transfer Descriptors to be processed, per
2539 Section 6.6.5.
2540 The Host Controller shall have only one Ring Headers registers section per Host Controller Interface,
2541 containing only one Preamble, with up to eight Ring Bundle offsets (as defined by the Ring Header
2542 Descriptor registers). All Ring-specific registers are defined in the respective Ring Headers. Driver-
2543 allocated memory is pointed to by the Ring Base Address High and Low registers for the Command,
2544 Response, IBI, and Data Rings (Section 7.6.10.12 through Section 7.6.10.19).
2545 Registers related to Ring Bundle interrupts are defined in the Ring Header. Completion of a transfer (i.e.,
2546 one resulting from a Transfer Descriptor with the IOC bit set) triggers the TRANSFER_COMPLETION
2547 interrupt.
2548 The Driver may trigger the Ring Abort operation for a Ring Bundle by setting the ABORT bit to 1'b1 in
2549 register RH_CONTROL (see Section 7.6.10.9). See Section 6.6.6 for more details.

6.8.3 Data Byte Ordering
2563 For Transfer Commands, the data being sent or received is specific to the application and the particular
2564 Target Device, and interpreted as an opaque stream of bytes by the Host Controller. The Host Controller
2565 interface is defined in terms of DWORD entries (i.e., 32-bit wide data words) that are used to store up to 4
2566 bytes per entry.
2567 The particular byte within a DWORD that is read or written first (i.e., the lowest offset in the DWORD
2568 entry) is system dependent, and implementers should determine the correct ordering to use for a particular
2569 system architecture and its system bus. Systems that use the Least Significant Byte first are commonly
2570 called Little Endian, and systems that use the Most Significant Byte first are commonly called Big Endian.
2571 To make data transfers as efficient as possible, a Host Controller should accommodate the same byte
2572 ordering used by its connected Host system. Implementers should consider the integration options and offer
2573 byte ordering capabilities that automatically handle the byte ordering of data DWORDs in a manner best
2574 suited to the connected Host system.
2575 Field DATA_BYTE_ORDER_MODE in register HC_CONTROL (see Section 7.4.2) indicates the supported byte
2576 ordering mode. The Host Controller shall use this byte ordering mode with the following uses:
2577 • For PIO Mode:
2578 • For Write-Type transfers, all Data DWORDs written by the Host into the Tx Data Queue (i.e., the
2579 Transfer Data Port, register XFER_DATA_PORT; see Section 7.5.3)
2580 • For Read-Type transfers, all Data DWORDs read by the Host from the Rx Data Queue (i.e., the
2581 Transfer Data Port, register XFER_DATA_PORT; see Section 7.5.3)
2582 • For IBIs, all IBI Data DWORDs read by the Host from the IBI Port (i.e., register IBI_PORT; see
2583 Section 7.5.4)
2584 Note:
2585 The IBI Status Descriptor shall not be affected or otherwise changed by the current byte
2586 ordering mode when read from the IBI Port, as this data structure is a discrete 32-bit entity.
2587 • For DMA Mode:
2588 • For Write-Type transfers, all Data DWORDs read by the Memory Access Interface from Host system
2589 memory, at addresses indicated by the Transfer Descriptor (see Section 8.3)
2590 • For Read-Type transfers, all Data DWORDs written by the Memory Access Interface to Host system
2591 memory, at addresses indicated by the Transfer Descriptor (see Section 8.3)
2592 • For IBIs, all IBI Data DWORDs written by the Memory Access Interface to Host system memory, at
2593 addresses indicated by the IBI Data Ring’s Base Address and the Host Controller’s internal register of
2594 free chunks (see Section 6.9.2)
2595 The Host Controller shall not apply the byte ordering mode to change the contents of any other registers,
2596 descriptors, or data structures that are read/written via mailbox registers (such as Queues in PIO Mode) or
2597 within other direct memory operations (such as Rings in DMA Mode). Such other registers, descriptors,
2598 and data structures shall be read or written in their native byte ordering, as discrete entities that are defined
2599 in terms of 32-bit DWORDs on all systems.
2600 The order of data transmission of a data byte on the I3C Bus shall always follow the I3C Specification (i.e.,
2601 SDR Mode proceeds from bit 7 to bit 0), regardless of the current byte ordering mode.
94 Copyright © 2018–2023 MIPI Alliance, Inc.

2602 Little-Endian Byte Ordering Mode
2603 For Write-Type transfers, the I3C Bus Controller Logic shall drive Data bytes from each DWORD entry in
2604 the Tx Data Buffer, starting with the least significant byte (i.e., Bits[7:0]) and continuing on to the most
2605 significant byte (i.e., Bits[31:24]).
2606 If the transfer length is not DWORD-aligned (i.e., is not an even multiple of 4 bytes) then the I3C Bus
2607 Controller Logic might end the transfer before reaching the most significant byte within the last DWORD
2608 entry, according to the framing and data transfer coding for the I3C Mode.
2609 For Read-Type transfers, the I3C Bus Controller Logic shall read Data bytes from the Target Device and
2610 store them into the Rx Data Buffer, starting with the least significant byte and continuing on to the most
2611 significant byte. If the read transfer ends before the DWORD boundary, then the remaining byte locations
2612 in that DWORD entry shall not be used.
2613 Figure 22 shows the order in which the Data bytes appear on the I3C Bus during a Transfer Command’s
2614 transaction.

6.8.4 Host Controller Abort Operation
2632 The Driver may initiate a Host Controller Abort operation at any time, while enqueued Command
2633 Descriptors are waiting to be processed and also while the I3C Bus Controller Logic is currently processing
2634 active transfers. For certain situations, the Driver might initiate the Host Controller Abort on detecting an
2635 incorrect result or other status received for a Read-Type transfer (i.e., a Private Read, a Direct Read CCC,
2636 or a Direct GET CCC) that would not halt operation automatically (i.e., a NACK error) or is not necessarily
2637 an I3C Bus error, but would have otherwise been determined to be an error or a sign of operations
2638 diverging from an expected result (i.e., from software).
2639 The Driver may initiate the global Host Controller Abort operation by setting the ABORT bit to 1'b1 in
2640 register HC_CONTROL (see Section 7.4.2). The Host Controller shall receive this request and process it
2641 according to the current operating mode. In effect, setting the ABORT bit acts as a method for cancelling the
2642 I3C Bus Controller Logic’s current transfer, and also for preventing the I3C Bus Controller Logic from
2643 processing any other enqueued transfers in any Rings/Queues (per the operating mode), or for Scheduled
2644 Commands (if supported; see Section 6.16).
2645 • In any operating modes:
2646 • The Host Controller shall abort (i.e., shall terminate) any in-progress transfers that the I3C Bus
2647 Controller Logic is currently driving or receiving, at the earliest opportunity.
2648 The I3C Bus Controller Logic shall terminate transfers according to the requirements of
2649 the I3C Specification for the current I3C Mode (i.e., without causing any I3C Bus errors).
2650 The transactions that were aborted are indicated accordingly in the corresponding
2651 Response Descriptors, with field ERR_STATUS having a value of 0x8 (HC_ABORTED) or
2652 another transfer-type specific value; and the Host Controller shall also assert the
2653 TRANSFER_ABORT_STAT interrupt (if enabled for notification) for the current operating
2654 context(s) affected by the Host Controller Abort operation:
2655 • For PIO Mode this is register PIO_INTR_STATUS (see Section 7.5.9).
2656 • For DMA Mode this is register RH_INTR_STATUS (see Section 7.6.10.4) in the Ring Header for
2657 the Ring Bundle that was currently active for processing.
2658 • Once received, a Host Controller Abort request cannot be cancelled by the Driver (i.e., before it is
2659 either processed or propagated, as defined below).
2660 • The Host Controller shall enter the ABORTED state:
2661 • Bit ABORT in register HC_CONTROL shall read with a value of 1'b1 while the Host Controller remains
2662 in the ABORTED state.
2663 • Additionally, in PIO Mode:
2664 • If the Command Queue contains any subsequent Command Descriptors that might have been enqueued
2665 after the aborted transfers (i.e., those that were stopped, and indicated as aborted with a Response
2666 Descriptor typically having a value of 0x8 (HC_ABORTED) or another transfer type specific value), then
2667 these subsequent Command Descriptors shall remain in the Command Queue. The Driver shall
2668 determine whether to leave such Command Descriptors intact, or whether to reset the Command
2669 Queue (i.e., by using register RESET_CONTROL; see Section 7.4.5).
2670 • The Host Controller shall effectively propagate the global Abort signal to the PIO Queues (as well as to
2671 any other operating contexts, such as Scheduled Commands).
2672 • The Host Controller shall remain in ABORTED state until the Driver clears the global ABORTED state
2673 and the ABORTED state for the PIO Queues.
2674 • Once the Driver writes a value of 1'b0 to clear the ABORT bit in register HC_CONTROL, the Driver
2675 shall also clear the ABORTED state of the PIO Queues by writing a value of 1'b0 to clear the ABORT
2676 bit in register PIO_CONTROL (Section 7.5.13). After this, processing shall be resumed (if such
2677 Command Descriptors remain enqueued).

2678 • Additionally, in DMA Mode:
2679 • The Host Controller Abort operation acts as though the Ring Abort operation (see Section 6.6.6) were
2680 triggered for all Ring Bundles that were currently valid (i.e., enabled and running) when the Host
2681 Controller received the request:
2682 • Each Ring Bundle that is affected by the Host Controller Abort operation shall report its state as
2683 ABORTED, per Section 6.6.6 and Section 7.6.10.8.
2684 • Any other Ring Bundles that were not valid (i.e., not running, not enabled, or already in ABORTED
2685 state) shall not be affected (i.e., shall not enter the ABORTED state).
2686 • The Host Controller shall effectively propagate the global Abort signal to all such Ring Bundles (as
2687 well as any other operating contexts, such as Scheduled Commands). Each affected Ring Bundle shall
2688 enter the ABORTED state simultaneously, and each must be recovered individually.
2689 • The Host Controller shall remain in ABORTED state until the Driver clears the global ABORTED state:
2690 • Reads from bit ABORT in register HC_CONTROL shall return a value of 1'b1 while the Host Controller
2691 remains in the ABORTED state.
2692 • Once the Driver writes a value of 1'b0 to clear the ABORT bit in register HC_CONTROL, the Driver
2693 shall also clear the ABORTED state for the Ring Bundles that entered the ABORTED state.
2694 • The Driver shall follow the same procedure to perform Ring recovery steps, for each Ring Bundle in
2695 ABORTED state (per Section 6.6.6).
2696 • As each such Ring Bundle is recovered and brought out of ABORTED state, it shall become available
2697 for Ring Bundle Servicing (per Section 6.6.5) if and only if the Host Controller was also brought out
2698 of the global ABORTED state.
2699 • For any other Ring Bundles that were not Aborted: If the Driver later enables such a Ring Bundle
2700 (i.e., one that was not enabled when the Host Controller Abort operation was processed), or causes a
2701 Ring Bundle that was not running to enter running state (i.e., one that was stopped when the Host
2702 Controller Abort operation was processed), then:
2703 • If bit ABORT in register HC_CONTROL still has a value of 1'b1, then the Host Controller shall remain
2704 in an ABORTED state, and no Ring Bundles shall be serviced (i.e., until this is first cleared at the Host
2705 Controller level).
2706 • If bit ABORT in register HC_CONTROL was cleared (i.e., written with a value of 1'b0), then such a
2707 Ring Bundle shall become available for Ring Bundle Servicing. No other action to clear any other
2708 ABORTED state is necessary for this Ring Bundle, as it was not previously ABORTED.

6.8.5 Support for I3C ‘Short’ Read-Type Transfers
2713 A Host Controller shall support ‘short’ Read-Type transfers, as defined in Section 6.2.7 of the I3C TCRI
2714 Specification [MIPI06]. Additionally, the Host Controller shall support any Transfer Command types that
2715 allow the software to select whether to consider a ‘short’ Read-Type transfer as a transfer error.
2716 Note:
2717 A ‘short’ Read-Type transfer might not necessarily be an error, as some I3C content protocols might
2718 depend on variable-length Private Read transfers. From the perspective of this I3C HCI
2719 Specification, it is left to the Driver or higher-level software to decide whether to (a) Indicate that
2720 ‘short’ Read-Type transfers will be treated as a transfer error by the Host Controller, and stop any
2721 processing of subsequent Transfer Commands; or (b) Indicate that ‘short’ Read-Type transfers that
2722 do not otherwise generate any other errors should not stop processing of subsequent Transfer
2723 commands. However, in case (b) the ultimate decision of whether or not the ‘short’ Read-Transfer
2724 was actually an error (i.e., unexpected result) is left to the Driver: in some cases, the Driver might
2725 inspect the Response data to decide whether this transfer was an error. If so, then the Driver could
2726 also initiate a Host Controller Abort operation to stop processing at some later time.
6.8.6 Support for Transfer Termination and HDR Mode Configuration
2727 A Host Controller shall optionally support special handling of I3C data transfers where either the I3C
2728 Target(s) or a Monitoring Device can terminate the transfer. If supported, then the Host Controller shall
2729 support configuration flows using Command Descriptors of type Internal Control Command (see
2730 Section 8.4.2) with value 0x6 in field MIPI_CMD (see Table 135 and Table 141). In this section and its
2731 subsections, such a Command Descriptor is referred to as a Configuration Command Descriptor.
6.8.6.1 Use with HDR Mode Configuration
2732 If the I3C Bus has one or more Targets that support special handling for Early Transfer Termination in one
2733 or more HDR modes, then the Host Controller allows software to configure such I3C Targets (using the
2734 ENDXFER CCC, per the I3C Specification [MIPI02] at Section 5.1.9.3.25). After such I3C Targets are
2735 configured appropriately, then software may construct a command sequence using a Configuration
2736 Command Descriptor followed by one or more Transfer Commands in the indicated HDR Mode.
2737 To use this special handling, software shall first enqueue a Configuration Command Descriptor with a value
2738 of 0x1 (for HDR-DDR Mode) or 0x2 (for HDR-Ternary Modes) in field END_XFER_TYPE (i.e., Bits[15:12],
2739 see Table 141), and the configuration byte previously sent to such Targets with the ENDXFER CCC in field
2740 END_XFER_CONFIG (i.e., Bits[23:16]). This Configuration Command Descriptor temporarily configures the
2741 I3C Bus Controller Logic to support the provided configuration parameters for that HDR Mode, which
2742 shall apply for the rest of the command sequence. These configuration parameters vary per the HDR Mode,
2743 and may include:
2744 • Whether the Controller and Target(s) use, or expect to handle, a particular Early Termination Pattern
2745 during the transfer, giving the receiver an opportunity to either continue or terminate the transfer;
2746 • Whether the Controller or Target(s) will send any additional structured protocol elements after an Early
2747 Termination Pattern was initiated by the receiver (for both Writes and Reads); and
2748 • Whether the Controller and Target(s) will use flow control for certain transfer types (i.e., an equivalent of
2749 ACK/NACK in that HDR Mode protocol).
2750 As this Configuration Command Descriptor is always used in a command sequence, any subsequent
2751 Transfer Commands in that HDR Mode will be sent with the appropriate parameters, until the next STOP
2752 condition. To use special handling, software should send one or more Transfer Commands in the sequence,
2753 where the last such Transfer Command contains the value 1'b1 in the TOC field, and any previous Transfer
2754 Commands contain the value 1'b0 in the TOC field (i.e., continuous framing, as defined in Section 6.12).
2755 After exiting the HDR Mode with the HDR Exit Pattern (which ends with the STOP condition), the I3C
2756 Bus Controller Logic shall return to its default configuration parameters.
Copyright © 2018–2023 MIPI Alliance, Inc. 99
Public Release Edition

Specification for I3C HCI Version 1.2
15-Feb-2023
2757 Note:
2758 For HDR-DDR Mode and HDR-Ternary Modes, the special handling and Early Transfer Termination
2759 support is new for v1.1 of the I3C Specification, and certain I3C Targets may choose to support
2760 these capabilities. Since other Targets might not support these capabilities (including legacy I3C
2761 Targets that only comply with version 1.0 of the I3C Specification), the Configuration Command
2762 Descriptor only applies the provided configuration parameters to the current command sequence,
2763 and the I3C Bus Controller Logic uses its default parameters for subsequent transfers (i.e.,
2764 subsequent Transfer Commands after the STOP). This allows software to discover which I3C
2765 Targets will support this special handling, optionally configure them with the ENDXFER CCC to use
2766 special handling, and then enqueue command sequences for these I3C Targets, starting with the
2767 Configuration Command Descriptor. However, software must first configure any I3C Targets with
2768 the ENDXFER CCC before using the Configuration Command Descriptor that uses special
2769 handling. When enqueueing command sequences for other I3C Targets (i.e., those that do not
2770 support special handling, or those that were not configured to use it), software shall not use the
2771 Configuration Command Descriptor in the command sequence.
6.8.6.2 Use with Monitoring Device Early Termination
2772 If the I3C Bus has one or more Targets or Monitoring Devices that can terminate a transfer using
2773 Monitoring Device Early Transfer Termination, then the Host Controller allows software to construct a
2774 command sequence that enables this Early Termination capability for the I3C Bus, using a Configuration
2775 Command Descriptor followed by one or more Transfer Commands in the indicated I3C Mode.
2776 To use this special handling, software shall first enqueue a Configuration Command Descriptor with a value
2777 of 0x3 in field END_XFER_TYPE (i.e., Bits[15:12], see Table 141), and the configuration parameter byte in
2778 field END_XFER_CONFIG (i.e., Bits[23:16]). This Configuration Command Descriptor will temporarily
2779 configure the I3C Bus Controller Logic to support the Early Termination capability for the indicated I3C
2780 Modes, which shall apply for the rest of the command sequence. Additionally, the Host Controller will
2781 begin the SDR Frame by automatically sending the ENDXFER CCC with the same configuration parameter
2782 byte, such that it enables all Monitoring Devices to use the parameters for subsequent transfers.
2783 Note:
2784 The value in field END_XFER_CONFIG is used directly by the I3C Bus Controller Logic, when it
2785 sends the ENDXFER CCC with Defining Byte 0xFC to configure the I3C Bus.
2786 As this Configuration Command Descriptor is always used in a command sequence, any subsequent
2787 Transfer Commands in that I3C Mode will be sent with the appropriate parameters, until the next STOP
2788 condition. Once the I3C Bus Controller Logic is ready to use Early Transfer Termination, software should
2789 send one or more Transfer Commands in the sequence, where the last such Transfer Command contains the
2790 value 1'b1 in the TOC field, and any previous Transfer Commands contain the value 1'b0 in the TOC field
2791 (i.e., continuous framing, as defined in Section 6.12). After ending transfers with either the STOP condition
2792 (for SDR Mode) or the HDR Exit Pattern (for HDR Modes), the I3C Bus Controller Logic shall return to its
2793 default configuration parameters.

6.9 IBI Handling
2794 This Section specifies IBI Handling in PIO Mode and DMA Mode.
2795 For both PIO Mode and DMA Mode, all IBI Data Bytes shall be stored as DWORDs in the current byte
2796 ordering mode (as indicated by field DATA_BYTE_ORDER_MODE in register HC_CONTROL, see
2797 Section 7.4.2).
6.9.1 IBI Handling in PIO Mode
2798 In PIO Mode, the IBI-related information shall be enqueued to the IBI Queue and consumed by reading the
2799 IBI Port (see Section 7.5.4). IBI reception shall be indicated via the IBI Status Port Threshold Status bit
2800 (field IBI_STATUS_THLD_STAT) in the Interrupt Status register (register PIO_INTR_STATUS, see
2801 Section 7.5.9).
2802 The Driver shall first read out an IBI Status Descriptor structure from the IBI Port (register IBI_PORT, see
2803 Section 7.5.4). Next, the Driver shall read consecutive data DWORDs from the IBI Port, using the
2804 DATA_LENGTH field provided via the IBI Status Descriptor (see Section 8.6).
2805 Note:
2806 Both the IBI Status Descriptor and the IBI Data DWORD(s) are read from the same IBI Port. IBI
2807 Data DWORD(s) shall be read from the IBI Port, according to the current byte ordering mode per
2808 Section 6.8.3.
2809 For some IBIs, multiple IBI Status Descriptors might be needed to describe a single IBI event. If field
2810 LAST_STATUS in the previous IBI Status Descriptor is set to 1'b0, then the Driver shall continue reading
2811 from the IBI Port to read the next IBI Status Descriptor.
2812 In cases with multiple back-to-back IBI Requests, the Driver should provide appropriate values in fields
2813 IBI_STATUS_THLD and IBI_DATA_SEGMENT_SIZE of register QUEUE_THLD_CTRL (see Section 7.5.5), in
2814 order to ensure that IBI reception is not blocked due to the IBI Queue becoming completely full before it
2815 can be read by the Driver via the IBI Port. The Driver should choose values that balance overall system
2816 latency and performance concerns, with knowledge of the size of the IBI Queue. The recommended values
2817 might vary, depending on the frequency of IBI Requests as well as the expected data payload length for
2818 IBIs from different I3C Target Devices.
2819 Note:
2820 The Host Controller shall buffer incoming IBI payload data before populating the IBI Status
2821 Descriptor into the IBI Queue, since the IBI Status Descriptor contains the length of the data that
2822 follows it (i.e., as read from the IBI Queue via the IBI Port).
2823 If the IBI Status Threshold value is set to a value that is too high for the Driver to be made aware of
2824 incoming IBI Status Descriptors in a timely manner, then the Driver might not receive notifications
2825 and would not know to drain the IBI Queue in time for subsequent IBI Requests. In this case, if the
2826 IBI Queue were to become completely full, then the Host Controller would not be able to accept an
2827 incoming IBI Request from an I3C Target Device, so in such a case the Host Controller shall NACK
2828 all IBI Requests (including Hot-Join Requests and Controller Role Requests) until the IBI Queue is
2829 drained by the Driver.

6.9.2 IBI Handling in DMA Mode
2830 Note:
2831 This section applies only for Host Controller implementations that implement DMA Mode, and thus
2832 connect to a System Bus that supports memory-mapped IO and DMA.
2833 In DMA Mode, after an IBI is fully processed on the Bus, the Host Controller shall trigger an
2834 IBI_READY_STAT interrupt to the Driver. For an IBI from a Target that is present in the DAT table, the IBI
2835 shall be enqueued into the Ring Bundle indicated by field RING_ID in that Target’s DAT table entry. For an
2836 IBI from an unknown Target, the IBI shall be enqueued into Ring Bundle 0.
2837 Per Section 6.6.3.1, the IBI Status Ring’s Enqueue Pointer indicates that one or more IBI Status Descriptor
2838 structures have been populated on IBI Status Ring. The Driver shall process one or more of these IBI Status
2839 Descriptor structures, and upon completion shall update the IBI Status Ring’s Dequeue Pointer to notify the
2840 Host Controller that the structure has been freed.
2841 If an IBI Status Descriptor structure also indicates that it has an allocation of one or more Data Chunks
2842 containing IBI payload data, then the Driver shall also process the IBI payload data, and then shall notify
2843 the Host Controller that the Data Chunks have been freed (see Section 6.6.3.2).
2844 Note:
2845 IBI payload data shall be written into the Chunks comprising the IBI Data Ring, according to the
2846 current byte ordering mode that was selected when the IBI was received and processed by the
2847 Host Controller’s I3C Bus Controller Logic per Section 6.8.3.
2848 The Driver shall also increment field CHUNK_COUNTER in register CHUNK_CONTROL (see Section 7.6.10.3)
2849 to inform the hardware how many Data Chunks were freed (i.e., the Driver shall add the number of Data
2850 Chunks for the processed IBI Status Descriptor(s) to the current value of field CHUNK_COUNTER). This
2851 approach relieves the Host Controller of the need to directly inspect the IBI Status Descriptors that the
2852 Driver frees.
2853 To process one or more IBI Status Descriptor structures on the IBI Status Ring, along with any associated
2854 Data Chunks on the IBI Data Ring, the Driver shall:
2855 1. Ensure that the Enqueue Pointer is ahead of the Dequeue Pointer
2856 2. Read the Chunk Counter field and save the cached value
2857 3. Read the first IBI Status Descriptor (i.e., the one at the position pointed to by the Dequeue Pointer)
2858 from the IBI Status Ring
2859 4. Determine whether this is the last IBI Status Descriptor for an IBI event (i.e., check field
2860 LAST_STATUS)
2861 5. Determine how many Data Chunks are associated with this IBI Status Descriptor (i.e., check field
2862 CHUNKS) and process these Data Chunks appropriately (i.e., copy contents of Data Chunks from the
2863 IBI Data Ring into other Host system memory)
2864 6. Advance the Dequeue Pointer by one position
2865 7. Add the number of Data Chunks to the cached value of the Chunk Counter field, and write this new
2866 value back to the Chunk Counter field
2867 8. Optionally repeat steps 2–7, as long as the Dequeue Pointer has not yet reached the Enqueue Pointer.
2868 The Driver may also optimize this procedure, by freeing several adjacent IBI Status Descriptors with one
2869 update (i.e., advancing the Dequeue Pointer by multiple positions) and then freeing all Data Chunks for
2870 such IBI Status Descriptors with a single write to field CHUNK_COUNTER in register CHUNK_CONTROL, as
2871 long as it adds the total number of all Data Chunks for all such IBI Status Descriptors.

6.9.3 Timestamping
2877 The TS field of a DAT table entry indicates whether the corresponding Target supports Timestamping. If a
2878 Target supports Timestamping, then the Host Controller hardware shall include two additional QWORDs
2879 (thus 4 DWORDs in total) in the IBI Data buffer, containing Controller Timestamp information (C_REF and
2880 C_C2) for the IBI event on the I3C Bus. These Controller Timestamp counters are sent before the IBI
2881 Mandatory Byte, and the IBI Payload Length is increased by 4 DWORDs in order to accommodate them.
2882 The exact means of implementing C_REF and C_C2 and its Synchronization to any System timer is
2883 implementation-specific and beyond the scope of this Specification.
2884 Note:
2885 The Host Controller does not interpret or otherwise process any counters directly provided by any
2886 Target (T_C1 and T_C2). The software shall handle correlation of C_REF and C_C2 with T_C1 and
2887 T_C2, based on the definitions given in the I3C Specification [MIPI02] and any additional private
2888 contract between the Controller and the Target.
2889 In PIO Mode, the C_REF and C_C2 counters appear after the initial IBI Status Descriptor structure from the
2890 IBI Queue Port.
2891 In DMA Mode, where the IBI Status Descriptor structure is put on the IBI Status Ring, the first chunk in
2892 the IBI Data Ring starts with the C_REF and C_C2 counter values.
2893 The IBI Status Descriptor structure indicates the presence of Controller timestamping counters in the IBI
2894 Data Queue or IBI Data Ring by setting the TS field to 1'b1. In cases where this IBI payload is spread
2895 across multiple chunks (for DMA Mode) and more than one IBI Status Descriptor structure is inserted into
2896 the IBI Status Ring, all such IBI Status Descriptor structures shall have the TS field set to 1'b1, but the
2897 Controller counters shall be coalesced just once at the beginning of the first portion of the IBI Data buffer
2898 (i.e., in the first chunk only for DMA Mode).

6.9.4 IBI Data Abort Operation
2900 If field IBI_DATA_ABORT_EN in register HC_CAPABILITIES (Section 7.4.4) has a value of 1'b1, then the Host
2901 Controller also supports the IBI Data Abort operation, which allows the Driver to abort reception of an
2902 ongoing IBI data payload.
2903 The Driver may enable or disable the IBI Data Abort monitoring logic by setting or clearing bit
2904 IBI_DATA_ABORT_MON in register IBI_DATA_ABORT_CTRL (Section 7.4.18). When monitoring is enabled,
2905 the Host Controller shall watch for subsequent writes to this register with Bit[8] set to 1'b1. If an IBI is
2906 received (i.e., if it is accepted) by the Bus Controller Logic, then the Host Controller shall allow the Driver
2907 to abort the IBI data payload once the Host Controller has received the first IBI Status Descriptor. The
2908 Driver must provide matching field values when writing to this register, as follows:
2909 • Field MATCH_IBI_ID must match the value provided in field IBI_ID from the IBI Status Descriptor (i.e., the
2910 Target’s Dynamic Address with RnW = 1'b1); and
2911 • Field MATCH_STATUS_TYPE must match the value provided in field STATUS_TYPE from the IBI Status
2912 Descriptor, with restrictions:
2913 • Only values 3'b000 (REGULAR_IBI) and 3'b100 (AUTOCMD_READ) are supported.
2914 If the Host Controller sees a write to this register with the matching fields above, and if the same IBI data
2915 payload or Auto-Command Read is still in progress, then the I3C Bus Controller shall terminate the read at
2916 the next opportunity (i.e., at a byte boundary) and shall then send at least one final IBI Status Descriptor
2917 (with any other unsent data bytes). The last IBI Status Descriptor shall have field LAST_STATUS set to 1'b1.
2918 Note:
2919 Since HCI register writes are not synchronous, if the IBI Data payload or Auto-Command read
2920 transfer had previously ended before the Host Controller could process the requested IBI Data
2921 Abort operation, then the Host Controller shall take no additional action. Writes to the indicated
2922 fields of register IBI_DATA_ABORT_CTRL shall not be ‘sticky’, and shall not affect any subsequent
2923 incoming IBIs.
2924 If the Driver writes non-matching values to the indicated fields of register IBI_DATA_ABORT_CTRL,
2925 then the Host Controller shall take no action.
2926 The I3C Bus Controller Logic shall end the IBI data payload at the soonest opportunity (i.e., shall
2927 abort the transfer on a byte boundary), and shall report any additional bytes using IBI Status
2928 Descriptor(s) and additional DWORDs. If the IBI data payload is aborted, then at least one
2929 additional IBI Status Descriptor shall be generated, the last of which shall have field LAST_STATUS
2930 set to 1'b1.
2931 Note:
2932 The Driver should monitor the incoming IBI Status Descriptor and data DWORDs as it determines
2933 whether to request the IBI Data Abort operation. This decision might depend on either the length of
2934 the IBI data payload, or whether the Driver matches a specific data pattern in the IBI data payload.
2935 Once the Driver writes to register IBI_DATA_ABORT_CTRL and requests the IBI Data Abort
2936 operation, the Host Controller shall end the transfer in the proper manner for the current I3C Mode
2937 (for example, to end an IBI data payload in SDR Mode, the I3C Bus Controller Logic would use the
2938 T-Bit). Similar data transfer ending procedures shall be used for HDR Modes, for Auto-Command
2939 read transfers in any HDR Modes.
2940 The IBI Data Abort operation is most useful for longer IBI data payloads or Auto-Command read
2941 transfers. Additionally, the Driver must configure the Host Controller to send quicker notification of
2942 the first IBI Status Descriptor, and then the Host Controller should send the successive data
2943 DWORDs at more frequent opportunities, which might not be the most efficient strategy if
2944 monitoring were not enabled. For example, in PIO Mode effective use of the IBI Data Abort
2945 operation depends on the IBI Queue threshold settings (i.e., register QUEUE_THLD_CTRL, see
2946 Section 7.5.5).
