8.3.1 Data Buffer Descriptor
7055 The Data Buffer Descriptor is a structure that is directly used in a Transfer Descriptor. This structure
7056 contains a pointer in fields BUFFER_PTR_HI / BUFFER_PTR_LO. Field BLP indicates whether this pointer is:
7057 • A direct pointer to a single Data Buffer for the entire transfer (i.e., a single region of physically
7058 contiguous memory); or
7059 • A pointer to an array of Data Buffer Pointers that are set up as a Scatter-Gather List (i.e., an array of
7060 Memory Descriptor structures), each having their own with a pointer to a block of physical memory to be
7061 used as a portion of the Data Buffer for the transfer.
7062 Note:
7063 Scatter-Gather Lists always use the Memory Descriptor structure (see Section 8.7). The Data
7064 Buffer Descriptor is always contained within the Transfer Descriptor.

8.4 Command Descriptor
7066 The write-only Command Descriptor structure defines a transaction, including its parameters, and is sent by
7067 the Driver to schedule a command to a Device(s) on the I3C Bus while the Host Controller is operating in
7068 Active Controller mode.
7069 The method for writing a Command Descriptor depends on the operating mode (see Section 6.8):
7070 • PIO Mode: A Command Descriptor is added to the Command Queue via writes to the Command Queue
7071 Port (per Section 6.8.1)
7072 • DMA Mode: A Command Descriptor is included in the Transfer Descriptor, and the Transfer Descriptor is
7073 placed on the Command Ring (per Section 6.8.2)
7074 The Command Descriptor is 64 bits (2 DWORDs) in length, and supports a number of common transfer
7075 types (see Section 6.7).
7076 All Command Descriptors can be grouped into the supported Command Types shown in Table 133. This
7077 specification defines a Command Descriptor structure for each listed Command Type, at the indicated
7078 Section. Table 133 also shows the value of the CMD_ATTR field, for each listed Command Type.
7079 • The Address Assignment Command type is used for assigning Dynamic Addresses to I3C Targets.
7080 • The Internal Control Command type is used for controlling the Host Controller itself, not for I3C
7081 Transfer Commands. However, specific sub-commands may affect the way that the I3C Bus Controller
7082 processes certain Transfer Commands.

8.4.1 Address Assignment Command
7097 This section defines the Command Descriptor structure for I3C Address Assignment commands. This
7098 Command Type supports the modal flow for I3C Dynamic Address Assignment, using the ENTDAA CCC
7099 (see Section 5.1.4.2 and Section 5.1.9.3.4 of the I3C Specification [MIPI02]); and also supports the
7100 command to set an I3C Target’s Dynamic Address from its assigned Static Address, using the SETDASA
7101 CCC (see Section 5.1.4.2 and Section 5.1.9.3.10 of the I3C Specification [MIPI02]).
7102 The Address Assignment Command relies on the Driver to provide a Dynamic Address in one or more DAT
7103 entries as part of Device Context (see Section 6.3.3 and Section 8.1). It is the only method for assigning a
7104 Dynamic Address using the SETDASA and ENTDAA CCCs (per Section 6.4).
7105 Note:
7106 The Address Assignment Command does not support the SETAASA Broadcast CCC.

8.4.1.1 Usage for DAA with ENTDAA CCC
7108 The Address Assignment Command supports Dynamic Address Assignment with the ENTDAA CCC and its
7109 procedure, for I3C Target Devices that support Dynamic Address Assignment using the ENTDAA procedure
7110 (per the I3C Specification [MIPI02] at Section 5.1.4.2).
7111 This variant of the Address Assignment Command requires a standard DAT and DCT having at least one
7112 entry in each table (although more entries are strongly recommended). If the Host Controller supports the
7113 DAT and DCT as part of Device Context that must be allocated in Host System memory, then the
7114 appropriate base address registers must first be programmed by the Driver (see Section 7.4.19 and
7115 Section 7.4.20) as part of initializing the Host Controller for operation (per Section 6.1).
7116 Before initiating Dynamic Address Assignment with the ENTDAA CCC and its procedure, the Driver shall
7117 allocate DAT entries for the number of Target Devices that are expected to be found. These might be a set
7118 of contiguous entries in the DAT; if so, then the Driver can prepare these in a sequence and use a single
7119 Address Assignment Command to assign them all in a single pass. Alternatively, this might be a single
7120 entry in the DAT, used either for a single expected command, or for multiple invocations of the same
7121 command (subject to some restrictions).
7122 For each DAT entry, the Driver shall set the DEVICE field to indicate the Device’s type (i.e., I3C), and then
7123 set the DYNAMIC_ADDRESS field to the desired Dynamic Address. The Driver shall not set an assigned
7124 Static Address in the STATIC_ADDRESS field, as no Static Address is assigned to such Target Devices. If
7125 DMA Mode is used, then the Driver may also choose a specific Ring Bundle ID to use for any incoming
7126 IBI Requests by writing a Ring Bundle ID that has been configured with a Ring IBI Status/Data Pair (per
7127 Section 6.6.3) into field RING_ID.
7128 The Driver should also initialize the DCT index for each invocation of an Address Assignment Command
7129 with ENTDAA, by writing a value of 0x0 to field TABLE_INDEX in register DCT_SECTION_OFFSET
7130 (Section 7.4.12).
7131 • For most cases the default index value of 0x0 should be written, as this allows the Host Controller to start
7132 at the first DCT entry for each invocation of an Address Assignment Command with ENTDAA. A value
7133 of 0x0 is strongly recommended, and the Driver should generally not override this recommendation.
7134 • Use of other index values might be possible for certain use cases. However, the Host Controller shall
7135 increment the value of field TABLE_INDEX upon each successful assignment of a Dynamic Address to a
7136 Target Device during the ENTDAA procedure. In some cases, the index value might wrap around back to
7137 the initial value (i.e., index 0x0) after it increments past the last DCT entry (i.e., if the number of found
7138 Devices is greater than TABLE_SIZE minus TABLE_INDEX).
Copyright © 2018–2023 MIPI Alliance, Inc. 375
Public Release Edition

Specification for I3C HCI Version 1.2
15-Feb-2023
7139 To use the ENTDAA CCC and its procedure, the Driver shall prepare a Command Descriptor of the
7140 appropriate format, with the following specified field values:
7141 • For Bits[31:0]:
7142 • Field CMD_ATTR shall contain the value 0x2 (ADDR_ASSGN_CMD).
7143 • Field TID may have any value chosen by software.
7144 • Field CMD shall contain 0x07, the assigned Common Command Code value for ENTDAA (per the I3C
7145 Specification [MIPI02] at Section 5.1.9.3).
7146 • Field DEV_INDEX shall indicate the DAT table index, for the first (or only) DAT entry that contains a
7147 Dynamic Address configured earlier:
7148 • If only a single DAT entry is expected to be used, then the Driver shall provide the index to the DAT
7149 entry, and shall then write a value of 0x1 into field DEV_COUNT.
7150 • If several contiguous DAT entries are expected to be used, then the Driver shall provide the index to
7151 the first DAT entry, and shall then write a value into field DEV_COUNT for the number of contiguous
7152 DAT entries (i.e., the number of Target Devices to configure with ENTDAA).
7153 • Field WROC shall contain the value 1'b1 (i.e., Response Status is required).
7154 • Field TOC shall contain the value 1'b1 (i.e., issue the STOP [P] condition at the end of the transfer).
7155 • For Bits[63:32]:
7156 • These bits are reserved, and shall contain all-zero values.
7157 Once the Host Controller receives this Command Descriptor, it shall validate that it matches the specified
7158 format. If a Command Descriptor is received that does not match the specified format, then it shall be
7159 rejected and field ERR_STATUS of the Response Descriptor shall contain the value 0xA (NOT_SUPPORTED),
7160 per Section 8.5. If the Command Descriptor does match the specified format, then the Host Controller’s
7161 Controller Logic shall shall start the Dynamic Address Assignment modal flow using the ENTDAA CCC
7162 with Broadcast CCC Framing in SDR Mode. The Controller logic shall assign the Dynamic Addresses to
7163 any I3C Target Devices that respond to the Dynamic Address Assignment procedure, in the same order as
7164 the provided DAT entries. The Controller Logic shall start at the DAT entry indicated by DEV_INDEX and
7165 proceed incrementally, until it encounters a failure (i.e., a NACK) or until the ENTDAA procedure has
7166 completed.
7167 The ENTDAA procedure shall end either when no additional I3C Target Devices that have not been
7168 assigned a Dynamic Address respond to the modal flow, or when the Controller Logic has assigned all
7169 Dynamic Addresses from the range of contiguous DAT entries, as indicated by field DEV_COUNT in the
7170 Command Descriptor.
7171 Note:
7172 Dynamic Address Assignment with the ENTDAA CCC is not guaranteed to be predictable, since
7173 the Arbitration phase of the ENTDAA procedure affects the order in which I3C Target Devices
7174 might win the arbitration. A changing I3C Bus configuration could mean that the same inputs to DAT
7175 entries might not cause the Host Controller’s I3C Bus Controller Logic to assign the same Dynamic
7176 Addresses to the same Target Devices, if new Target Devices are added to an I3C Bus that might
7177 affect the Arbitration during the ENTDAA procedure.
376 Copyright © 2018–2023 MIPI Alliance, Inc.
Public Release Edition

Version 1.2 Specification for I3C HCI
15-Feb-2023
7178 If the Address Assignment Command was accepted and processed without any error, then field
7179 ERR_STATUS of the Response Descriptor shall contain a value of 0x0 (SUCCESS) for either of the following
7180 two cases:
7181 1. During the ENTDAA procedure, the I3C Bus Controller Logic was able to assign the Dynamic
7182 Addresses from some or all of the indicated DAT entries, for a number of found Target Devices less
7183 than or equal to the value of field DEV_COUNT, with no additional eligible Target Devices remaining
7184 without a Dynamic Address.
7185 • In this case, field DATA_LENGTH of the Response Descriptor shall contain a value of 0x0 to indicate
7186 no remaining Target Devices (i.e., that the ENTDAA procedure was not terminated early).
7187 2. During the ENTDAA procedure, the I3C Bus Controller Logic was able to assign the Dynamic
7188 Addresses from all of the indicated DAT entries, for a number of found Target Devices equal to the
7189 value of field DEV_COUNT, and was forced to terminate the ENTDAA procedure since there were
7190 additional eligible Target Devices remaining without a Dynamic Address.
7191 • In this case, field DATA_LENGTH of the Response Descriptor shall contain the value 0x1, to indicate at
7192 least one remaining Target Device. Note that the true count of remaining Target Devices cannot be
7193 detected by the I3C Bus Controller Logic, since the process of Arbitration during the ENTDAA
7194 procedure indicates only that some additional Target Devices are present, not how many there are.
7195 • In this case, the Driver should prepare additional DAT entries (i.e., with unused Dynamic Addresses)
7196 and then send a new Address Assignment Command to start a new ENTDAA procedure, in order to
7197 assign Dynamic Addresses to any remaining Target Devices.
7198 Note:
7199 The case where the I3C Bus Controller Logic might terminate the ENTDAA procedure early might
7200 happen frequently, for situations where the Host Controller has a smaller DAT and must make
7201 decisions about which Target Devices might need to be assigned a dedicated DAT entry. This case
7202 might also happen frequently for situations where the Driver might not know the total count of
7203 Target Devices on the I3C Bus, and might also need to examine each found Target Device and
7204 assign it a Dynamic Address based on its PID, BCR, and DCR values, that would account for its
7205 relative priority on the I3C Bus. However, the Driver would first need to assign a temporary
7206 Dynamic Address using the DAT entry, in order to use the Host Controller and the ENTDAA
7207 procedure to learn about the Target Device. For this situation, the Driver would use repeated
7208 invocations of the Address Assignment Command for the ENTDAA procedure, with field
7209 DEV_COUNT set to a value of 0x1; followed by other Transfer Commands with the SETNEWDA
7210 CCC, to re-assign the temporary Dynamic Address to a longer-term Dynamic Address.
7211 In both cases, the Driver should read the current value from field TABLE_INDEX in register
7212 DCT_SECTION_OFFSET (Section 7.4.12), and compare with the original value written to the same field, in
7213 order to determine the number of successful assignments. The Driver should also read the Dynamic
7214 Address, PID, BCR, and DCR values from the appropriate DCT entries (or from the single DCT entry) that
7215 were written by the Host Controller for each successful assignment, in order to save the values in memory.
7216 Note:
7217 If the original and current values from field TABLE_INDEX are identical, then the ENTDAA procedure
7218 did not assign any Dynamic Addresses. The Driver should detect this result and handle it
7219 appropriately.
7220 If a Target Device did not ACK the Dynamic Address that the I3C Bus Controller Logic assigned to it, then
7221 the Host Controller shall stop the ENTDAA procedure and indicate this as an error. In such a situation, field
7222 ERR_STATUS of the Response Descriptor shall contain a value of 0x5 (NACK). Note that a partial success
7223 might still generate a NACK error, with some DCT entries being written with Dynamic Address, PID,
7224 BCR, and DCR values for those assignments that succeeded before the I3C Bus Controller Logic received a
7225 NACK.

8.4.1.2 Usage for DAA with SETDASA CCC
7226 The Address Assignment Command supports Dynamic Address Assignment with the SETDASA CCC, for
7227 I3C Target Devices that have an assigned Static Address and also support the SETDASA CCC.
7228 This variant of the Address Assignment Command requires a standard DAT having at least one entry in the
7229 table, although more DAT entries are usually recommended for most use cases. If the Host Controller
7230 supports the DAT as part of Device Context that must be allocated in Host System memory, then the
7231 appropriate base address registers must first be set by the Driver (see Section 7.4.19 and Section 7.4.20) as
7232 part of initializing the Host Controller for operation (per Section 6.1).
7233 Before initiating Dynamic Address Assignment with the SETDASA CCC, the Driver shall allocate DAT
7234 entries for such Target Devices that are known to have assigned Static Addresses. These might be a set of
7235 contiguous entries in the DAT; if so, the Driver can prepare these in a sequence, and use a single Address
7236 Assignment Command to assign them all in a single pass.
7237 For each DAT entry, the Driver shall set the DEVICE field to indicate the Device’s type (i.e., I3C), and then
7238 set the DYNAMIC_ADDRESS field to the desired Dynamic Address. The Driver shall then set the assigned
7239 Static Address in the STATIC_ADDRESS field. If DMA Mode is used, then the Driver may also choose a
7240 specific Ring Bundle ID to use for any incoming IBI Requests, by writing a Ring Bundle ID that has been
7241 configured with a Ring IBI Status/Data Pair (as specified in Section 6.6.3) into field RING_ID.
7242 To use the SETDASA CCC, the Driver shall prepare a Command Descriptor of the appropriate format, with
7243 the following specified field values:
7244 • For Bits[31:0]:
7245 • Field CMD_ATTR shall contain the value 0x2 (ADDR_ASSGN_CMD).
7246 • Field TID may have any value chosen by software.
7247 • Field CMD shall contain the value the assigned Common Command Code value for SETDASA (i.e.,
7248 0x87; see the I3C Specification [MIPI02] at Section 5.1.9.3).
7249 • Field DEV_INDEX shall indicate the DAT table index, for the first (or only) DAT entry that contains the
7250 Dynamic Address and Static Address configured earlier:
7251 • If this is for a single Target Device with a single DAT entry, then the Driver shall provide the index
7252 to the DAT entry, and shall then write a value of 0x1 into field DEV_COUNT.
7253 • If this is for several Target Devices with a range of contiguous DAT entries, then the Driver shall
7254 provide the index to the first DAT entry, and then write a value into field DEV_COUNT for the number
7255 of contiguous DAT entries (i.e., the number of Target Devices to configure with SETDASA).
7256 • Field WROC shall contain the value 1'b1 (i.e., Response Status is required).
7257 • Field TOC shall contain the value 1'b1 (i.e., issue the STOP [P] condition at the end of the transfer).
7258 • For Bits[63:32]:
7259 • These bits are reserved, and shall contain all-zero values.
7260 Once the Host Controller receives this Command Descriptor, it shall validate that it matches the specified
7261 format. If a Command Descriptor is received that does not match the specified format, then it shall be
7262 rejected and field ERR_STATUS of the Response Descriptor shall contain the value 0xA (NOT_SUPPORTED),
7263 per Section 8.5. If the Command Descriptor does match the specified format, then the Host Controller’s
7264 I3C Bus Controller Logic shall start the SETDASA CCC with Direct CCC Framing in SDR Mode, using
7265 the values of Static Addresses and Dynamic Addresses from the provided DAT entries. The I3C Bus
7266 Controller Logic shall start at the DAT entry indicated by DEV_INDEX and proceed incrementally, until it
7267 encounters a failure (i.e., a NACK) or until all DAT entries have been processed and all Dynamic Addresses
7268 successfully assigned.

7269 If the Address Assignment Command was accepted and processed without any error, then field
7270 ERR_STATUS of the Response Descriptor shall contain a value of 0x0 (SUCCESS). However, if any Target
7271 Devices did not ACK the SETDASA CCC, then field ERR_STATUS of the Response Descriptor shall contain
7272 a value of 0x5 (NACK). The Host Controller shall also indicate how many Target Devices were remaining
7273 from the Address Assignment Command that were not assigned a Dynamic Address.
7274 • If field DATA_LENGTH has a value of 0x0, then all Target Devices indicated by field DEV_COUNT were
7275 assigned the Dynamic Address in the DAT entry (or entries).
7276 • If field DATA_LENGTH has a non-zero value, then one or more Target Devices did not receive their
7277 Dynamic Address. Field DATA_LENGTH therefore gives an indirect indication of a Target Device that did
7278 not respond to the SETDASA CCC and did not ACK a Static Address:
7279 • The indicated DAT entry at index DEV_INDEX + DEV_COUNT – DATA_LENGTH shall be the DAT entry
7280 for the Target Device that returned a NACK for the SETDASA CCC.
7281 • If field DATA_LENGTH is greater than 1, then the subsequent DAT entries after this entry were not
7282 processed by the Host Controller, since the I3C Bus Controller Logic ended the Direct CCC framing
7283 after receiving the NACK. Target Devices indicated by these subsequent DAT entries have not received
7284 a Dynamic Address, and must still be addressed by their assigned Static Addresses.

8.4.2.1  Sub-Command 0x1: Ring Bundle Lock/Unlock
7303  If field MIPI_CMD in the Internal Control Command’s Command Descriptor contains 0x1, then the sub-
7304  command  is  Ring  Bundle  Lock/Unlock.  This  sub-command  is  used  by  software  to  lock  the  Ring
7305  Controller’s  arbitration  logic  to  only  process  Transfer  Descriptors  for  a  specific  Ring  Bundle’s
7306  Command/Response Ring Pair, and not process any enqueued Transfer Descriptors for any other valid Ring
7307  Bundle.
7308  This sub-command is valid for DMA Mode only, and shall only be used if the Host Controller has multiple
7309  Ring Bundles. While locked, the Ring Controller shall switch to other valid Ring Bundles until software
7310  subsequently unlocks the arbitration logic. See Section 6.6.5.2.
7311  This sub-command uses Bit[12] of field MIPI_RESERVED for sub-field ON_OFF.

8.4.2.2 Sub-Command 0x2: Broadcast Address Enable/Disable
7313 If field MIPI_CMD in the Internal Control Command’s Command Descriptor contains 0x2, then the sub-
7314 command is Broadcast Address Enable/Disable. This sub-command is used by software to inform the Host
7315 Controller to either enable or disable automatic transmission of the I3C Broadcast Address and its header
7316 (i.e., START, 7'h7E, W followed by Repeated START) for every Transfer Command that indicates a Private
7317 Write or Private Read in SDR Mode, and would otherwise drive a START condition (i.e., starting from Bus
7318 Free condition or longer).
7319 This sub-command uses Bit[12] of field MIPI_RESERVED for sub-field ON_OFF.
7320 This sub-command acts similarly to field IBA_INCLUDE in register HC_CONTROL (see Section 7.4.2), but
7321 acts only on a particular operating context.
7322 The particular operating context depends on the operating mode:
7323 • For PIO Mode: The operating context is the PIO Command Queue. Software may send this sub-
7324 command as an Internal Control Command, by enqueueing the Command Descriptor into the Command
7325 Queue Port (per Section 6.8.1). The Host Controller shall keep the persistent setting (i.e., Broadcast
7326 Address transmission enabled or disabled) for subsequent Transfer Commands.
7327 • For DMA Mode: The operating context is the Command Ring for the Ring Bundle that receives the sub-
7328 command. Software may send this sub-command as an Internal Control Command, by enqueueing a
7329 Transfer Descriptor containing this Command Descriptor into the Command Ring (per Section 6.8.2).
7330 The Host Controller shall keep the persistent setting (i.e., Broadcast Address transmission enabled or
7331 disabled) for subsequent Transfer Commands on the same Ring Bundle.
7332 If the Host Controller supports multiple Ring Bundles (per Section 6.6.5) then it shall keep persistent
7333 settings for each Command Ring in a Ring Bundle, and apply them on switching back to that Ring
7334 Bundle to process subsequent Transfer Descriptors (per Section 6.6.5.1).
7335 Note:
7336 In many cases, using this sub-command might be preferable to setting or clearing field
7337 IBA_INCLUDE, as the update of the Broadcast Address transmission setting using this sub-
7338 command shall be “in-line” with the Transfer Commands that follow the update.

8.4.2.4 Sub-Command 0x4: Target Reset Pattern
7360 If field MIPI_CMD in the Internal Control Command Command Descriptor contains 0x4, then the sub-
7361 command is Target Reset Pattern. This sub-command is used by software to either drive a Target Reset
7362 Pattern, or to inform Host Controller of the start of a sequence of commands for several types of flows
7363 involving the RSTACT CCC and the Target Reset Pattern (see the I3C Specification [MIPI02] at
7364 Section 5.1.11.2 and Section 5.1.9.3.26).
7365 This command and any subsequent Transfer Commands for the RSTACT CCC (for certain flows that use
7366 the Target Reset Pattern after the RSTACT CCC) shall follow the steps defined in Section 6.15.1. For such
7367 flows that also involve the RSTACT CCC, this command shall instruct the Host Controller to enter a
7368 Critical Section, where the Host Controller shall handle this command and subsequent Transfer Commands
7369 according to special rules until the end of the sequence of commands, or unless the command sequence is
7370 ended prematurely (i.e., due to an error by software or a delay from the Host).

8.4.2.6 Sub-Command 0x6: Enable End Transfer Termination and HDR Mode
Configuration
7387 Note:
7388 This sub-command is new for this version of the I3C HCI Specification, and is required if the Host
7389 Controller supports either the End Transfer Termination capabilities for selected HDR Modes or
7390 support for Monitoring Devices on the I3C Bus. However, if the Host Controller does not support
7391 any of these capabilities, then this sub-command shall not be implemented.
7392 If field MIPI_CMD in the Internal Control Command’s Command Descriptor contains 0x6, then the sub-
7393 command is used to configure the I3C Bus Controller Logic to enable special handling of End Transfer
7394 Termination for selected HDR Modes and for Monitoring Devices. This sub-command is used by software
7395 as part of command sequences that use I3C transfers where these capabilities will be used by I3C Targets
7396 on the Bus.
7397 Use of this sub-command for HDR Mode Configuration requires the Host to have previously configured
7398 the relevant I3C Targets to support the indicated configuration, by sending the ENDXFER CCC with
7399 appropriate options (see the I3C Specification [MIPI02] at Section 5.1.9.3.25). The options provided to this
7400 sub-command must match the configuration of the Target(s) that will be addressed in subsequent I3C
7401 transfers that follow this sub-command.
7402 For specific information about the configuration of HDR Mode transfers, refer to the I3C Specification
7403 [MIPI02]:
7404 • For HDR-DDR Mode, see Section 5.2.2.3.4
7405 • For HDR-Ternary Modes, see Section 5.2.3.3.2
7406 Use of this sub-command for Monitoring Device Early Termination shall apply to various I3C Modes,
7407 including SDR Mode, HDR-DDR Mode, and HDR-Ternary Modes (see the I3C Specification [MIPI02] at
7408 Section 5.1.12.2.1). For this type of configuration, the I3C Bus Controller sends the ENDXFER CCC to
7409 enable Monitoring Devices for subsequent transfers, and configures the I3C Bus Controller Logic to
7410 appropriately handle situations where a Monitoring Device terminates the data transfer.
7411 The Host may send one or more sub-commands of this type with different configuration parameters as part
7412 of a command sequence; additionally, such sub-commands must precede any transfers in the HDR Mode
7413 that will rely on such parameters (i.e., before the I3C Bus enters that HDR Mode). After the I3C Bus
7414 Controller Logic accepts each sub-command, the provided parameters will remain in force until the next
7415 STOP condition on the I3C Bus.
7416 Note:
7417 After the next STOP condition (which typically happens at the end of the command sequence), the
7418 special handling is disabled: the I3C Bus Controller Logic shall return to its default configuration
7419 parameters. However, implementers may choose to define one or more optional Extended
7420 Capability structures with registers to set the default configuration for such HDR Modes. If so, then
7421 such configuration parameters will then become the default after the next STOP condition (i.e.,
7422 instead of disabling the special handling).
7423 This sub-command’s use of field MIPI_RESERVED is:
7424 • Bits[15:12] for sub-field END_XFER_TYPE
7425 • Bits[23:16] for sub-field END_XFER_CONFIG

8.4.2.7 Sub-Command 0x7: Controller Role Handoff Procedure with GETACCCR CCC
7428 Note:
7429 This sub-command is new for this version of the I3C HCI Specification, and is required if the Host
7430 Controller supports Standby Controller mode (i.e., with Secondary Controller Logic).
7431 If field MIPI_CMD in the Internal Control Command’s Command Descriptor contains 0x7, then this sub-
7432 command is Controller Role Handoff Procedure with the GETACCCR CCC. The Driver uses this sub-
7433 command to pass the Controller Role to a chosen Controller-capable Device (i.e., a Secondary Controller
7434 Device) on the I3C Bus. This sub-command shall only be used while in the special transitional state to
7435 prepare for Controller Role Handoff which is used to prepare for entering Standby Controller mode (per
7436 Section 6.17.2).
7437 The Host Controller shall only accept this sub-command in this transitional state, and shall reject this sub-
7438 command if it is not operating in the transitional state. Additionally, the Host Controller shall always
7439 generate a Response Descriptor, and shall return one of several error codes in field ERR_STATUS depending
7440 on the results of the sub-command and its attempt to drive the GETACCCR CCC to the chosen Secondary
7441 Controller Device, per Table 143. If the Host Controller returns 0x0 (SUCCESS) in field ERR_STATUS of the
7442 Response Descriptor, then this typically indicates a successful transition from Active Controller mode to
7443 Standby Controller mode; however, other interrupt conditions are typically sent along with the change of
7444 roles on the I3C Bus.
7445 As the Host Controller processes this sub-command, it uses the GETACCCR CCC and also subsequently
7446 drives the Controller Role Handoff Procedure, which uses the I3C Bus Controller Logic and also engages
7447 the I3C Secondary Controller Logic during the passing of the Controller Role. This procedure is defined in
7448 the I3C Specification [MIPI02] at Section 5.1.7.2, and is required for any Host Controller that supports
7449 Standby Controller mode.
7450 This sub-command’s use of field MIPI_RESERVED is:
7451 • Bits[18:12] for sub-field STBY_CR_DYN_ADDR
7452 • Bits[20:19] for sub-field HANDOFF_RETRY

8.4.2.8 Sub-Command 0xD: Attempt Dead Bus Recovery
7459 Note:
7460 This sub-command is new for this version of the I3C HCI Specification, and is recommended for
7461 Host Controllers that need to detect their role when initializing on an I3C Bus where it is not initially
7462 known if the Bus already has an Active Controller.
7463 If field MIPI_CMD in the Internal Control Command’s Command Descriptor contains 0xD, then the sub-
7464 command is Attempt Dead Bus Recovery. This sub-command is used by the Driver to engage the Dead Bus
7465 Recovery Mechanism under the following circumstances:
7466 • Before finishing Host Controller initialization steps (i.e., when field BUS_ENABLE in register
7467 HC_CONTROL is 1'b0), when the presence or current status of an Active Controller on the I3C Bus (i.e.,
7468 not this Host Controller) is not yet known;
7469 If Standby Controller mode is also supported, then the Driver also shall not write 1'b1 to
7470 field ACR_FSM_OP_SELECT in register STBY_CR_CONTROL (Section 7.7.11.1) before
7471 engaging the Dead Bus Recovery Mechanism.
7472 • While operating in Standby Controller mode (if Secondary Controller Logic is supported), if the Host
7473 Controller is not the Active Controller, and if the Host suspects that the Active Controller on the I3C Bus
7474 has stopped responding (or has crashed, been disconnected, or has encountered another condition that
7475 renders it inoperable).
7476 Additionally, the Host Controller shall always generate a Response Descriptor, and shall return one of
7477 several error codes in field ERR_STATUS, depending on the results of the sub-command and its attempt to
7478 detect the state of the I3C Bus and claim the Active Controller role, per Table 145. If the Host Controller
7479 returns 0x0 (SUCCESS) in field ERR_STATUS of the Response Descriptor, then this typically indicates a
7480 successful attempt; however, other interrupt conditions are typically sent due to the conditions on the I3C
7481 Bus.
7482 This sub-command’s use of field MIPI_RESERVED is:
7483 • Bit[15] for sub-field TRY_STANDBY
7484 • Bits[14:12] for sub-field DBR_PROC

8.4.3 Common Aspects of Transfer Commands
7490 The I3C TCRI Specification contains the full normative definition of Transfer Command types (see
7491 [MIPI06] at Section 7.1.2).
7492 However, a Host Controller shall also observe the following requirements:
7493 • For Transfer Commands with field MODE = 0x5: This indicates HDR-Ternary Mode. Selection of
7494 HDR-TSP Mode vs. HDR-TSL Mode depends on the value of field I2C_DEV_PRESENT in register
7495 HC_CONTROL. The Host Controller shall use the appropriate Broadcast CCC when entering HDR-Ternary
7496 Mode, based on this field.
7497 • If field I2C_DEV_PRESENT is 1'b0, then the Host Controller shall use the ENTHDR1 CCC and enter
7498 HDR-TSP Mode. Note that this is only supported for a Pure Bus: no Legacy I2C Devices are allowed
7499 to be on the I3C Bus when HDR-TSP Mode is used.
7500 • If field I2C_DEV_PRESENT is 1'b1, then the Host Controller shall use the ENTHDR2 CCC and enter
7501 HDR-TSL Mode. This HDR Mode may be used if Legacy I2C Devices are on the I3C Bus.
7502 • Field WROC controls whether Response Status is conditionally required after successful completion of the
7503 transfer. The successful completion shall be read from register RESPONSE_QUEUE_PORT. Upon
7504 unsuccessful transfer, the Response Status shall always be sent:
7505 • In PIO Mode: A value of 1'b0 may optionally be used for Write-Type transfers, if the Driver does not
7506 wish to receive a Response Descriptor for a successful transfer. However, if there is a transfer error,
7507 then the Host Controller shall generate a Response Descriptor regardless of the value in this field. In
7508 most cases, the Driver should use a value of 1'b1.
7509 • In DMA Mode: The Host Controller shall always generate a Response Descriptor, and the Driver shall
7510 always set this field to 1'b1.
7511 • All Transfer Commands will use a data buffer, based on the currently selected operating mode:
7512 • For PIO Mode: The data buffer is available through Transfer Data Port (RX Data Port and TX Data
7513 Port). For Immediate Data Transfer commands, these are defined as Write-type transfers so only the
7514 TX Data Port is used. The Driver must write to or read from register TX_DATA_PORT (see Section 6.5
7515 and Section 7.5.3), and prevent both overflow and underflow conditions from occurring during the
7516 transfer.
7517 • For DMA Mode: The buffer is provided in the Transfer Descriptor that contains the Command
7518 Descriptor. The Driver must allocate sufficient Host system memory to hold the transfer data (per
7519 Section 6.6).
7520 • For Transfers with No Data Bytes (i.e., zero-length): These are only intended for special uses, such
7521 as CCCs that simply send the Command Code to the Target and then use ACK/NACK alone to
7522 determine whether the CCC was successfully received. For most other typical Transfer Commands,
7523 software should provide a non-zero value in field DATA_LENGTH.
7524 • Support for Combo Transfer Commands is optional: an implementer may choose whether to implement
7525 support for Combo transfers, per the specific use case. If so, then field COMBO_COMMAND in register
7526 HC_CAPABILITES shall have a value of 1'b1 (per Section 7.4.4). If not, then field COMBO_COMMAND shall
7527 instead have a value of 1'b0.

8.5 Response Descriptor
7528 The Response Descriptor is a read-only structure describing the success or failure of a Command, and the
7529 amount of data transferred.
7530 This structure is used in two different ways:
7531 • For PIO Mode: The Response Descriptor is read from Response Queue (i.e., via reads from Response
7532 Queue Port).
7533 • For DMA Mode: The Response Descriptor is read from the Response Ring.
7534 The Response Descriptor is 32 bits (i.e., 1 DWORD) in length, and is normatively defined in Section 7.1.3
7535 of the I3C TCRI Specification [MIPI06]. Table 146 summarizes the relevant fields.

8.6 IBI Status Descriptor
7537 The IBI Status Descriptor is a read-only structure describing the outcome of I3C Bus activity or other
7538 related actions that are not the result of the Host Controller processing a normally enqueued Command
7539 Descriptor and generating a corresponding Response Descriptor. In general, the IBI Status Descriptor is
7540 used for describing IBI Requests and other types of requests that can be raised by I3C Targets, or other
7541 events/actions that might be unexpected or autonomously generated within the Host Controller.
7542 Note:
7543 In version 1.1 of this I3C HCI Specification, the IBI Status Descriptor structure was only used to
7544 report IBI Requests with data payloads. In this version of the I3C HCI Specification, the structure
7545 has been extended to report additional event types.
7546 Table 147 defines the fields in the IBI Status Descriptor data structure. Field STATUS_TYPE indicates the
7547 source of the status data in the IBI Status Descriptor, and also defines the usage of other fields in the data
7548 structure.
7549 The following sub-sections define the uses of the fields of the IBI Status Descriptor, as indicated by the
7550 value of field STATUS_TYPE:
7551 • 3’b000: (REGULAR_IBI):
7552 • Regular IBI Request notification with data payload, see Section 8.6.2
7553 • Notification of Hot-Join Request or Controller-Role Request, see Section 8.6.3
7554 • 3’b001: (CREDIT_ACK): Target IBI credit update acknowledgement or error, see Section 8.6.4
7555 • 3’b010: (SCHEDULED_CMD): Scheduled Command execution report, see Section 8.6.5
7556 • 3’b100: (AUTOCMD_READ): Auto-Command read notification with data payload, see Section 8.6.6
7557 • 3’b111: (STBY_BR_BCAST_CCC): Broadcast CCCs received in Standby Controller mode, see
7558 Section 8.6.7

7560 Note:
7561 In version 1.1 of this I3C HCI Specification, field HW_CONTEXT (i.e., Bits[28:26]) was defined as a
7562 3-bit field that allowed for the I3C Bus Controller Logic to describe hardware-specific context for IBI
7563 processing. Implementers had the option to use this field to provide more information to the SW
7564 driver. However, actual use of this field proved to be limited, and implementers did not define a
7565 standard encoding for it. In this version of the I3C HCI Specification, field HW_CONTEXT has been
7566 removed since Bits[28:27] are now allocated to an expanded STATUS_TYPE field. This allows
7567 additional reporting of events from other sources beyond just IBI Requests. Considering
7568 Bits[29:27], the existing values with Bits[28:27] set to 2'b00 have the same meaning as previous
7569 versions of the HCI Specification.

8.6.1 Common Usage
7570 The following fields in the IBI Status Descriptor shall be used commonly across multiple types of events:
7571 • Field LAST_STATUS shall indicate whether this is the last IBI Status Descriptor for the event.
7572 • In cases where a data payload requires multiple chunks, all chunks except the last shall have
7573 LAST_STATUS set to 1'b0, and the last chunk shall have LAST_STATUS set to 1'b1.
7574 • Field CHUNKS:
7575 • In DMA Mode, this field shall indicate the number of valid data Chunks in the IBI Ring that are
7576 associated with this IBI Status Descriptor.
7577 • In PIO Mode, this field shall not be used.
7578 • Field DATA_LENGTH shall describe the length of data enqueued to the IBI Queue/Ring that is associated
7579 with this IBI Status Descriptor:
7580 • In PIO Mode, this field shall contain the number of bytes for this chunk.
7581 • In DMA Mode, this field shall contain the number of bytes in the last Data Chunk only. If there are any
7582 preceding Data Chunks, then they shall have the maximum number of data bytes.
8.6.2 Usage for Regular IBIs
7583 The Host Controller shall generate IBI Status Descriptors for IBI Requests that are received from I3C
7584 Targets on the Bus. Such IBI Status Descriptors shall have field STATUS_TYPE set to 3'b000
7585 (REGULAR_IBI), and the other fields in the structure shall be used as follows:
7586 • Field IBI_STS shall indicate whether the IBI Request was ACKed or NACKed by the Host Controller:
7587 • If the Host Controller ACKed the IBI Request, then field IBI_STS shall be set to 1'b0.
7588 • If the Host Controller NACKed the IBI Request, then field IBI_STS shall be set to 1'b1.
7589 • Field ERROR:
7590 • Shall be set to 1'b0 (NORMAL) if the IBI data payload ended normally (i.e., was not terminated by the
7591 Host Controller), or
7592 • Shall be set to 1'b1 (TERMINATED) if the Host Controller terminated the IBI data payload for any of the
7593 following reasons:
7594 • The Host Controller shall terminate the IBI data payload if the IBI Queue/Rings become full and
7595 cannot accept any new IBI Status Descriptors or associated data DWORDs.
7596 • If the Target IBI credit counting mechanism is supported and enabled (per Section 6.9.5), then the
7597 Host Controller shall terminate the IBI data payload if there is insufficient credit for that Target
7598 during an IBI payload (per the value of field TERM_READ_ZERO_CREDIT).
7599 • If the Host Controller is using coalesced data reporting for the Auto-Command read transfer after the
7600 IBI data payload (per Section 6.11.3), then the Host Controller shall terminate the read transfer if it
7601 encounters any of the following errors during the Auto-Command read transfer:
7602 • CRC Error or Parity Error (for HDR Modes only)
7603 • Target NACKs its Dynamic Address
7604 • Broadcast Address (7'h7E) NACK
7605 • Field TS shall be set to 1'b1 if a Timestamp is available for the IBI (per Section 6.9.3) as part of the data
7606 payload, or 1'b0 if no Timestamp is available for the IBI.
7607 • For field IBI_ID, Bits[15:9] shall contain the Target’s Dynamic Address, and Bit[8] shall contain the RnW
7608 bit (i.e., RnW = 1 for a regular IBI).
7609 • Fields DATA_LENGTH and CHUNKS shall be used to describe the length of the read data for this IBI Status
7610 Descriptor (per Section 8.6.1).
7611 If the IBI has a data payload, then the Host Controller shall enqueue the data payload bytes in one or more
7612 DWORDs per the current operating mode, using chunks (per Section 8.6.1).

8.6.3 Usage for Hot-Join Requests and Controller-Role Requests
7613 The Host Controller shall generate IBI Status Descriptors for either Hot-Join Requests or Controller-Role
7614 Requests that are received from I3C Targets on the Bus. Such IBI Status Descriptors shall have field
7615 STATUS_TYPE set to 3'b000 (REGULAR_IBI), and the other fields in the structure shall be used as follows:
7616 • Field IBI_STS shall indicate whether the request was ACKed or NACKed by the Host Controller:
7617 • If the Host Controller ACKed the request, then field IBI_STS shall be set to 1'b0.
7618 • If the Host Controller NACKed the request, then field IBI_STS shall be set to 1'b1.
7619 • Fields ERROR, TS, LAST_STATUS, and DATA_LENGTH shall be set to 1'b0 always.
7620 • Field IBI_ID:
7621 • For Hot-Join Requests, Bits[15:9] of this field shall contain the Hot-Join ID (i.e., 7'h02 always), and
7622 Bit[8] of this field shall contain 1'b0 (i.e., RnW = 0)
7623 • For Controller-Role Requests, Bits[15:9] of this field shall contain the Secondary Controller’s
7624 Dynamic Address, and Bit[8] of this field shall contain the RnW bit (i.e., RnW = 0 for a Controller-
7625 Role Request).
7626 Note:
7627 Bit[8] (i.e., the RnW bit) differentiates these request types from a regular IBI Request. Additionally,
7628 these request types do not have a data payload.
8.6.4 Usage for Target IBI Credit Counter Updates
7629 If the Target IBI credit counting mechanism is supported and enabled (per Section 6.9.5), then the Host
7630 Controller shall generate IBI Status Descriptors to report the processing of Target IBI credit update
7631 requests. Such IBI Status descriptors shall have field STATUS_TYPE set to 3'b001 (CREDIT_ACK).
7632 If such a request is successfully processed, then the other fields in the structure shall be used as follows:
7633 • Field IBI_STS shall be set to 1'b0 (UPDATED) to report a successful update.
7634 • Field LAST_STATUS shall be set to 1'b0.
7635 • For field IBI_ID, Bits[15:9] shall be set to the Target’s Dynamic Address, and Bit[8] shall be set to 1'b0.
7636 • Field DATA_LENGTH shall be set to 4 (i.e., a single DWORD).
7637 • If DMA Mode is used, then field CHUNKS shall report the number of data chunks in this report (i.e.,
7638 1 chunk for 1 DWORD of data).
7639 • All other fields shall be set to zero.
7640 The data payload for this IBI Status Descriptor shall be a single DWORD that contains the updated credit
7641 counter for the IBI Target in Bits[15:0], and zero in Bits[31:16].
7642 • If PIO Mode is used, then this DWORD shall be enqueued into the IBI Queue after this IBI Status
7643 Descriptor (per Section 6.9.1).
7644 • If DMA Mode is used, then this DWORD shall be enqueued into the corresponding IBI Data Ring (per
7645 Section 6.9.2).
7646 If such a request is not successfully processed (i.e., dropped by the Host Controller), then the other fields in
7647 the structure shall be used as follows:
7648 • Field IBI_STS shall be set to 1'b1 (DROPPED) to report an unsuccessful update.
7649 • Field LAST_STATUS shall be set to 1'b0.
7650 • For field IBI_ID, Bits[15:9] shall be set to the Target’s Dynamic Address, and Bit[8] shall be set to 1'b0.
7651 • Field DATA_LENGTH shall be set to 0 (i.e., no data).
7652 • All other fields shall be set to zero.

8.6.5 Usage for Scheduled Command Execution Reports
7653 If the Scheduled Commands logic is supported and enabled (per Section 6.16) then the Host Controller
7654 shall generate IBI Status Descriptors to report the execution of Transfer Commands by the Scheduled
7655 Commands logic. Such IBI Status Descriptors shall have field STATUS_TYPE set to 3'b010
7656 (SCHEDULED_CMD), and the other fields in the structure shall be used as follows:
7657 • Field IBI_STS shall be set to 1'b0 always.
7658 • Field ERROR:
7659 • Shall be set to 1'b0 (NO_ERROR) if the Transfer Command was executed normally (i.e., if no errors
7660 were detected by the Host Controller), or
7661 • Shall be set to 1’b1 (ERROR) if the Host Controller detected an error during Transfer Command
7662 execution.
7663 • Field IBI_ID shall identify the context, which depends on the Handler Type of the specific Scheduled
7664 Commands instance:
7665 • If the Transfer Command was processed by Handler Type 1, then see Section 7.7.8.6.
7666 • If the Transfer Command was processed by Handler Type 2, then see Section 7.7.9.7.
7667 • If the Transfer Command was processed by Handler Type 3, then see Section 7.7.10.9.
7668 • Fields DATA_LENGTH and CHUNKS shall be used to describe the length of the read data for this IBI Status
7669 Descriptor (per Section 8.6.1).
7670 If the Transfer Command was a Read-Type transfer, then the Host Controller shall enqueue the read data
7671 payload bytes in one or more DWORDs per the current operating mode, using chunks (per Section 8.6.1).
404 Copyright © 2018–2023 MIPI Alliance, Inc.
Public Release Edition

Version 1.2 Specification for I3C HCI
15-Feb-2023
8.6.6 Usage for Auto-Command Read Data
7672 If Auto-Command is supported and enabled, and if the Host Controller supports separated reporting of
7673 Auto-Command read data (per Section 6.11.3), then the Host Controller shall generate IBI Status
7674 Descriptors to contain data from an Auto-Command read transfer from a Target Device on the I3C Bus.
7675 Such IBI Status Descriptors shall have field STATUS_TYPE set to 3'b100 (AUTOCMD_READ). For Auto-
7676 Command read, the Target would have previously initiated an IBI Request with a matching Mandatory
7677 Data Byte (MDB) to indicate a Pending Read; as a result, the first instance of an IBI Status Descriptor of
7678 type AUTOCMD_READ shall always follow one or more IBI Status Descriptors of type REGULAR_IBI (since
7679 the IBI data payload and Auto-Command data payload would be reported separately).
7680 The other fields in such an IBI Status Descriptor structure shall be used as follows:
7681 • Field IBI_STS shall indicate whether the Auto-Command read was ACKed or NACKed by the Target that
7682 raised the read transfer (i.e., the Pending Read IBI that triggered the Host Controller to perform the Auto-
7683 Command read):
7684 • If the Target ACKed the read transfer, then field IBI_STS shall be set to 1'b0.
7685 • If the Target NACKed the read transfer, then field IBI_STS shall be set to 1'b1.
7686 • Field ERROR:
7687 • Shall be set to 1'b0 (NORMAL) if the Auto-Command read data payload ended normally (i.e., was not
7688 terminated by the Host Controller), or
7689 • Shall be set to 1'b1 (TERMINATED) if the Host Controller terminated the Auto-Command read data
7690 payload, for any of the following reasons:
7691 • The Host Controller shall terminate the Auto-Command read transfer if the IBI Queue/Rings become
7692 full and cannot accept any new IBI Status Descriptors or associated data DWORDs.
7693 • If the Target IBI credit counting mechanism is supported and enabled (per Section 6.9.5) then the
7694 Host Controller shall terminate the Auto-Command read data payload if there is insufficient credit
7695 for that Target during an IBI payload (per the value of field TERM_READ_ZERO_CREDIT).
7696 • The Host Controller shall terminate the Auto-Command read transfer if it encounters any of the
7697 following errors during the Auto-Command read transfer:
7698 • CRC Error or Parity Error (for HDR Modes only)
7699 • Broadcast Address (7'h7E) NACK
7700 • Field TS shall be set to 1'b0 always.
7701 • For field IBI_ID, Bits[15:9] shall contain the Target’s Dynamic Address, and Bit[8] shall contain the RnW
7702 bit (i.e., RnW = 1 for an Auto-Command read).
7703 • Fields DATA_LENGTH and CHUNKS shall be used to describe the length of the read data for this IBI Status
7704 Descriptor (per Section 8.6.1).
7705 If the Auto-Command read has a data payload (i.e., is not a zero-length read transfer), then the Host
7706 Controller shall enqueue the data payload bytes in one or more DWORDs per the current operating mode,
7707 using chunks (per Section 8.6.1).

8.6.7 Usage for Broadcast CCCs Received in Standby Controller Mode
7708 If the Host Controller supports Standby Controller mode and is currently operating as a Secondary
7709 Controller (i.e., not the Active Controller), then the current Active Controller of the I3C Bus may send
7710 Broadcast CCCs that will be received by the Host Controller. The Host Controller shall generate IBI Status
7711 Descriptors to contain data from such Broadcast CCCs from the Active Controller of the I3C Bus (per
7712 Section 6.17.3.2). Such IBI Status Descriptors shall have field STATUS_TYPE set to 3'b111
7713 (STBY_CR_BCAST_CCC), and the other fields in the structure shall be used as follows:
7714 • Fields IBI_STS, ERROR, and TS shall be set to 1'b0 always.
7715 • For field IBI_ID, Bits[15:9] shall be set to the Broadcast Address (7’h7E), and Bit[8] shall be set to 1'b0.
7716 • Fields DATA_LENGTH and CHUNKS shall be used to describe the length of the read data for this IBI Status
7717 Descriptor (per Section 8.6.1).
7718 The Host Controller shall also capture the CCC data payload (see Section 6.17.3.2) and enqueue the data
7719 payload bytes in one or more DWORDs per the current operating mode, using chunks (per Section 8.6.1).

9 System Bus Implementations
7729 This Section describes the requirements and details of Host Controllers that implement connection to
7730 various types of System Buses.
9.1 System Bus Requirements
7731 The generic Host Controller Interface definition (listed in earlier Sections of this Specification) is applied in
7732 accordance to the features available in a particular implementation’s System Bus. Some I3C HCI features
7733 do not map well to all System Bus types, so the capabilities available in a particular System Bus may
7734 dictate which features in a Host Controller can be implemented, and which ones cannot be supported.
7735 The following System Bus features are prerequisites for any Host Controller implementation:
7736 • A method for the Host to discover the Host Controller on the System Bus, configure its System Bus
7737 interface logic for the Host to access, and enumerate its capabilities correctly
7738 • A method for the Host to access the Host Controller registers, using read/write commands with a register
7739 offset
7740 The following System Bus features are optional, but their presence or absence may determine which
7741 features or capabilities of a Host Controller are supported (or even chosen to be implemented), as well as
7742 the method for performing transfers, receiving interrupts including IBI Status notifications, or performing
7743 advanced operations to manage the Host Controller:
7744 • Direct memory access (or similar) capability that allows the Host Controller to access Host system
7745 memory.
7746 • This capability allows the Device to use a Memory Access Engine (i.e., a DMA engine) to request
7747 access to Host system memory, without direct software involvement from the Host. The Device also
7748 has a Memory Access Interface (see Figure 3) to manage internal requests to specific memory
7749 addresses for defined purposes, each configured by the Driver with regions of allocated system
7750 memory.
7751 • Such a capability requires corresponding data access logic within the Host system’s System Bus
7752 controller logic, or other entities that might serve as a “Hub”, “Router”, and/or “Switch” between the
7753 System Bus controller logic and the Host Controller (i.e., things necessary to connect the Device to a
7754 specific Port on the System Bus) to respond to such requests initiated by a Device, and fulfill them on
7755 behalf of the Host System’s memory controller(s).
7756 • A method for the Host to poll for interrupt notifications, or be proactively notified by the Host Controller
7757 when an interrupt notification condition is satisfied
7758 • A method for the Host to send requests, according to the capabilities of the System Bus interface
7759 specification, to access certain features in the Host Controller
7760 • Support for one or more Host Controller Interface instances within the same Host Controller may be
7761 exposed:
7762 • Either within a single interface, as a single mapping of HCI registers with a Multi-Bus Instance
7763 extended capability
7764 • Or as separate interfaces, i.e., multiple independent mappings of HCI registers using System-Bus-
7765 specific methods to direct requests to different interfaces

9.2 Implementation Specifics
7766 This Section lists the implementation details for common types of System Buses.
9.2.1 PCI and PCI-Compatible Buses
7767 Although PCI devices have largely been supplanted by PCI-Express devices, the higher-level software
7768 compatibility with PCI has been largely preserved. Therefore this Specification will not cover the lower-
7769 level electrical details, but will focus instead on the logical details from a software perspective. The term
7770 “PCI*” will refer to a System Bus that maintains logical compatibility with PCI.
7771 PCI* Devices generally support memory-mapped IO (MMIO) from the Host system address map, and
7772 enable interrupt Device-initiated interrupt notifications via one of several methods: Legacy (INTx), MSI, or
7773 MSI-X. This enables a basic method of interacting with a PCI* I3C Host Controller, for Host Controller
7774 implementations that implement PIO Mode by the use of basic MMIO requests comprising simple register
7775 read/write accesses as smaller packets initiated via Host transactions, to produce entries in the Command
7776 Queue and read Response Queue entries and IBI Notifications directly.
7777 In most System Bus implementations, PCI* Devices also have the ability to access Host system memory
7778 via “upstream” read and write requests using Bus Mastering (this is the feature name as used by PCI SIG).
7779 A PCI* I3C Host Controller might be implemented with DMA engines, in order initiate read/write requests
7780 to Host System memory without software involvement. The combination of these advanced capabilities
7781 also enables a higher-performance method of interacting with a PCI* I3C Host Controller, for Host
7782 Controller implementations that implement DMA Mode by the use of upstream memory accesses and also
7783 possess a Ring Controller, which can enable pipelined processing of transaction streams.
7784 Depending on the choices made by an implementer and the System Bus designer, a PCI* I3C Host
7785 Controller may therefore implement DMA Mode and/or PIO Mode.
7786 For all PCI* I3C Host Controller options:
7787 • Host Controller configuration and enumeration uses a PCI Configuration Space, including PCI
7788 Configuration Registers.
7789 • HCI register read/write access is enabled using memory-read and memory-write requests. As the System
7790 Bus supports byte-enables, most registers will most likely be accessed by Byte, Word (i.e., 16-bit), or
7791 DWORD (i.e., 32-bit) transactions.
7792 • For specific registers that act as mailbox registers to a Queue, FIFO, or Buffer (e.g., the PIO Queue
7793 registers in Section 7.5) and have special actions that either produce or consume entries on these
7794 structures, the Host Controller shall only allow DWORD transactions. The byte-enables for such
7795 transactions must select all 4 bytes comprising the 32-bit mailbox register. Any transactions not
7796 selecting all 4 bytes shall not be supported, and should be dropped or rejected as an unsupported
7797 request.
7798 • The DAT and DCT may be exposed either within the HCI register map, or stored in Host system memory
7799 (allocated by the Driver) that requires DMA capability within the Host Controller (i.e., the Memory
7800 Access Engine).
7801 • Interrupt notifications are sent via a supported PCI* interrupt method.
7802 For a PCI* I3C Host Controller that supports PIO Mode:
7803 • The PIO Mode registers are also implemented.

7804 For a PCI* I3C Host Controller that supports DMA Mode:
7805 • If PIO Mode is also supported, then PIO registers must be blocked from register read/write access, if the
7806 Device is configured to use DMA Mode.
7807 • The Ring Headers Registers are also implemented, with at least one Ring Bundle.
7808 • A Ring Controller is implemented, and uses the DMA capability within the Host Controller (i.e., the
7809 Memory Access Engine) to automatically manage transfers enqueued via Ring Bundles that are enabled
7810 and running.
7811 • The Memory Access Interface automatically initiates read and write requests to Host system memory,
7812 to appropriate memory addresses provided in Transfer Descriptors, using the Memory Access
7813 Interface.
7814 A PCI* I3C Host Controller may be the sole “function” or Interface within a PCI* Device, or it may be one
7815 of many Interfaces within a PCI* Device. If the I3C Host Controller is part of a multi-function Device, then
7816 the implementer shall appropriately define the Device’s interface logic to use separate PCI Bus, Device,
7817 and/or Function numbers for each “function” to ensure that the I3C Host Controller appears as a unique
7818 “function” so that it can be bound to its own software Driver.
7819 For PCI-Express (“PCIe”), specific other implementation details may apply, such as the configuration of
7820 the PCIe Root Port, or any other PCIe Switch devices that might be used to connect the I3C Host Controller
7821 as a Device to the PCIe Root Port.
9.2.1.1 PCI* Configuration Registers
7822 Per PCI SIG [PCISIG01], compliance to this MIPI I3C Host Controller Interface Specification is indicated
7823 in the PCI header with Base Class equal to 0xCh, Sub Class equal to 0xAh, and Programming Interface
7824 equal to 0x0h.
7825 The Device’s System Bus interface logic shall enable decode to enable read/write access the HCI registers
7826 defined in the Register Map section, via memory-mapped BAR0. The PCI configuration registers shall
7827 correctly enable such MMIO access, once the System Bus interface logic is configured to enable Bus
7828 Mastering (this is the feature name as used by PCI SIG) and MMIO access. The System Bus interface logic
7829 shall ensure that the Host Controller is correctly enumerated by the Host system’s BIOS or Firmware, in
7830 order to assign a valid system address range to BAR0 and properly configure any upstream PCI/PCIe
7831 compliant root ports, bridges or switches to steer access to the assigned system address range to this
7832 Device.
7833 The Host Controller may implement support for either 32-bit or 64-bit addressing at the discretion of the
7834 implementer. The Host Controller shall expose all HCI registers in this memory-mapped BAR, starting at
7835 the initial offset (0x0) for the first I3C Bus Controller instance. The register offsets for all HCI registers
7836 must fit within the BAR0 size specified in the PCI configuration.

9.2.2 Universal Serial Bus (USB)
7837 An I3C Host Controller may also be implemented as a USB Device, conforming to USB 2.0 [USB01],
7838 USB 3.2 [USB02], or beyond.
7839 The details of exposing an I3C Host Controller as a USB Device are defined in the USB-IF’s USB I3C
7840 Device Class Specification [USB03] (see Section 9.2.2.1).
7841 USB Devices do not have the ability to directly access Host system memory, and generally cannot initiate
7842 any such transactions from the Device. Since the Host’s USB Host Controller (e.g., EHCI, xHCI) directs
7843 the flow of all Bus operations, a USB I3C Host Controller must rely on Host-initiated requests to drive all
7844 transactions, including IBI Status notifications.
7845 USB defines the use of a default Control endpoint (EP #0) that supports both standard request types, “class-
7846 specific” request types, and “vendor-specific” request types. USB also defines Interrupt endpoints, which
7847 are used by USB Host Controllers and their drivers to automate the delivery of interrupt notifications while
7848 still working within the Host-initiated traffic model.
7849 The combination of these System Bus capabilities enables a basic method of interacting with a USB I3C
7850 Host Controller, for Host Controller implementations that either (A) implement PIO Mode through the use
7851 of USB requests that comprise simple register read/write accesses, or (B) provide another mechanism for
7852 interacting with the Host Controller that does not directly use PIO Mode.
7853 USB also supports the use of Bulk Transfer endpoints, which allow for packets with large data payloads (up
7854 to 512 bytes for USB 2.0 “High-Speed”, or 1024 bytes for USB 3.x “SuperSpeed” and its derivatives). In
7855 this case the USB device might provide a method to send large USB Bulk packets to PIO Mode queues, or
7856 it might enable a higher-level transaction-based command/response flow (i.e., another operating mode) that
7857 uses USB Bulk packets for performance, together with other USB protocol-specific packets for efficient
7858 flow control.
7859 For All USB I3C Host Controller Options:
7860 • Device configuration and enumeration may use USB descriptors, including at least one I3C-specific
7861 descriptor that exposes the I3C Interface details and Host Controller configuration.
7862 • HCI register read/write access may be enabled using USB request types via an endpoint.
7863 • The DAT and DCT may be exposed either within the HCI register map, or else stored within an internal
7864 structure (local context) that is accessed solely using USB requests. These requests might use an endpoint
7865 created specifically for DAT and DCT access.
7866 • Interrupt notifications may be queued within the Device, and delivered via an Interrupt endpoint that is
7867 regularly polled by the Host.
7868 DMA Mode (i.e., accessing Host system memory in order to initiate an I3C transfer) is not supported, since
7869 the necessary features to enable Direct Memory Access by a Device are not supported by USB. Note that
7870 DMA engines might be used internally to access USB Device local memory (i.e., cache within the USB
7871 device), however this shall not be presented to the USB Host as “DMA Mode” as defined by this I3C HCI
7872 Specification.
7873 For all the descriptors, request types, data structures, and flows listed in this Specification, an implementer
7874 may either define their own (“vendor-specific”) specification, or else conform to the “Device Class”
7875 specification (USB I3C Device Class Specification [USB03]). The Device Class Specification refers to this
7876 I3C HCI Specification, and provides additional details that are specific to a conforming USB I3C Host
7877 Controller.
7878 A USB I3C Host Controller might be the sole “function” or Interface within a USB Device, or it might be
7879 one of many Interfaces within a USB “Composite Device”. If the I3C Host Controller is part of such a
7880 multi-function Composite Device, then the implementer should use the appropriate conventions from the
7881 USB device framework and descriptor hierarchy, to ensure that each Interface can be found by its correct
7882 Driver.

9.2.2.1 USB Descriptors and Endpoints (Conforming to Device Class)
7883 A USB I3C Host Controller that conforms to the Device Class Specification indicates this via its Device
7884 Descriptor, or for a multi-function Composite Device, via its Interface Descriptor, by using the standard
7885 Class Code and SubClass Code values defined in that Device Class specification. Per the USB I3C Device
7886 Class Specification [USB03], a conforming USB I3C Host Controller shall have an Interface Descriptor
7887 with a Class Code equal to 0x3C.
7888 The USB I3C Host Controller contains an Interface Descriptor to contain all the USB endpoints associated
7889 with a given Bus Controller instance. Each Interface Descriptor might also have other “class-specific”
7890 accompanying descriptors that describe each Interface in more detail and enumerate the capabilities of an
7891 Interface’s supported operating modes or other parameters.
7892 For a USB Device that implements multiple Bus Controller instances, each instance might have its own
7893 Interface Descriptor for an I3C Interface, with separate endpoints for Interrupts and Bulk Transfer.
7894 Alternately, some implementations with multiple Bus Controller instances might use shared Interrupt
7895 endpoints for consolidated delivery of interrupt notifications to the Host. The use of multiple Interface
7896 Descriptors per USB Device replaces the use of the Multi-Bus Instance Extended Capability structure (see
7897 Section 7.7.4), which is not recommended or supported for use by the Device Class specification.
7898 The Device Class Specification defines the particular “mapping” used by the USB function logic within the
7899 Device, which allows the Host to enqueue sequences of one or more I3C Transfer Commands using packets
7900 sent via the Bulk Transfer “outbound” endpoint. The USB function logic uses the I3C Bus Controller Logic
7901 to drive the Transfer Commands on the I3C Bus, and then return the responses to the Host, using packets
7902 sent via the Bulk Transfer “inbound” endpoint. The Device Class specification defines the specific framing
7903 and data structure formats for such USB Bulk packets that contain I3C Transfer Commands and responses,
7904 as well as I3C In-Band Interrupt notifications.
7905 The Device Class Specification also defines “class-specific” request types that are supported by the
7906 Device’s default Control endpoint (EP #0) to enable or disable certain Host Controller features, access other
7907 data structures or perform commands for initialization and configuration.
7908 The USB endpoint logic within the Device shall steer all class-specific requests to the correct Interface
7909 using the “wIndex” field.

9.2.3 AMBA Interfaces
7910 An implementation of an I3C Host Controller may use any of the publicly available Arm AMBA
7911 specifications (Advanced Microcontroller Bus Architecture), to implement I3C Bus Controller functionality
7912 as a peripheral of an on-chip interconnect (i.e., a block that is integrated into the SoC).
7913 I3C Host Controller implementations should use either of the following AMBA standards:
7914 • AMBA 5 AHB standard (i.e., as defined in the AMBA 5 AHB specification)
7915 • AMBA 5 APB standard (i.e., as defined in the AMBA 5 APB specification)
7916 A Host Controller that complies with either of these AMBA standards typically includes a subordinate-type
7917 interface (i.e., a target) that can be addressed by one or more manager-type interfaces (i.e., initiators) for
7918 HCI register access, including the PIO Queue Port registers (if PIO Mode is supported). Additionally, if
7919 such a Host Controller implements DMA Mode and/or has access to Host system memory on the same
7920 AMBA interface (i.e., for Device Context) then it would also use a DMA engine (i.e., Memory Access
7921 Engine). For operation in DMA Mode, the Memory Access Interface logic would drive memory read/write
7922 transactions using the DMA engine, which might be external to the Host Controller block.

Annex A Implementation Guidance (Informative)
A.1 Relationship to the I3C Transfer Command/Response Interface
(TCRI) Specification
7923 A Host Controller as defined in this I3C HCI Specification contains an implementation of I3C Bus
7924 Controller Logic, and also supports the Transfer Command/Response Interface as defined in the I3C TCRI
7925 Specification (see [MIPI06]). The remainder of the normative definitions in this I3C HCI Specification
7926 comprise the Application (as that term is defined in the I3C TCRI Specification), along with the Driver or
7927 other upper-level software that would run on the connected Host system and enqueue Transfer Commands
7928 to be processed.
7929 The I3C TCRI Specification defines the requirements for processing Transfer Commands and Transfer
7930 Responses, whether issued individually or in continuous sequences. The mechanisms for enqueueing and
7931 dequeuing such Transfer Commands and Transfer Responses (i.e., the HCI-defined operating modes) are
7932 specific to this I3C HCI Specification, including the use of a Transfer Data Port (for PIO Mode) or Host
7933 system memory accessed via a Transfer Descriptor (for DMA Mode).
7934 To understand the full set of normative requirements for a Host Controller and its I3C Bus Controller
7935 Logic, implementers of a Host Controller should read this I3C HCI Specification in conjunction with the
7936 I3C TCRI Specification. Where possible, this I3C HCI Specification contains references to the particular
7937 relevant sections of the I3C TCRI Specification. However, a full reading of the I3C TCRI Specification is
7938 strongly recommended.
7939 In addition, the I3C Bus Controller Logic shall also comply with the electrical and protocol requirements in
7940 version 1.1.1+ of the I3C Specification (see [MIPI05]). Implementers are strongly recommended to always
7941 use the latest I3C Specification version, including any future updates or Errata that MIPI Alliance might
7942 publish.
A.2 Variable Data Rates and Queue/FIFO Fill Levels
7943 An implementer might choose to dynamically adjust the clock rates or effective data transfer rates, within
7944 the limits set by the I3C Specification, in order to slow down the rate of data transmission during a transfer
7945 and prevent underrun or overrun conditions for an internal Queue, Tx Data Buffer, or Rx Data Buffer. This
7946 might be an advisable capability for PIO Mode, which would help to mitigate issues where the Driver
7947 allowed such a Queue or Buffer to approach an underrun or overrun condition due to system latency.
7948 If such a capability is needed, then the implementer should provide control over this capability to software,
7949 exposed as registers in a vendor-defined Extended Capability structure. At minimum, such an optional
7950 capability should include an enable/disable control, as well as threshold values for “nearly full” and “nearly
7951 empty” (or similar) to set the points at which the I3C Bus Controller Logic should start ramping down from
7952 its current transfer rate to a lower rate, in order to avoid encountering the overrun/underrun condition at the
7953 programmed rate.
